                                                              no wording makes this impossible; additionalProperties:false does

(a) and (e) look similar and are not. Both are format complaints, but (a) is about prose a person reads and (e) is about a field your code consumes. Prompting is the right tool for the first and cannot solve the second. No phrasing makes an extra field impossible, and additionalProperties: false does. The test is who reads the output.

(b) is the one where prompt engineering is genuinely the answer, and the technique is unobvious. The fix is not "be more accurate" but giving the model somewhere to go when the source lacks the fact. A model with no way to express "not in the record" produces something anyway. Adding the escape hatch and restricting it to the provided source removes the pressure that caused the invention.

(c) is the most surprising, and it is why the section includes an ordering rule at all. The instinct on a bad summary is to rewrite the instruction. The measured intervention is to move the document above the query. That change has no wording in it, and it is worth up to 30% on complex multi-document inputs in Anthropic's testing. It also happens to be where a cache breakpoint wants the document anyway (§9.3), so it is free twice.

(d) is not a defect. "Can you suggest some changes" is a request for suggestions, and it got them. The current models follow instructions precisely, which means imprecise instructions are followed precisely too. This is the clearest case of the section's governing test: a colleague handed that sentence would also have sent suggestions.

The pattern across all five. Three of the five are not prompting problems: (e) is a constraint problem, (c) is a layout problem, and (d) is a specification problem. Reaching for better wording first is the reflex worth unlearning. The question to ask before rewording is which layer can make this impossible and not just unlikely.

SECTION 4

Structured Outputs

Start with a puzzle. You ask a model to read a customer's message and reply in JSON. JSON is a plain-text way of writing a record, such as {"intent": "refund"}: each field's name in double quotes, followed by its value. Your program reads the reply with json.loads, Python's JSON reader, and passes it to the handler for that intent. Here are two replies that came back:

{"intent": "refund", "urgency": "high"}

{"intent": "money back"}

json.loads reads both without a single complaint. Is your program safe? Guess before you read on. §4.1 runs both replies, and shows what each one does to the code that receives it.

That puzzle is the whole subject in small. Most of the time you do not want prose from a model. You want a record, a small piece of data with named fields: a classification, an extracted field, or a decision your code can branch on. Getting one out of a language model used to take three steps:

  1. asking politely for JSON in the prompt;
  2. parsing the reply, meaning turning its text into a Python value;
  3. handling every case where the model wrapped it in a sentence, used single quotes, or invented a field.

Structured outputs remove that entire category of failure. They do it not by asking more firmly but by constraining what the model is allowed to emit. Here is how it works:

  • You describe the shape you want in a schema: which fields, what type each one has, and which values are allowed.
  • The API turns your schema into a grammar, a set of rules saying which characters may come next at every point of the reply.
  • It compiles that grammar, meaning it converts it once into a fast form the server checks the reply against.
  • The model then writes its reply under those rules.

So a response that violates the schema is not merely unlikely. It is unreachable.

There are two features, and you can use them independently or together:

  • JSON outputs (output_config.format) constrain the response, the reply the model writes for you.
  • Strict tool use (strict: true, taught in full in §6.8) constrains tool inputs. A tool is a function your code offers the model. The model asks for it to be run, with inputs it writes itself; §1 called that request a tool call.

This section covers both and, more importantly, where the guarantee stops. It has eight subsections, in five parts:

  1. what goes wrong without it (§4.1);
  2. the feature itself, and what a schema may contain (§4.2, §4.3);
  3. the three cases where the guarantee stops (§4.4);
  4. two smaller behaviours: the order of fields, and tool inputs (§4.5, §4.6);
  5. what it costs, and when not to use it (§4.7, §4.8).

Here is the picture for the whole section. In §1 you met the model as a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. In §2 you filled in the telegram office's order form, and in §3 you wrote the brief. §3.5 ended with a promise: a brief can ask the writer nicely for a neat table, but a printed form with boxes leaves the writer no other way to fill it in. This section is that form: a printed reply card. Instead of a blank sheet, you send the writer a card with labelled boxes. And the office fits the writer's telegraph key with a stencil, a cover with holes cut in it, so that only the characters that fit the card can be sent at all.

Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

On the reply card In structured outputs Section
A blank sheet, with a polite note asking for boxes asking for JSON in the prompt §4.1
The card's labelled boxes, each marked "words" or "number" a JSON schema §4.2
The stencil on the telegraph key the compiled grammar §4.2
A box with its allowed answers printed beside it an enum §4.2
No margin to scribble anything else in additionalProperties: false §4.2
A box marked "number" that cannot say "between 0 and 1" no numeric or string constraints §4.3
The telegram running out of words halfway across the card max_tokens truncation §4.4
The writer refusing, and sending the card back unfilled a refusal §4.4
An allowed answer copied out with one letter capitalised enum capitalisation §4.4
Required boxes filled in first property ordering §4.5
A stencilled request slip for your clerk strict tool use §4.6
A sheet of instructions stapled to every card, and the stencil kept in a drawer for a day what it costs §4.7
A love letter written in a form's one big box when not to use it §4.8

Two examples call the real API (§4.2 and §4.6), so running them needs an API key, and the model may word its reply a little differently. Every other example is plain Python, and prints the same thing on every machine.

4.1 The Problem, Stated Honestly

Before the mechanism, it is worth seeing precisely what goes wrong without it, because the failure modes are not the ones people expect. In the picture, this is the blank sheet with a polite note asking for boxes.

The example below collects six replies a model can really produce when the prompt asks for JSON. It asks three questions of each one:

  • Does json.loads accept it at all?
  • Is the intent one of the three your code handles? A fixed list of allowed values like that is an enum, short for enumeration.
  • Does it hold only the fields you expect, with nothing stray?

The try/except catches the error json.loads raises on text that is not JSON, and counts that reply as failing all three:

import json

# Six real shapes a model can produce when you ask for JSON in the prompt.
RESPONSES = [
    ('{"intent": "refund", "confidence": 0.9}', "clean"),
    ('Sure! Here is the JSON:\n{"intent": "refund"}', "prose wrapper"),
    ('```json\n{"intent": "refund"}\n```', "markdown fence"),
    ("{'intent': 'refund'}", "single quotes"),
    ('{"intent": "refund", "urgency": "high"}', "extra field"),
    ('{"intent": "money back"}', "value outside the enum"),
]

VALID_INTENTS = {"refund", "order_status", "cancel_order"}
EXPECTED_FIELDS = {"intent", "confidence", "order_id"}

print(f"{'shape':<24}{'parses?':<10}{'valid enum?':<14}{'no stray fields?'}")
for raw, label in RESPONSES:
    try:
        parsed = json.loads(raw)
        parses = True
        good_enum = parsed.get("intent") in VALID_INTENTS
        no_stray = set(parsed) <= EXPECTED_FIELDS
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        parses = good_enum = no_stray = False
    print(f"{label:<24}{str(parses):<10}{str(good_enum):<14}{no_stray}")

print()
print("the last two parse perfectly and are still wrong, in different ways")

shape                   parses?   valid enum?   no stray fields?
clean                   True      True          True
prose wrapper           False     False         False
markdown fence          False     False         False
single quotes           False     False         False
extra field             True      True          False
value outside the enum  True      False         True

the last two parse perfectly and are still wrong, in different ways

Read the table row by row:

  • The first row is the reply you hoped for, and it passes all three checks.
  • The next three do not parse at all. "Sure! Here is the JSON:" is a sentence in front of the record. A markdown fence is the line of three backticks that chat formats use to frame code. And single quotes are not legal JSON, which requires double quotes.
  • The last two parse perfectly. Each one still fails a check.

The parse failures are the easy half. A wrapper or a fence around the JSON is annoying and detectable. You write a regex (a pattern that finds text, here the part between the braces), you feel dirty, and it works.

The dangerous rows are the last two, and they are the two replies from the opening puzzle:

  • {"intent": "refund", "urgency": "high"} is valid JSON with an extra field. Your code never asked for urgency, so what happens to it is now down to luck.
  • {"intent": "money back"} is valid JSON with a value outside your enum. Your code has no handler called "money back", so it silently routes a refund request to no handler at all.

Both parse. Both flow into your code. Neither raises anything, so nothing tells you. The program in the puzzle was not safe, twice over.

Every one of these becomes impossible under a constrained grammar. In the picture, a card with no margin has nowhere to write urgency, and a box with three printed answers cannot hold "money back". The figure sums up the table:

4.2 JSON Outputs

Before the real API, here is the stencil idea in a few lines of plain Python. It is a toy: a real grammar works on tokens, the pieces of words from §1, and not on single characters. But the rule is the same. At every step, only the characters that can still lead to an allowed value get through.

The function allowed_next takes the text written so far and returns every character that may come next. It looks at each enum value that starts with that text, and takes the value's next character:

ENUM = ["refund", "order_status", "cancel_order"]


def allowed_next(written):
    """The characters the stencil lets through after `written`."""
    return sorted({value[len(written)] for value in ENUM
                   if value.startswith(written) and len(value) > len(written)})


for written in ["", "r", "c", "o", "order_"]:
    print(f"after {written!r:<10} the stencil allows {allowed_next(written)}")

print()
print("can the reply start with 'm' (for 'money back')?",
      "m" in allowed_next(""))

after ''         the stencil allows ['c', 'o', 'r']
after 'r'        the stencil allows ['e']
after 'c'        the stencil allows ['a']
after 'o'        the stencil allows ['r']
after 'order_'   the stencil allows ['s']

can the reply start with 'm' (for 'money back')? False

Line by line:

  • Before anything is written, only c, o and r are allowed, because the three values start with those letters.
  • After r, the only value left is refund, so only e may follow.
  • After c and after o, there is again exactly one way to go on.
  • After order_, only s may follow, on the way to order_status.
  • The last line is the puzzle's second reply. "money back" starts with m, and m is never allowed, so the model cannot even begin to write it.

That is what "unreachable" means. The model is not asked to avoid "money back". The stencil has no hole for it.

Now the real feature. output_config.format takes a json schema and guarantees the response conforms to it. A JSON schema is a description of the shape you want, written in JSON itself. The json schema is the specification, and it has four parts:

  • the properties, meaning the fields;
  • their types, such as string (text) or number;
  • which ones are required;
  • and the enum values a string may take.

The example below sends one customer question with a schema attached. It is a real API call, so it needs the anthropic package and an API key, as in §2. The one new line is output_config={"format": SCHEMA}, and the program prints the raw reply, then each field of the parsed record:

import anthropic
import json

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "intent": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["refund", "order_status", "cancel_order"]},
            "order_id": {"type": "string"},
            "confidence": {"type": "number"},
        },
        "required": ["intent", "confidence"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    output_config={"format": SCHEMA},
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Where has my order ORD-4471 got to?"}],
)

raw = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print("raw text  :", raw)

record = json.loads(raw)
print("intent    :", record["intent"])
print("order_id  :", record["order_id"])
print("confidence:", record["confidence"])
print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)

raw text  : {"intent":"order_status","confidence":0.94,"order_id":"ORD-4471"}
intent    : order_status
order_id  : ORD-4471
confidence: 0.94
stop_reason: end_turn

Read the output line by line:

  • The first line is the raw text, exactly as the model wrote it: one JSON object, holding the three fields.
  • The next three lines are those fields, read out of the parsed record. The model picked order_status from the enum, and copied the order id out of the question.
  • The last line is the stop reason from §2.6. end_turn means the model finished on its own.

Three things to notice.

The JSON arrives in an ordinary text block. There is no new block type, and content[0].text is a JSON string. You still call json.loads, and it cannot fail.

additionalProperties: false is required for objects. This is not optional styling, because the API rejects a schema without it. It is also what makes the "extra field" row from §4.1 impossible. In the picture, it is the card with no margin.

Changing the format invalidates your prompt cache for that conversation. A prompt cache, from §1, keeps the start of a long prompt on file, so that sending it again is cheaper and faster. Structured outputs inject an additional system prompt describing the expected format. So output_config.format is part of the cached prefix, the start of the prompt that the cache matches on (§9.5). Alternating between two schemas on the same conversation means alternating between two prefixes.

The SDK also offers messages.parse. The SDK is the Python library from §2 that sends requests for you, and messages.parse is a helper in it that validates the response for you. It works with schema libraries such as Pydantic, a popular Python library that describes the shape of data as classes. The value you get back is then a typed object and not a string. Use it where it fits. The manual form above is shown because it makes the mechanism visible.

Reach for messages.parse when you already have a schema library in the project. The manual json.loads is fine when you do not.

One note on what "guaranteed" means precisely: schema conformance covers structure and types. Schema conformance is not validation, and §4.3 is the whole of that distinction. The response will be an object with your required properties at your declared types. It will not necessarily be an object whose values are in range, and that is §4.3's subject. In the picture, the stencil makes sure a number goes in the number box. It cannot make sure the number is a sensible one.

4.3 What the Schema May Contain

The grammar is compiled, and compilation constrains what can be expressed. Not every rule you can write in a JSON schema can be turned into a stencil. The supported subset is generous and the gaps are specific, so it is worth knowing them and not discovering them as 400s, the "fix your form" errors from §2.9.

Here is the whole list:

Supported
Not supported
All basic types; enum (scalars only); const; anyOf and allOf; $ref, $def and definitions (internal only); default; required; additionalProperties: false; string formats date-time, date, time, duration, email, hostname, uri, ipv4, ipv6, uuid; array minItems of 0 or 1.
Recursive schemas; complex types inside enum; external $ref; numeric constraints (minimum, maximum, multipleOf); string constraints (minLength, maxLength); array constraints beyond minItems 0 or 1; additionalProperties set to anything but false.

A few of those names, in plain words:

  • anyOf means "any one of these shapes", and allOf means "all of these shapes at once".
  • $ref points at a shape defined somewhere else. Internal means somewhere in the same schema; external means another file or web address.
  • A recursive schema is one that contains itself, such as a comment whose replies are comments.
  • minItems is the least number of items an array, a JSON list, must hold.

The omission that surprises people most is numeric and string constraints. You cannot say "confidence between 0 and 1" or "at most 200 characters" in the schema. Those still have to be validated in your code. The grammar guarantees a number, and not a number in range.

The example below makes that concrete for three fields. For each one it prints what the grammar guarantees, and what you must still check yourself:

SCHEMA_PROPS = {
    "confidence": {"type": "number"},
    "summary": {"type": "string"},
    "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
}
GUARANTEED = {"confidence": "is a number",
              "summary": "is a string",
              "tags": "is an array of strings"}
NOT_GUARANTEED = {"confidence": "is between 0 and 1",
                  "summary": "is under 200 characters",
                  "tags": "has at most 5 entries"}

print(f"{'field':<12}{'the grammar guarantees':<28}{'you must still check'}")
for field in SCHEMA_PROPS:
    print(f"{field:<12}{GUARANTEED[field]:<28}{NOT_GUARANTEED[field]}")

print()
print("the schema removes parse errors and type errors, not validation")

field       the grammar guarantees      you must still check
confidence  is a number                 is between 0 and 1
summary     is a string                 is under 200 characters
tags        is an array of strings      has at most 5 entries

the schema removes parse errors and type errors, not validation

Each row splits a field in two. The left half is about the type, and the stencil enforces it. The right half is a rule about the value, and nothing enforces it but your own code. Exercise 4.1 asks you to write that code.

A schema may also give a string a pattern, a regex the string must match. Regex pattern is supported for the common cases:

  • anchored and partial matching (an anchored pattern, written with ^ and $, must match the whole string);
  • *, + and ?, meaning zero or more, one or more, and zero or one;
  • simple {n,m}, meaning between n and m repetitions;
  • character classes and groups.

It does not support backreferences, lookahead or lookbehind, or \b. Those are the regex features that match an earlier match again, peek ahead or behind without moving on, or mark a word boundary. A complex pattern is a 400 and not a silent degradation. That is the good kind of failure: you find out on the first request, not in production.

There are also complexity limits, and they are shared across the whole request and not per schema. An optional parameter is a field your schema does not list as required. You get at most:

  • 20 strict tools;
  • 24 optional parameters in total;
  • 16 parameters using union types, where a union type means "one of several types", written with anyOf.

That last one is low because anyOf makes compilation cost grow exponentially: each one added multiplies the work, instead of adding to it. The limits add up faster than you expect. Four strict tools with six optional parameters each already reach the 24 limit, which is the kind of thing that fails on the day you add the fourth tool.

4.4 Where the Guarantee Stops

This is the part to read twice. The documentation states "guaranteed schema-compliant" with three exceptions, and each one produces output your parser will choke on. In the picture, these are the three ways a card can come back wrong even with the stencil on.

The example below shows a good reply and the first two exceptions, each with the stop reason that arrives with it. It tries json.loads on each one:

import json

CASES = [
    ("end_turn", '{"intent": "refund", "confidence": 0.9}',
     "conforms"),
    ("max_tokens", '{"intent": "refund", "confi',
     "cut off mid-token; not valid JSON at all"),
    ("refusal", "",
     "empty content; the refusal takes precedence over the schema"),
]

print(f"{'stop_reason':<14}{'parses?':<10}{'what happened'}")
for stop, raw, note in CASES:
    try:
        json.loads(raw)
        parses = True
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError):
        parses = False
    print(f"{stop:<14}{str(parses):<10}{note}")

print()
print("guaranteed conformance applies to a COMPLETED, non-refused response")

stop_reason   parses?   what happened
end_turn      True      conforms
max_tokens    False     cut off mid-token; not valid JSON at all
refusal       False     empty content; the refusal takes precedence over the schema

guaranteed conformance applies to a COMPLETED, non-refused response

Line by line:

  • The end_turn reply parses.
  • The max_tokens reply stops in the middle of the word "confidence", so it is not JSON at all.
  • The refusal reply is empty, and empty text is not JSON either.
  • The last line is the rule for this whole subsection.

max_tokens truncation produces invalid JSON. max_tokens, from §2.6, is the most tokens the reply may use, and the model stops there even in the middle of a word. The grammar constrains which tokens may be emitted, but it cannot make the response finish. Cut it off and you get a fragment. In the picture, the telegram runs out of words halfway across the card. So a structured-output call still needs stop_reason checked before parsing. That is the same rule as §2.6, and the one most likely to be skipped precisely because the output is "guaranteed".

A refusal takes precedence over the schema. A refusal is the model declining to answer, for example because the request asks for something harmful. You get stop_reason: "refusal", a 200, and content that does not match. A 200 is HTTP's "OK" code, so nothing about the reply looks like an error. Note that, unlike the pre-output refusals in §14.6 (refusals that happen before the model writes anything), you are billed for tokens generated here.

Enum capitalisation is not guaranteed. This one is genuinely surprising. The model may return a value that differs from your enum only in capitalisation, typically the first letter of a word after a space. The response completes normally with no error and no special stop reason. Given ["Conversation topic 3"] you may receive "Conversation Topic 3". In the picture, the writer copies an allowed answer out by hand, and capitalises one letter on the way.

The example below compares that returned value with the enum in two ways: exactly, and after lowering every letter with .lower(). Its second half looks at a different enum, one whose own members differ only in capitalisation:

ENUM = ["Conversation Topic 1", "Conversation Topic 2", "Conversation topic 3"]
RETURNED = "Conversation Topic 3"          # note the capital T

print("declared in the schema:", repr(ENUM[2]))
print("actually returned     :", repr(RETURNED))
print("exact match           :", RETURNED in ENUM)
print("case-insensitive match:", RETURNED.lower() in {v.lower() for v in ENUM})
print()

# A separate hazard: an enum whose own members collide when case is ignored.
# Then NO comparison strategy can recover the intended member.
COLLIDING = ["Draft", "draft", "DRAFT"]
lowered = [v.lower() for v in COLLIDING]
print("an enum that cannot be repaired:", COLLIDING)
print("distinct members            :", len(set(COLLIDING)))
print("distinct once lowercased    :", len(set(lowered)))
print("case-insensitive comparison is ambiguous:",
      len(set(lowered)) < len(set(COLLIDING)))

declared in the schema: 'Conversation topic 3'
actually returned     : 'Conversation Topic 3'
exact match           : False
case-insensitive match: True

an enum that cannot be repaired: ['Draft', 'draft', 'DRAFT']
distinct members            : 3
distinct once lowercased    : 1
case-insensitive comparison is ambiguous: True

Line by line:

  • The first two lines show the declared value and the returned one. They differ by one letter, the T.
  • An exact comparison says False, so code using in would reject a perfectly good answer.
  • After lowering both sides, they match.
  • The second half has three members, Draft, draft and DRAFT. Lowered, all three become draft, so three members become one.

These are two separate rules, and the block shows why they are separate. Compare enum values case-insensitively. That repairs the first case, where the returned value differs from a schema member only in capitalisation. And never define two enum values that differ only in capitalisation. That is the second block, where case-insensitive comparison collapses three distinct members into one and no strategy recovers the intended value. The first rule saves you, and the second is a hole the first rule cannot patch.

Here are all three exceptions handled in one place. read_record takes the stop reason and the raw text of a reply. It turns away the two kinds that cannot be parsed. For the rest, it maps the returned enum value back to the declared one, through a dictionary keyed by the lowered value:

import json

TOPICS = ["Conversation Topic 1", "Conversation Topic 2", "Conversation topic 3"]


def read_record(stop_reason, raw):
    """Return (record, None) for a usable reply, or (None, why) for any other."""
    if stop_reason == "refusal":
        return None, "refused: nothing to parse"
    if stop_reason == "max_tokens":
        return None, "cut off: retry with a larger max_tokens"
    record = json.loads(raw)
    by_lower = {value.lower(): value for value in TOPICS}
    record["topic"] = by_lower[record["topic"].lower()]
    return record, None


REPLIES = [
    ("end_turn", '{"topic": "Conversation Topic 1"}'),
    ("end_turn", '{"topic": "Conversation Topic 3"}'),
    ("max_tokens", '{"topic": "Conver'),
    ("refusal", ""),
]
for stop_reason, raw in REPLIES:
    record, why = read_record(stop_reason, raw)
    print(f"{stop_reason:<11} -> {record or why}")

end_turn    -> {'topic': 'Conversation Topic 1'}
end_turn    -> {'topic': 'Conversation topic 3'}
max_tokens  -> cut off: retry with a larger max_tokens
refusal     -> refused: nothing to parse

Line by line:

  • The first reply is fine as it is.
  • The second reply said Conversation Topic 3, and the record now holds the declared Conversation topic 3. Code that branches on it sees a value it knows.
  • The cut-off reply and the refused one never reach json.loads. Each returns a reason instead, and the caller decides what to do next.

That repair works only because no two TOPICS differ only in capitalisation. Build the same dictionary from Draft, draft and DRAFT and it holds a single entry, so two of the three members could never come back out.

The figure sums up where the guarantee stops:

4.5 Property Ordering

Here is a small behaviour with a large capacity to confuse: required properties are emitted first, then optional ones, each group in schema order. Emitted means written out by the model, and schema order is the order you listed the properties in. In the picture, the writer fills in every required box first, then goes back for the optional ones.

The example below works out the order for a schema of four properties, two of them required. It builds the list in two passes, the required properties first and then the rest:

SCHEMA_ORDER = ["notes", "name", "email", "age"]
REQUIRED = ["name", "email"]

emitted = ([p for p in SCHEMA_ORDER if p in REQUIRED]
           + [p for p in SCHEMA_ORDER if p not in REQUIRED])

print("declared in the schema :", SCHEMA_ORDER)
print("required               :", REQUIRED)
print("emitted in this order  :", emitted)
print()
print("if order matters to you, mark everything required —")
print("or stop depending on the order of keys in a JSON object")

declared in the schema : ['notes', 'name', 'email', 'age']
required               : ['name', 'email']
emitted in this order  : ['name', 'email', 'notes', 'age']

if order matters to you, mark everything required —
or stop depending on the order of keys in a JSON object

The schema lists notes first, but notes is optional, so it comes out third, after the two required fields. age is optional too, and stays last.

This matters in exactly two situations:

  • when you are diffing JSON as text, meaning comparing two replies line by line, where a different key order looks like a change;
  • when a downstream consumer, the next program to read the record, is order-sensitive.

Both are worth avoiding on their own merits, because the order of a JSON object's keys is not supposed to mean anything. If you cannot avoid them, marking every property required restores schema order.

4.6 Strict Tool Use, and Using Both Together

Recall the tool call from §1. The model writes a request such as "run lookup_order with this order id", and your program decides whether to run it. The request's inputs are JSON too, so they can go wrong in all the ways §4.1 showed.

§6.8 teaches strict: true in full, once tools have been introduced properly. It is the same constrained-decoding machinery applied to tool inputs and not to the response, and the two work together. Constrained decoding is the stencil's proper name: generating the reply under the grammar. In the picture, the request slip the writer sends to your clerk is stencilled too.

The example below uses both at once:

  • The tool's order_id has a pattern: ORD-, then exactly four digits.
  • The response has its own schema, with a status enum.

The program prints the tool input the model asked for. Then it checks that input against the pattern with re.fullmatch, which is true only when the whole string matches:

import anthropic
import json

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "lookup_order",
    "description": "Look up an order by id.",
    "strict": True,
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string",
                                    "pattern": "^ORD-[0-9]{4}$"}},
        "required": ["order_id"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}]

RESPONSE_SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "status": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["shipped", "delivered", "cancelled"]},
            "eta_days": {"type": "integer"},
        },
        "required": ["status"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    tools=TOOLS,
    output_config={"format": RESPONSE_SCHEMA},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Where is ORD-4471?"}],
)

call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
print("tool input :", call.input)
print("matches the pattern:",
      bool(__import__("re").fullmatch(r"ORD-[0-9]{4}", call.input["order_id"])))

tool input : {'order_id': 'ORD-4471'}
matches the pattern: True

The model asked for ORD-4471, and the check confirms it matches. With the stencil on, a request for order 4471 could not have been written.

The tool input is constrained on the way in, and the final response is constrained on the way out. A pattern on the tool's order_id means the model cannot even propose a malformed id. That is stronger than validating it in your executor, the code of yours that actually runs the tool. Still, §14.4's argument stands: validate anyway, because the executor is reachable by other callers. Other code can call the same function without going through the model, and no stencil protects it there.

There are two incompatibilities to remember:

  • Strict tools cannot be used with programmatic tool calling (§7.6), where the model writes a small program that calls your tools for it. So a tool that needs to be callable from inside code execution cannot also be schema-guaranteed.
  • The 20-strict-tool limit is a limit on the request. So a large tool surface, meaning the full set of tools you offer, has to choose which tools get the guarantee.

4.7 What It Costs

Constrained decoding is not free, and the costs are unusual enough to be worth naming. There are two of them:

  • every request carries some extra input tokens;
  • every new schema pays a one-off wait while its grammar is compiled.

The example below works out the first cost for three schema sizes, at 50,000 requests a day for 30 days, at $5 per million input tokens. Then it prints the compile wait, and the changes that throw a compiled grammar away:

SCHEMA_SIZES = [("a 3-field classification", 180, 40),
                ("a 12-field extraction", 640, 140),
                ("a nested report schema", 2_100, 460)]
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00
REQUESTS_PER_DAY, DAYS = 50_000, 30

print(f"{'schema':<26}{'chars':>8}{'injected tokens':>17}{'$/month':>10}")
for name, chars, injected in SCHEMA_SIZES:
    monthly = injected * REQUESTS_PER_DAY * DAYS / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK
    print(f"{name:<26}{chars:>8,}{injected:>17,}{'$%.0f' % monthly:>10}")

print()
FIRST_MS, CACHED_MS = 340, 0
print(f"grammar compilation on first use : ~{FIRST_MS} ms of extra latency")
print(f"on every subsequent use          :  {CACHED_MS} ms — cached for 24 hours")
print()
print("the cache is invalidated by:")
for cause in ("changing the schema structure",
              "changing the SET of tools in the request",
              "(but NOT by changing only a name or description)"):
    print(f"  - {cause}")

schema                       chars  injected tokens   $/month
a 3-field classification       180               40      $300
a 12-field extraction          640              140     $1050
a nested report schema       2,100              460     $3450

grammar compilation on first use : ~340 ms of extra latency
on every subsequent use          :  0 ms — cached for 24 hours

the cache is invalidated by:
  - changing the schema structure
  - changing the SET of tools in the request
  - (but NOT by changing only a name or description)

Read the money column first. Each $/month figure is the injected tokens times 50,000 requests times 30 days, priced at $5 per million. So 40 tokens make 60 million a month, which is $300, and 460 tokens make 690 million, which is $3450.

A system prompt describing the format is injected on your behalf, so your input token count rises. It is small per request and real at volume. In the picture, the office staples a sheet of instructions to every card it sends, and you pay for the sheet's words.

The grammar is compiled and cached for 24 hours from last use. The first request with a new schema pays compilation latency, the extra waiting time, and the rest do not. This is a separate cache from prompt caching, with separate invalidation rules. Note that changing only a name or description does not invalidate it, while changing the set of tools does. In the picture, the office cuts the stencil once and keeps it in a drawer for a day.

The practical consequence is this: do not generate schemas dynamically per request. A schema assembled from user input is a new grammar every time, so you pay compilation on every call and never hit the cache. Define a fixed set of schemas and choose between them.

Here is that rule as a toy. It models the rules above, not the server's real cache. structure removes every description from a schema, since descriptions do not count. send keeps every structure it has seen in a set, and reports a compile the first time it meets each one:

import json

compiled = set()


def structure(schema):
    """The schema without its descriptions: the part the grammar is built from."""
    if isinstance(schema, dict):
        return {k: structure(v) for k, v in schema.items() if k != "description"}
    if isinstance(schema, list):
        return [structure(v) for v in schema]
    return schema


def send(label, schema):
    key = json.dumps(structure(schema), sort_keys=True)
    if key in compiled:
        print(f"{label:<34} cache hit")
    else:
        compiled.add(key)
        print(f"{label:<34} compile (~340 ms)")


BASE = {"type": "object",
        "properties": {"intent": {"type": "string",
                                  "description": "What the customer wants."}},
        "required": ["intent"], "additionalProperties": False}
REWORDED = json.loads(json.dumps(BASE))
REWORDED["properties"]["intent"]["description"] = "The customer's goal."
WIDER = json.loads(json.dumps(BASE))
WIDER["properties"]["order_id"] = {"type": "string"}

send("first request", BASE)
send("same schema again", BASE)
send("only the description changed", REWORDED)
send("a field added", WIDER)
print()
for user in ["ana", "bruno", "carla"]:
    per_user = json.loads(json.dumps(BASE))
    per_user["properties"][f"note_for_{user}"] = {"type": "string"}
    send(f"schema built for {user}", per_user)
print()
print("grammars compiled:", len(compiled), "for 7 requests")

first request                      compile (~340 ms)
same schema again                  cache hit
only the description changed       cache hit
a field added                      compile (~340 ms)

schema built for ana               compile (~340 ms)
schema built for bruno             compile (~340 ms)
schema built for carla             compile (~340 ms)

grammars compiled: 5 for 7 requests

Line by line:

  • The first request compiles, and sending the same schema again is a hit.
  • Rewording a description is still a hit, because the structure did not change.
  • Adding a field is a new structure, so it compiles.
  • The last three requests each build a schema for one user. Each one is new, so each one compiles, and the cache never helps.

Three of the five compiles came from the per-user schemas, and that is exactly the cost the rule tells you to avoid.

The figure puts both costs side by side:

4.8 When Not to Use It

Structured outputs are so clearly better than prompting for JSON that the failure mode becomes using them where prose was the right choice. Here is the rule of thumb, in four rows:

Use it
Whenever the output feeds code. Classification, extraction, routing, scoring, anything with an enum. This is the large majority of production LLM traffic and it should all be constrained.
Consider a forced tool
When you also want the model to choose whether to answer. §6.7's tool_choice pattern predates this feature and remains useful when structure is one option among several.
Do not use it
When a person reads the output. Constraining generation to a grammar is a constraint on how the model can express itself; for an explanation or a draft, that is a cost with no benefit.
Do not use it
To smuggle prose into a field. A schema whose only property is {"answer": {"type": "string"}} has bought you a pair of braces and paid an injected system prompt for them.

A forced tool, in the second row, means telling the model it must call one particular tool, so that its answer arrives as that tool's input (§6.7).

That last row is a real pattern and worth naming. Wrapping a free-text answer in a one-field object gives the appearance of structure with none of its properties:

  • Nothing is validated.
  • Nothing is enumerated.
  • The parse could not have failed anyway.

If the schema has no enum, no required numeric field and no branching, ask whether you wanted structure at all. In the picture, that is a love letter written in a form's one big box. It pays for the stencil, and the stencil does nothing for it.

Back to the opening puzzle one last time. Send §4.2's schema with output_config.format, and neither reply can be written. The card has no margin for urgency, and the stencil has no hole for the m of "money back". What is left for your code is what §4.3 and §4.4 listed: ranges and lengths, truncation, refusals and capitalisation.

Exercises

Exercise 4.1 — Fix this schema. It fails with a 400. Find every reason, then write the version that works and say what you still have to validate yourself.

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "score": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 10},
            "summary": {"type": "string", "maxLength": 200},
            "category": {"type": "string",
                         "enum": ["Bug Report", "Feature request",
                                  "bug report"]},
            "related": {"$ref": "https://example.com/schemas/ticket.json"},
            "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"},
                     "maxItems": 5},
        },
        "required": ["score"],
    },
}
Solution 
FIXED = {
    "type": "json_schema",
    "schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            # 1. numeric constraints are not supported: state the range in the
            #    description, and check it in code.
            "score": {"type": "number",
                      "description": "Severity from 0 to 10 inclusive."},
            # 2. string constraints are not supported either.
            "summary": {"type": "string",
                        "description": "One sentence, at most 200 characters."},
            # 3. two enum values differing only in capitalisation are
            #    unresolvable; and casing is not guaranteed anyway.
            "category": {"type": "string",
                         "enum": ["bug_report", "feature_request"]},
            # 4. external $ref is not supported; inline it or drop it.
            "related_ticket": {"type": "string",
                               "pattern": "^TICKET-[0-9]{4}$"},
            # 5. maxItems is not supported (only minItems, and only 0 or 1).
            "tags": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"},
                     "description": "At most 5 tags."},
        },
        "required": ["score", "summary", "category"],
        # 6. required for every object, and missing from the original.
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}


def validate(record):
    """What the grammar cannot express, and therefore what you still own."""
    problems = []
    if not 0 <= record["score"] <= 10:
        problems.append(f"score {record['score']} outside 0-10")
    if len(record["summary"]) > 200:
        problems.append(f"summary is {len(record['summary'])} chars")
    if len(record.get("tags", [])) > 5:
        problems.append(f"{len(record['tags'])} tags, max 5")
    return problems


SAMPLES = [
    {"score": 7.5, "summary": "Login fails on Safari.",
     "category": "bug_report", "tags": ["auth", "safari"]},
    {"score": 12, "summary": "x" * 240, "category": "bug_report",
     "tags": ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]},
]
for record in SAMPLES:
    problems = validate(record)
    print(f"score={record['score']:<5} -> {problems or 'ok'}")

print()
print("enum after the fix:", FIXED["schema"]["properties"]["category"]["enum"])
print("required          :", FIXED["schema"]["required"])
print("additionalProperties:", FIXED["schema"]["additionalProperties"])

score=7.5   -> ok
score=12    -> ['score 12 outside 0-10', 'summary is 240 chars', '6 tags, max 5']

enum after the fix: ['bug_report', 'feature_request']
required          : ['score', 'summary', 'category']
additionalProperties: False

Six defects, and they fall into two kinds.

Four are unsupported features and produce a 400 immediately: minimum/maximum, maxLength, an external $ref, and maxItems. Each is easy to fix once you know the list, and each has the same replacement. Say it in the description so the model still knows the intent, and enforce it in code.

One is the missing additionalProperties: false, which objects must set. This is the most common single cause of a rejected schema.

And one is not a 400 at all, which makes it the interesting one. ["Bug Report", "Feature request", "bug report"] contains two values that differ only in capitalisation. §4.4's rule says enum casing is not guaranteed, so receiving "Bug report" is possible, and there is no comparison, case-sensitive or insensitive, that maps it to the right member. The fix is not clever matching. It is choosing enum values that are distinguishable. Lowercase identifiers with underscores are a good default because they have no capitalisation to get wrong.

What you still validate yourself. That is range, length and cardinality (how many items), which is everything the grammar cannot express. That is why the solution ships a validate() alongside the schema and does not treat "structured" as "checked". The schema is a type system, not a validator, and the distinction is exactly the one between int and "an integer between 0 and 10".

One judgement call. I made summary and category required. The original required only score, which permits a response that is technically conformant and useless. If a field is needed for the record to mean anything, requiring it is free and removes a branch from every consumer.

Exercise 4.2 — Should these be structured? For each, decide and justify: (a) classify a support ticket into one of six queues; (b) draft a reply to a customer; (c) extract line items from an invoice image; (d) explain why a deploy failed; (e) decide whether to escalate, with a reason.

Solution 
DECISIONS = [
    ("a  classify into 6 queues", "YES — JSON outputs",
     "The output is an enum that routes code. Constrain it, and the whole "
     "class of unroutable values disappears."),
    ("b  draft a customer reply", "no",
     "A person reads it. Constraining generation to a grammar buys nothing "
     "and costs expressiveness plus an injected system prompt."),
    ("c  extract invoice line items", "YES — JSON outputs",
     "An array of typed objects feeding an accounting system. The canonical "
     "case, and the arrays are where hand-parsing hurts most."),
    ("d  explain a deploy failure", "no",
     "Prose is the deliverable. A one-field {\"explanation\": string} schema "
     "is 4.8's anti-pattern in its purest form."),
    ("e  escalate, with a reason", "YES — mixed",
     "The decision is an enum the code branches on; the reason is prose for "
     "a human. One schema holds both, and only the enum is load-bearing."),
]

for task, verdict, why in DECISIONS:
    print(f"{task:<30} -> {verdict}")
    print(f"{'':30}    {why}")

ESCALATION = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "escalate": {"type": "boolean"},
        "tier": {"type": "string", "enum": ["none", "l2", "l3", "oncall"]},
        "reason": {"type": "string",
                   "description": "One sentence, for the receiving engineer."},
    },
    "required": ["escalate", "tier", "reason"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
print()
print("(e) the schema that gets both halves right:")
for field, spec in ESCALATION["properties"].items():
    kind = spec.get("enum") or spec["type"]
    print(f"  {field:<10} {kind}")

a  classify into 6 queues      -> YES — JSON outputs
                                  The output is an enum that routes code. Constrain it, and the whole class of unroutable values disappears.
b  draft a customer reply      -> no
                                  A person reads it. Constraining generation to a grammar buys nothing and costs expressiveness plus an injected system prompt.
c  extract invoice line items  -> YES — JSON outputs
                                  An array of typed objects feeding an accounting system. The canonical case, and the arrays are where hand-parsing hurts most.
d  explain a deploy failure    -> no
                                  Prose is the deliverable. A one-field {"explanation": string} schema is 4.8's anti-pattern in its purest form.
e  escalate, with a reason     -> YES — mixed
                                  The decision is an enum the code branches on; the reason is prose for a human. One schema holds both, and only the enum is load-bearing.

(e) the schema that gets both halves right:
  escalate   boolean
  tier       ['none', 'l2', 'l3', 'oncall']
  reason     string

(a) and (c) are unambiguous yeses, and they are most of what structured outputs exist for. In (a) the enum means an unroutable value is unreachable and not merely rare, which is a failure your code no longer needs a branch for. In (c) the win is arrays of typed objects, which is where prompt-and-parse is at its worst: a single malformed row in a twelve-row invoice used to poison the whole extraction.

(b) and (d) are noes for the same reason. A human reads the output, so the only thing a grammar can do is constrain how the model expresses itself. That is a real cost, because constrained decoding changes phrasing around the constrained region. And it is bought for a parse that was never going to happen, because nobody is parsing.

(e) is the interesting one, and it is the shape most production decisions take. There is a machine-readable decision and a human-readable justification, and it is tempting to treat that as two different problems. One schema handles both: escalate and tier are constrained and load-bearing, and reason is a free string with guidance in its description. The grammar does nothing useful for reason, and that is fine. It is along for the ride, and putting it in the same response means the reason is guaranteed to accompany the decision and does not need a second call.

The general test. Ask what would happen if the model returned something unexpected. If the answer is "my code takes a wrong branch or throws", constrain it. If the answer is "a person reads a slightly odd sentence", do not.

SECTION 5

Thinking and Effort

Start with a puzzle. You ask a model a small question about a train: it leaves at 14:05, arrives at 17:40, and stops twice on the way. The answer it shows you is one short sentence:

3 hours and 19 minutes of moving time.

The bill for that reply says 312 output tokens. A token is the unit the API counts and bills, roughly a piece of a word (§1.2). A sentence that short is only a dozen or so tokens. So where did the other three hundred go, and do you pay for them? Guess before you read on. §5.1 runs the request and shows where they went, and §5.3 says exactly what you were billed for.

That puzzle is the whole subject in small. A model that answers in one pass has to be right immediately:

  • it has no scratch work;
  • it cannot check an intermediate result;
  • it has no way to change course halfway.

For a hard problem, that matters. Think of a proof, a subtle bug, or a long agentic task, one where the model does things in a loop, calling tools and reading their results (§3.9). For problems like these, the first approach is often not the best one. A model with no room to discover that produces a confident wrong answer.

Thinking removes that constraint. With thinking active, the model first works through the problem in its own words. It restates the problem, tries approaches, checks intermediate results, and abandons paths that do not hold up. That reasoning arrives in thinking content blocks ahead of the response. A content block is one typed piece of a reply's content list, as §2.5 showed.

It is not free, and the cost is not where people expect:

  • Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, at output prices.
  • They count against max_tokens alongside the answer. max_tokens, from §2.6, is the most tokens one reply may use.

So the question is never "should I enable thinking" but "how much reasoning is this task worth". The API gives you two separate controls for that.

This section has six subsections, in four parts:

  1. the two controls, and how far each one reaches (§5.1, §5.2);
  2. reading what thinking sends back (§5.3);
  3. thinking inside a tool loop, and over a long conversation (§5.4, §5.5);
  4. choosing an effort level with numbers (§5.6).

Here is the picture for the whole section. Since §1 the model has been a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. In §2 you filled in the telegram office's order form, in §3 you wrote the brief, and in §4 you sent a printed reply card. This section is about the writer's scrap paper. A good writer does not compose a hard letter straight onto the telegram form. They draft on scrap paper first: they try an opening, cross it out, check a date, and start again. Then they copy the finished reply onto the form. And the office charges for every word the writer writes, scrap paper included.

Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram office In thinking and effort Section
The writer drafting on scrap paper before writing your reply thinking §5.1
The office charging for every word, scrap paper included thinking billed as output tokens §5.1
The telegram's word limit, which the scrap words count against max_tokens §5.1
Whether the writer may use scrap paper at all the thinking mode §5.1
How long you tell the writer to spend: a quick note, or the whole afternoon effort §5.2
A note about the scrap pages, written by a different clerk summarised thinking §5.3
The scrap pages themselves, in a sealed envelope the signature §5.3
A scrap page the censor blacked out, still in the envelope redacted_thinking §5.3
The writer waiting mid-letter for a clerk's errand, scrap pages still on the desk thinking with tools §5.4
The file handed to a different writer switching models §5.4
Old scrap pages piling up in the file thinking in the context window §5.5
Paying the writer by the hour, when each extra hour buys less choosing an effort level §5.6

Two examples call the real API, one in §5.1 and one in §5.2, so running them needs an API key, and the model may word its reply differently and spend a different number of tokens. Every other example is plain Python, and prints the same thing on every machine.

5.1 Two Controls, and Which One You Want

Two settings decide how much reasoning you pay for. They sound alike, and they are not the same kind of thing:

  • thinking decides whether the model reasons in thinking blocks.
  • effort decides how much work goes into the whole response, meaning text, tool calls and thinking together.

In the picture, thinking is whether the writer may use scrap paper at all. effort is how long you tell the writer to spend on your letter: a quick note, or the whole afternoon. That time covers everything the writer does, the drafting, the letter itself, and every errand they send a clerk on. The grid puts the two side by side:

thinking
A mode. {"type": "adaptive"} lets the model decide when and how deeply to think. {"type": "disabled"} turns it off where the model allows that. It is not a dial.
output_config.effort
The dial, and the one to reach for. Five levels from low to max. It scales everything the model spends tokens on, including how many tool calls it makes.

That second property is what makes effort the better control in agentic systems: lower effort means fewer tool calls, and not merely shorter thinking. A tool call is the model asking your program to run one of its functions (§1.1), and each one costs a round trip and more tokens. No thinking-specific parameter can do that. In the picture, telling the writer "a quick note, please" also means fewer errands for the clerk.

Whether a model thinks before you ask it to depends on the model.

On Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, thinking is already on. No configuration is needed. What you usually want first on these models is to see it, because display defaults to "omitted" there. "omitted" means the reasoning is not shown to you; §5.3 covers display in full.

On Opus 4.8, 4.7, 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, thinking is off until you set thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}. Adaptive means the model decides for itself, request by request, when to think and how deeply.

There is also an older mode you will meet in inherited code: manual extended thinking, written {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}. There, budget_tokens reserves a fixed allowance of tokens for reasoning. Adaptive thinking replaced it, and the two differ in more than syntax:

  • A budget_tokens allowance is a number you must tune per task.
  • Adaptive thinking decides per request.

Note also that a top-level budget_tokens argument is not a thing at all. It belongs inside thinking. Passed at the top level, it raises a TypeError, for the same reason that §2's Exercise 2.1 gets one from temperature=0.7: messages.create() rejects a keyword it does not know.

Now back to the puzzle. The request below asks the train question. On Opus 5 thinking is already on, so passing thinking here changes one thing: "display": "summarized" asks for a readable summary of the reasoning instead of the default "omitted". The loop then prints each block of the reply by its type, and the last line prints the bill:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"},
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "A train leaves at 14:05 and arrives at 17:40, "
                          "stopping twice for 8 minutes each. What was its "
                          "moving time?"}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "thinking":
        print("thinking  :", block.thinking[:90])
        print("signature :", block.signature[:24] + "…")
    elif block.type == "text":
        print("answer    :", block.text)

print("output tokens (thinking INCLUDED):", response.usage.output_tokens)

thinking  : The train runs 14:05 to 17:40, which is 3 hours 35 minutes, or 215 minutes. Two stops of 8
signature : WaUjzkypQ2mUEVM36O2TxuHt…
answer    : 3 hours and 19 minutes of moving time.
output tokens (thinking INCLUDED): 312

Line by line:

  • The thinking line is the start of the reasoning summary. The model works out that 14:05 to 17:40 is 215 minutes before it gets to the stops. The example prints only the first 90 characters.
  • The signature line is a long encrypted string, cut to 24 characters here.
  • The answer line is the short sentence from the puzzle. 215 minutes, minus two stops of 8 minutes, is 199 minutes: 3 hours and 19 minutes.
  • The last line answers the puzzle. The 312 output tokens are the answer and the thinking. The thinking is most of them, and you pay for all of it at output prices.

In the picture, the answer is the clean reply on the telegram form, and the thinking is the scrap paper on the desk. The office counted the words on both.

Two fields on that block matter later:

  • thinking holds a summary of the reasoning, and never the raw chain of thought, on any setting. The chain of thought is the model's reasoning, word for word.
  • signature holds the full reasoning, encrypted, and it is what you pass back so the model can continue from where it left off (§5.4). Encrypted means scrambled with a key only the API holds: you can store it and send it back, but you cannot read it.

In the picture, the summary is a note about the scrap pages, and the signature is the scrap pages themselves, in a sealed envelope.

The bill has one more consequence: the thinking and the answer share max_tokens. Spend most of the allowance thinking, and there is little left for the answer. The example below is a small model of that documented rule, not the server. It gives one request a max_tokens of 4,096 and an answer that needs 250 tokens, and tries three amounts of thinking:

MAX_TOKENS = 4096

def share(thinking_used, answer_wanted):
    """A model of the documented rule: thinking and answer share max_tokens."""
    thinking = min(thinking_used, MAX_TOKENS)
    answer = min(answer_wanted, MAX_TOKENS - thinking)
    stop = "end_turn" if answer == answer_wanted else "max_tokens"
    return thinking, answer, stop

print(f"{'thinking':<10}{'answer':<8}stop_reason")
for thinking_used in (300, 3_900, 4_096):
    thinking, answer, stop = share(thinking_used, answer_wanted=250)
    print(f"{thinking:<10,}{answer:<8}{stop}")

thinking  answer  stop_reason
300       250     end_turn
3,900     196     max_tokens
4,096     0       max_tokens

Line by line:

  • With 300 tokens of thinking there is plenty of room, and the full 250-token answer fits.
  • With 3,900 tokens of thinking only 196 are left. The answer is cut off, and stop_reason says max_tokens.
  • With 4,096 tokens of thinking the whole allowance is gone. The reply holds thinking and no answer at all.

So set max_tokens for the thinking plus the answer, not for the answer alone. In the picture, the telegram's word limit counts the scrap paper too.

5.2 Effort Levels

effort is set inside output_config, as in output_config={"effort": "low"}. There are five levels. high is the default, and setting it explicitly is identical to omitting the parameter. In the picture, these are five ways to tell the writer how long to spend, from "a quick note" to "take as long as it needs":

max
No constraint on token spend. The deepest reasoning available. For problems where getting it right dominates everything else — and where overthinking is an acceptable price, because at this level the model will keep exploring a problem that a lower level would have closed.
xhigh
Extended, for long-horizon work — agentic and coding tasks running over thirty minutes with token budgets in the millions. Newer than max, and some models that support max do not support it.
high
The default. Complex reasoning, difficult coding, agentic tasks. Identical to omitting effort entirely.
medium
Balanced. Moderate token savings for agentic work that has to weigh speed and cost against quality.
low
Most efficient. Significant savings with some capability reduction. The right default for subagents (§11.8) and for graders (§13.5).

A few words in that grid, in plain terms:

  • Overthinking means long deliberation on a problem that did not need it.
  • Long-horizon work is a task that runs a long time, with many steps; here, over thirty minutes.
  • A subagent is a helper model that a main agent hands one small job to (§11.8).
  • A grader is a model that scores another model's answers against a written checklist (§13.5).

Effort is a behavioural signal, not a token budget. It tells the model how hard to try. It does not count anything. At low the model still thinks on a genuinely hard problem. It simply thinks less than it would at high for the same problem. If you need a hard ceiling, that is max_tokens, which is strict. In the picture, "a quick note, please" is advice the writer follows. The word limit on the telegram form is a rule the office enforces.

The request below asks one programming question twice, once at low and once at high. For each level it prints how many output tokens the reply used, and the first 44 characters of the answer:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

QUESTION = ("Given a list of 1,000,000 integers, find the two that sum to a "
            "target. Explain the approach you would choose and why.")

for level in ("low", "high"):
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5",
        max_tokens=4096,
        output_config={"effort": level},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": QUESTION}],
    )
    text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
    print(f"effort={level:<6} output_tokens={response.usage.output_tokens:>5}"
          f"  answer starts: {text[:44]!r}")

effort=low    output_tokens=  198  answer starts: 'Use a hash set: one pass, O(n) time and O(n)'
effort=high   output_tokens= 1364  answer starts: 'The choice is between sorting with two point'

Line by line:

  • At low, the reply used 198 output tokens. Its answer goes straight to the usual method: a hash set, a fast lookup table, in one pass over the list.
  • At high, it used 1,364, almost seven times as many. Its answer starts by weighing two methods against each other.

Both answers are reasonable. What changed is how much work went into them, and you paid for the difference.

Three practical notes follow, and the first two will save you a debugging session.

Do not pass adaptive as an effort value. adaptive is a thinking mode, and the effort levels are the five above. Mixing them up produces a 400 that reads confusingly. A 400 is the HTTP status code for "this request is malformed" (§2.9).

If the model is overthinking, lower the effort and do not instruct it not to. Overthinking means long deliberation on a problem that did not need it. It is a spend problem with a spend dial. Asking the model in prose to think less is a far weaker lever than the parameter that governs how many tokens it may use. In the picture, you do not add "please don't spend long on this" to the brief. You tell the office "a quick note".

Changing effort invalidates prompt cache. The prompt cache, from §1.3, keeps the start of a request, its prefix, so the next request that starts the same way is cheaper; §9.3 teaches it in full. Effort is rendered into the prompt, meaning the API writes it into the text the model reads. So changing it always invalidates message blocks and, on some models, tools and system too (§9.5). There is one exception: setting effort explicitly to the model's default is equivalent to omitting it and does not invalidate. So a request that alternates between low and high on the same conversation is two prefixes and not one.

The example below is a toy model of those rules, not the server's cache. It keys the cached prefix on the effort value alone, treats a missing effort as the default high, and sends five requests. A real cache entry also expires after a few minutes (§9.4), which the toy leaves out:

DEFAULT_EFFORT = "high"

def prefix_key(effort=None):
    """A model of the rule: effort is written into the prompt, and the
    default written out is the same as leaving it out."""
    return effort or DEFAULT_EFFORT

cached = set()
REQUESTS = [None, "high", "low", "high", "low"]
for effort in REQUESTS:
    key = prefix_key(effort)
    result = "hit" if key in cached else "MISS, new prefix written"
    cached.add(key)
    print(f"effort={effort!s:<5}  prefix={key:<5}  {result}")

print()
print(len(cached), "prefixes for", len(REQUESTS), "requests")

effort=None   prefix=high   MISS, new prefix written
effort=high   prefix=high   hit
effort=low    prefix=low    MISS, new prefix written
effort=high   prefix=high   hit
effort=low    prefix=low    hit

2 prefixes for 5 requests

Line by line:

  • The first request has no effort, which counts as high. Nothing is cached yet, so it writes a new prefix.
  • The second writes high out explicitly. That is the same as leaving it out, so it reuses the first prefix: a hit.
  • The third switches to low, a different prefix, so it misses.
  • From then on both prefixes exist, and each request hits one of them.

So five requests need two prefixes, one for each effort level you use.

5.3 Reading Thinking Output

You saw in §5.1 that a reply can carry a summary of the reasoning. Thinking display is controlled by the display field, which decides whether the summary text comes back at all. It has two values. The example below prints a table of what each value gives you, and which models use it by default:

BEHAVIOUR = [
    ("summarized", "a readable summary of the reasoning", "yes", "yes",
     "Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and earlier"),
    ("omitted", "an EMPTY thinking field", "no", "yes",
     "Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Fable 5, Mythos 5"),
]

print(f"{'display':<13}{'thinking field':<38}{'text?':<7}{'signature?':<12}"
      f"{'default on'}")
for value, what, text, sig, default_on in BEHAVIOUR:
    print(f"{value:<13}{what:<38}{text:<7}{sig:<12}{default_on}")

print()
print("BILLED THE SAME in both cases: omitting reduces latency, not cost")
print("the signature is IDENTICAL either way, and can be switched between turns")

display      thinking field                        text?  signature?  default on
summarized   a readable summary of the reasoning   yes    yes         Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and earlier
omitted      an EMPTY thinking field               no     yes         Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Fable 5, Mythos 5

BILLED THE SAME in both cases: omitting reduces latency, not cost
the signature is IDENTICAL either way, and can be switched between turns

Line by line:

  • "summarized" fills the thinking field with a readable summary. It is the default on Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and earlier.
  • "omitted" leaves the thinking field empty. It is the default on the newer models in the second row.
  • Both give you the signature, and both are billed the same.

In the picture, "summarized" means the office sends you a note about the scrap pages along with the sealed envelope. "omitted" means you get the sealed envelope alone.

display: "omitted" buys latency, not money. Latency is the time you wait. Thinking display is therefore an interface decision and not a cost one:

  • set it to "summarized" when you show reasoning to a user;
  • set it to "omitted" when you do not.

You are charged for every thinking token generated regardless. What it saves is time to first text token when streaming, meaning receiving the reply piece by piece as it is written (§2.7). The server skips streaming thinking tokens and delivers only the signature, so the answer starts sooner. If your interface does not show reasoning to users, this is a straightforward win.

Three further facts about summarised thinking change how you should read it.

It is never the raw chain of thought. No setting returns that. The summary is produced by a different model from the one you targeted, and the thinking model never sees the summary. In the picture, a different clerk reads the scrap pages and writes the note, and the writer never sees what the clerk wrote.

You are billed for the full thinking, not the summary. The billed output-token count will not match the tokens visible in the response. That is expected, and not a discrepancy to investigate. It is the second half of the puzzle's answer: the 312 tokens included reasoning you only ever saw a summary of.

Summarisation behaviour is subject to change. Do not build parsing on its shape. Parsing here means code that reads the summary's text and pulls facts out of it.

There is also a distinct block type worth knowing about, because it breaks naive filtering. When part of the reasoning is hidden for safety reasons, it arrives in a block of its own, redacted_thinking. The example below builds a reply's content list holding all three kinds of block, then filters it two ways. The naive filter keeps only blocks whose type is "thinking". The correct one keeps both thinking types:

# What a response's content list can hold when thinking is active.
BLOCKS = [
    {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "Let me work through this…",
     "signature": "WaUjzkypQ2mUEVM36O2Txu…"},
    {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "EncRypTedOpAqUeBlOb…"},
    {"type": "text", "text": "The moving time was 3 hours 19 minutes."},
]

naive = [b for b in BLOCKS if b["type"] == "thinking"]
correct = [b for b in BLOCKS if b["type"] in ("thinking", "redacted_thinking")]

print("blocks in the response      :", [b["type"] for b in BLOCKS])
print("kept by `type == 'thinking'`:", [b["type"] for b in naive])
print("kept by the correct filter  :", [b["type"] for b in correct])
print()
print("the naive filter silently drops redacted_thinking, which breaks the")
print("multi-turn protocol with a 400 on the NEXT request, not this one")

blocks in the response      : ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'text']
kept by `type == 'thinking'`: ['thinking']
kept by the correct filter  : ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking']

the naive filter silently drops redacted_thinking, which breaks the
multi-turn protocol with a 400 on the NEXT request, not this one

Line by line:

  • The reply holds three blocks.
  • The naive filter keeps one of them, and silently loses redacted_thinking.
  • The correct filter keeps both thinking blocks.
  • The last two lines say when the damage shows: not now, but on the next request.

redacted_thinking blocks appear when part of the reasoning is safety-redacted, meaning blanked out for safety reasons. The data field is opaque and encrypted, and the block must be passed back unchanged like any other. Opaque means you are not meant to read it or change it. In the picture, it is a scrap page the censor blacked out. It stays in the sealed envelope, and the envelope goes back whole.

Filtering on block.type == "thinking" alone drops it, and the failure surfaces one request later as a rejected message sequence. That is exactly the kind of bug that is hard to attribute, because the request that fails is not the one with the mistake in it.

5.4 Thinking With Tools

Thinking and tool use work together, with one rule that is absolute: within a tool-use turn, every thinking block must go back to the API complete and unmodified.

A turn is one message in the conversation, from you or from the model (§2.3). A tool-use turn is an assistant turn that asks for a tool: your program runs the tool and sends the result back, and the model carries on. §6.4 teaches that loop in full.

The reason for the rule is that a tool-use loop is one assistant turn. From the model's point of view it has not finished responding. It paused to wait for information. The reasoning that led to the tool call is part of the response it is still constructing.

In the picture, the writer is halfway through your letter and sends a clerk to look something up. The scrap pages stay on the desk. When the clerk comes back, the writer needs the desk exactly as it was left. If someone tidied a page away, or rewrote one, the writer cannot carry on, and the office refuses the job.

The example below sends one assistant turn back three ways: preserved exactly, with the thinking stripped out, and with the thinking edited. round_trip puts the assistant turn first and the tool result after it, as the API expects. The check on the last line stands in for the API: it accepts a turn only when it matches what the model produced, block for block:

def round_trip(assistant_content, tool_result):
    """Preserve the assistant turn exactly, then append the result."""
    return [
        {"role": "assistant", "content": assistant_content},
        {"role": "user", "content": [tool_result]},
    ]


ASSISTANT = [
    {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "I need the current weather first.",
     "signature": "sig_abc…"},
    {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "opaque…"},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "get_weather",
     "input": {"city": "Paris"}},
]
RESULT = {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01", "content": "20C"}

good = round_trip(ASSISTANT, RESULT)
stripped = round_trip([b for b in ASSISTANT if b["type"] == "tool_use"], RESULT)
edited = round_trip(
    [{**b, "thinking": "shortened"} if b["type"] == "thinking" else b
     for b in ASSISTANT], RESULT)

for label, turn in (("preserved", good), ("thinking stripped", stripped),
                    ("thinking edited", edited)):
    blocks = [b["type"] for b in turn[0]["content"]]
    ok = blocks == [b["type"] for b in ASSISTANT] and turn[0]["content"] == ASSISTANT
    print(f"{label:<20}{str(blocks):<58}{'accepted' if ok else 'REJECTED (400)'}")

preserved           ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'tool_use']             accepted
thinking stripped   ['tool_use']                                              REJECTED (400)
thinking edited     ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'tool_use']             REJECTED (400)

Line by line:

  • The preserved turn matches what the model produced, so it is accepted.
  • The stripped turn lost two blocks, so it is rejected with a 400.
  • The edited turn still has the same three block types, but one block's text changed. It is rejected too: the right types are not enough.

Modified thinking blocks are rejected with a 400. They are not silently ignored. Within the latest assistant message, the sequence of consecutive thinking blocks must match what the model generated. You cannot rearrange them, edit them, or drop some of them. The single exception is text placed in the empty thinking field of an omitted block, which is ignored and not rejected.

Across turns the rule relaxes. Once a tool-use turn is over and the conversation has moved on, older thinking is handled more loosely:

Required
Within a tool-use turn, pass thinking blocks back.
Recommended
Across turns, pass everything back. The API filters automatically, keeps what it needs, and bills input tokens only for the blocks actually shown to the model.
Allowed
Outside tool use, omit prior turns' thinking entirely.

Do not prune old thinking yourself. Pruning means cutting old blocks out of the history to make it shorter. Pass it all back, and the API decides what to keep. Which prior-turn blocks survive depends on the model:

  • Opus 4.5 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later, Fable 5 and Mythos 5 keep all prior turns.
  • Earlier Opus and Sonnet models and every Haiku through 4.5 keep only the last turn and strip the rest for you.

In the picture, you hand the office the whole file, and the office decides which old scrap pages the writer still needs.

One case demands manual stripping: switching models mid-conversation. Thinking blocks are tied to the model that produced them. After a fallback to a different model (§14.6), strip thinking and redacted_thinking from prior assistant turns. A fallback is sending the request to a second model when the first one fails; §14.6 teaches it. Other models will not reject the old blocks, because they silently ignore them, but ignored blocks still cost input tokens. In the picture, the file goes to a different writer, who cannot open the first writer's sealed envelopes, and you would still pay postage on them.

The function below does that stripping. It removes both thinking types from every assistant turn and leaves everything else alone:

THINKING = ("thinking", "redacted_thinking")


def strip_thinking(messages):
    """For a conversation moving to a different model: drop thinking
    from earlier assistant turns, and keep everything else."""
    cleaned = []
    for message in messages:
        content = message["content"]
        if message["role"] == "assistant":
            content = [b for b in content if b["type"] not in THINKING]
        cleaned.append({**message, "content": content})
    return cleaned


HISTORY = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Where is order 1042?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": [
        {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "Check the order first.",
         "signature": "sig_a…"},
