        {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "opaque…"},
        {"type": "text", "text": "It left the warehouse on Monday."},
    ]},
    {"role": "user", "content": "When will it arrive?"},
]

for label, messages in (("before", HISTORY), ("after", strip_thinking(HISTORY))):
    print(label)
    for m in messages:
        c = m["content"]
        shown = c if isinstance(c, str) else [b["type"] for b in c]
        print(f"  {m['role']:<11}{shown}")

before
  user       Where is order 1042?
  assistant  ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'text']
  user       When will it arrive?
after
  user       Where is order 1042?
  assistant  ['text']
  user       When will it arrive?

Line by line:

  • Before, the assistant turn holds two thinking blocks and its text.
  • After, it holds only the text. The user turns are untouched.
  • Everything either side actually said is still there.

Use it only when the model changes. On the same model, inside a tool-use turn, this is exactly the stripping the rule above forbids.

Interleaved thinking means reasoning between tool calls and not only before the first one. It is automatic with adaptive thinking on every model that supports it, and needs no beta header (a request header that opts in to a feature still in testing). That is worth stating because interleaved thinking used to require one. Under manual extended thinking it still does, and there it changes how the thinking budget is counted. Any guide that tells you to set a beta header for interleaved thinking is describing the manual mode.

On Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8 and Opus 4.7, reasoning between tool calls always appears in thinking blocks. Haiku 4.5 does not support it. Note that consecutive tool calls do not require interleaving. It changes where thinking appears, and not whether calls can chain. In the picture, interleaving is the writer adding scrap notes each time a clerk comes back, and not only at the start.

There is one incompatibility to know: forced tool use works with adaptive thinking and not with manual extended thinking. Forced tool use means setting tool_choice so that the model must call a tool (§6.7). Under thinking: {"type": "enabled"}, only a tool_choice of auto or none is accepted, and any and a named tool are errors. Adaptive thinking, including where it is on by default, supports forced tool use.

The figure sums up the rule for a tool loop:

5.5 Thinking and the Context Window

The context window is everything the model reads in one request: the system prompt, the tools, and the whole conversation so far, all counted in tokens (§1.2). Thinking occupies the window, and how much depends on when it was generated. In the picture, the window is the file the writer reads before each reply, and old scrap pages can pile up in it.

The example below adds up a 12-turn conversation, on top of a 1,200-token system prompt. Each turn adds a 60-token question, 900 tokens of thinking and a 260-token answer. It counts the context two ways:

  • keep-all models keep every earlier turn's thinking in the context;
  • last-turn-only models keep only the most recent turn's thinking.

It prints the context size at turns 1, 4, 8 and 12, and the gap between the two:

TURNS = 12
THINKING_PER_TURN = 900
TEXT_PER_TURN = 260
QUESTION = 60
SYSTEM = 1_200

keep_all, last_only = SYSTEM, SYSTEM
print(f"{'turn':>5}{'keep-all context':>19}{'last-turn-only':>17}{'gap':>9}")
for turn in range(1, TURNS + 1):
    keep_all += QUESTION + THINKING_PER_TURN + TEXT_PER_TURN
    last_only += QUESTION + TEXT_PER_TURN
    if turn in (1, 4, 8, 12):
        print(f"{turn:>5}{keep_all:>19,}{last_only + THINKING_PER_TURN:>17,}"
              f"{keep_all - last_only - THINKING_PER_TURN:>9,}")

print()
print(f"after {TURNS} turns, retained thinking accounts for "
      f"{TURNS * THINKING_PER_TURN:,} input tokens")
print("on keep-all models that is ordinary conversation history, billed as input")

 turn   keep-all context   last-turn-only      gap
    1              2,420            2,420        0
    4              6,080            3,380    2,700
    8             10,960            4,660    6,300
   12             15,840            5,940    9,900

after 12 turns, retained thinking accounts for 10,800 input tokens
on keep-all models that is ordinary conversation history, billed as input

Line by line:

  • At turn 1 the two are equal, because there is only one turn of thinking either way.
  • By turn 12 the keep-all context is 15,840 tokens, against 5,940. The gap, 9,900 tokens, is the eleven earlier turns of thinking.
  • In total, the 12 turns of thinking come to 10,800 tokens, and on keep-all models they are all still in the context.

The figure draws the same two lines:

On keep-all models, budget for thinking as if it were conversation history, because it is. Long agentic sessions accumulate it. The lever is clear_thinking_20251015 (§9.6), a setting that clears old thinking out of the context. Its cache interaction runs opposite to tool-result clearing, which §9.6 also teaches: keeping thinking blocks preserves the cache, and clearing them invalidates it at the clearing point.

Two hard limits worth having in mind:

max_tokens includes thinking and is strict. You saw the first half of that in §5.1. What happens when input plus max_tokens is larger than the window depends on the model:

  • On Claude 4.5 and newer, if input plus max_tokens exceeds the window, the request is accepted, and generation stops with stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded" if it actually reaches the limit.
  • On earlier models it is a validation error up front: the API rejects the request before the model writes anything.

Output caps are per model. An output cap is the largest max_tokens a model accepts:

  • Fable 5, Mythos 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 support up to 128k output tokens.
  • Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 support 64k.

The message batches API raises it further. That API runs many requests together, at a lower price, and returns the results later. A beta header there lifts the cap to 300k for several models, which is one of several reasons message batches suit thinking-heavy work (§15.2).

And here is a client-side rule that trips people: the SDKs require streaming when max_tokens exceeds 21,333, to avoid HTTP timeouts. The SDK is the anthropic library you call the API through, and an HTTP timeout is the connection giving up while it waits for a long reply. That is validation in the SDK and not an API restriction, and it is why §11.3's task-budget example uses .stream() with get_final_message().

The next figure belongs to §5.6, which works out its numbers. It shows, for one workload, what each effort level costs a month and what it buys:

5.6 Choosing an Effort Level

The decision is economic, and it is worth doing with numbers and not instinct. In the picture, you pay the writer by the hour, and you decide how many hours each kind of letter is worth.

The example below takes one workload: 40,000 requests a day for 30 days, each with 3,500 input tokens, at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens. For each effort level it has two numbers from that workload's profile: how many output tokens a reply used, and its accuracy, the share of answers that were right. It works out the monthly cost, and one more column, the cost of each extra accuracy point:

OUT_PER_MTOK, IN_PER_MTOK = 25.00, 5.00
INPUT_TOKENS = 3_500
REQUESTS_PER_DAY, DAYS = 40_000, 30

# Output token counts observed for one workload at each level.
PROFILE = [("low", 210, 0.71), ("medium", 640, 0.83),
           ("high", 1_450, 0.89), ("max", 3_900, 0.91)]

print(f"{'effort':<9}{'out tokens':>12}{'accuracy':>10}{'$/month':>12}"
      f"{'$ per accuracy point':>22}")
previous = None
for level, out_tokens, accuracy in PROFILE:
    monthly = ((INPUT_TOKENS / 1e6 * IN_PER_MTOK
                + out_tokens / 1e6 * OUT_PER_MTOK)
               * REQUESTS_PER_DAY * DAYS)
    if previous is None:
        marginal = "—"
    else:
        prev_cost, prev_acc = previous
        marginal = "$" + format((monthly - prev_cost)
                                / ((accuracy - prev_acc) * 100), ",.0f")
    previous = (monthly, accuracy)
    print(f"{level:<9}{out_tokens:>12,}{accuracy:>10.0%}"
          f"{'$' + format(monthly, ',.0f'):>12}{marginal:>22}")

print()
print("the last column is the cost of ONE more accuracy point at that step,")
print("not the average since `low` — the two tell very different stories")

effort     out tokens  accuracy     $/month  $ per accuracy point
low               210       71%     $27,300                     —
medium            640       83%     $40,200                $1,075
high            1,450       89%     $64,500                $4,050
max             3,900       91%    $138,000               $36,750

the last column is the cost of ONE more accuracy point at that step,
not the average since `low` — the two tell very different stories

Line by line:

  • At low, the month costs $27,300, and 71% of answers are right.
  • medium costs $12,900 more and adds 12 points: $1,075 per point.
  • high costs $24,300 more and adds 6 points: $4,050 per point.
  • max costs $73,500 more and adds 2 points: $36,750 per point.

Read the last column, not the third. Accuracy rises steadily with effort, and so does cost. What decides the level is the marginal cost of each additional point, meaning what the next point costs, and not the average of all of them. That column climbs from $1,075 to $36,750 across three steps. The last step buys two accuracy points for $73,500, which is nearly twice what the first eighteen points cost in total. "Diminishing returns" is too gentle a phrase for a 34-fold change in marginal price, and this shape is typical and not pathological. In the picture, the writer's first hours buy a much better letter. The last hours buy a slightly better comma.

That does not make max wrong. It makes it a choice you should make deliberately, and usually a per-request one. A router is a small piece of code, or a cheap model call, that decides which requests are hard. Using max on the 3% of requests a router judges hard, and low on the rest, is a far better system than either level applied uniformly. For a rough sense of scale: if a hard request cost what an average one does, that mix would cost 0.97 × $27,300 + 0.03 × $138,000 = $30,621 a month, against $138,000 for max everywhere. Hard requests usually use more tokens than average, so the real figure is higher, but the gap stays large.

Three defaults worth adopting:

low for graders and subagents. A judge applying an explicit rubric (§13.5) and a worker summarising a document (§11.8) are not the tasks that need deep reasoning, and both run at high volume. A rubric is the written checklist a grader scores against.

high, which means doing nothing, for the main path. It is the default because it is the right default. The main path is the request your users are waiting on.

xhigh for long-horizon agentic work, where the token budget is in the millions and the run takes half an hour. It exists for that shape specifically.

And measure it. The accuracy column above is a profile of one workload, and yours will differ. §13's eval harness (the program that runs your test cases and scores the results) is how you produce your own version of that table and do not inherit someone else's. Running an eval harness across two effort levels is an afternoon's work, and it replaces every guess in this subsection with your own numbers.

Back to the puzzle one last time. The 312 tokens were mostly scrap paper: thinking, billed as output, and shown to you only as a summary. Whether that scrap paper was worth paying for is the question this subsection answers, with numbers.

Exercises

Exercise 5.1 — Find the bug in this loop. An agent using thinking and tools works for one turn and then fails with a 400 saying thinking blocks cannot be modified. Find it.

while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    thinking = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "thinking"]
    calls = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": thinking + calls})
    results = [run(c) for c in calls]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
    response = client.messages.create(**kwargs, messages=messages)
Solution 
ORIGINAL = [
    {"type": "thinking", "thinking": "First I should check the order.",
     "signature": "sig_a…"},
    {"type": "redacted_thinking", "data": "opaque…"},
    {"type": "text", "text": "Let me look that up."},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_1", "name": "get_order",
     "input": {"id": "ord_1"}},
]


def buggy(content):
    thinking = [b for b in content if b["type"] == "thinking"]
    calls = [b for b in content if b["type"] == "tool_use"]
    return thinking + calls


def fixed(content):
    """Pass the assistant turn back exactly as it arrived."""
    return list(content)


for label, rebuilt in (("filtered", buggy(ORIGINAL)), ("verbatim", fixed(ORIGINAL))):
    types = [b["type"] for b in rebuilt]
    print(f"{label:<10}{str(types):<70}")
    print(f"{'':10}identical to what the model produced: {rebuilt == ORIGINAL}")
    dropped = [b["type"] for b in ORIGINAL if b not in rebuilt]
    print(f"{'':10}dropped: {dropped or 'nothing'}")
    print()

filtered  ['thinking', 'tool_use']                                              
          identical to what the model produced: False
          dropped: ['redacted_thinking', 'text']

verbatim  ['thinking', 'redacted_thinking', 'text', 'tool_use']                 
          identical to what the model produced: True
          dropped: nothing

The filter drops redacted_thinking. That is the bug, and it is the specific trap §5.3 named. block.type == "thinking" looks exhaustive and is not. When part of the reasoning is safety-redacted, it arrives as a redacted_thinking block, which must be passed back unchanged like any other. The rebuilt turn no longer matches what the model generated, and the API rejects it.

It also drops the text block, which is a second, quieter defect. The model often narrates before calling, with something like "Let me look that up.", and reconstructing the turn from thinking plus tool calls discards that. Here it happens not to be the thing that triggers the 400, but it does mean the conversation history no longer reflects what the assistant actually said.

The fix is not a better filter. It is not filtering. response.content is exactly what the API expects back. Every rule in §5.4 (do not rearrange, do not edit, do not partially drop) is satisfied for free by appending the list you were given. Any code that rebuilds an assistant turn from selected blocks will break the next time a block type is added, and block types keep being added.

Why it worked for one turn. The first request has no prior assistant turn to preserve, so the bug cannot fire. It fires on the second. That makes it look like a problem with the loop and not with the append, which is a good example of why the §13.10 trajectory tests matter: a single-turn test passes.

Exercise 5.2 — Choose the effort level. Three workloads. Pick a level for each and say what you would measure to confirm it: (a) a customer-facing chat assistant, 200,000 requests a day; (b) an LLM judge grading 5,000 eval cases per run; (c) an agent that refactors a module and opens a pull request, a few dozen runs a day.

Solution 
WORKLOADS = [
    ("a  customer chat", 200_000, "low or medium", 3_200, 240,
     "latency and cost dominate; answers are short and mostly routine"),
    ("b  LLM judge", 5_000, "low", 900, 60,
     "an explicit rubric is not a reasoning task; volume is what matters"),
    ("c  refactor + PR", 40, "xhigh", 28_000, 9_000,
     "long-horizon, high value per run, and a human gate catches errors"),
]
IN_PER_MTOK, OUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 25.00

print(f"{'workload':<20}{'runs/day':>10}  {'effort':<16}{'$/day':>10}{'$/run':>11}")
for name, runs, effort, in_tokens, out_tokens, _ in WORKLOADS:
    per_run = in_tokens / 1e6 * IN_PER_MTOK + out_tokens / 1e6 * OUT_PER_MTOK
    print(f"{name:<20}{runs:>10,}  {effort:<16}"
          f"{'$' + format(per_run * runs, ',.0f'):>10}{'$%.4f' % per_run:>11}")

print()
for name, _, _, _, _, reason in WORKLOADS:
    print(f"{name:<20}{reason}")

workload              runs/day  effort               $/day      $/run
a  customer chat       200,000  low or medium       $4,400    $0.0220
b  LLM judge             5,000  low                    $30    $0.0060
c  refactor + PR            40  xhigh                  $15    $0.3650

a  customer chat    latency and cost dominate; answers are short and mostly routine
b  LLM judge        an explicit rubric is not a reasoning task; volume is what matters
c  refactor + PR    long-horizon, high value per run, and a human gate catches errors

(a) Customer chat: low, moving to medium only if an eval says so. At 200,000 requests a day, this is the workload where effort is worth the most money, and it is also the one where deep reasoning helps least, because most turns are routine. The thing to measure is not cost, which is obvious, but quality on the tail. Run §13's suite at low and medium and look specifically at the hard cases, because the mean will barely move while the difficult 5% may move a lot. If it does, the answer is not a higher global effort. It is a router that escalates those cases.

(b) The judge: low, and I would not consider anything else. §13.5 makes the argument: grading against an explicit rubric is a classification and not a reasoning problem, and the rubric is doing the work that thinking would otherwise have to do. What to measure is Cohen's kappa against human labels (§13.6) at low. If it clears the bar, higher effort is spending money to agree with humans slightly more confidently.

(c) The refactor agent: xhigh, and this is what it exists for. Long-horizon coding over half an hour with a token budget in the millions is the documented shape for that level. At forty runs a day, the cost per run is what matters, and it is small against an engineer's time. The gate matters too. The pull request is a human review (§11.6), so an error is caught and not shipped, which is what makes spending on capability rational here and not in (a).

What I would measure in all three, and it is the same thing. Effort is a behavioural signal and not a budget, so the only way to know what a level costs you is to run your own workload at two levels and compare output tokens and quality. The profile in §5.6 is one workload's curve. The shape generalises, and the numbers do not.

And one thing I would not do: set effort globally and forget it. The largest gain available in (a) is not choosing between low and medium. It is routing, so that most requests run at low and the hard ones run at high. A single global level leaves most of the value on the table.

SECTION 6

Tool Use

Start with a puzzle. You ask a model one question: "Compare the weather in Lisbon and Reykjavik." You get one answer back, with the real temperatures in it. But when you count the messages your program built, there are three of them, not two. And the model never ran a line of code. So who fetched the weather, and where did the extra message come from? Guess before you read on. §6.4 runs the request and answers both questions.

Until now, every example has been one request and one answer. This section is where a language model stops being a text generator and becomes something you can build a system out of.

The mechanism is smaller than its reputation suggests:

  • There is no new endpoint. An endpoint is one address of the API, and you keep using the same one.
  • There is no agent runtime and no framework.
  • You add a tools array to the same request.

With that array, the model gains the ability to emit a structured request instead of prose. A structured request is a small piece of JSON, text with named fields (§4.1), that names a function and supplies its arguments. Your program decides what to do with it.

Hold that sentence, because every safety property in the rest of this course descends from it. The model never executes anything. It produces a block of JSON that names a function and supplies arguments. A loop you wrote decides three things:

  • whether to run it;
  • what to run it against;
  • what to say happened.

"The model deleted the row" is never true. What always happened is that "my loop passed the model's proposal to a function that deleted the row".

Here is the picture for the whole section. Since §1 the model has been a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. In §5 the writer drafted on scrap paper. This section is about the request slip. The writer never leaves the desk. When a letter needs a fact the writer does not have, such as today's weather in Lisbon, the writer cannot go and look. Instead, the writer fills in a request slip, "weather, Lisbon, please", and hands it out of the window. You read the slip, and you decide whether a clerk runs the errand. The clerk's report goes back to the writer, who finishes the letter.

Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram office In tool use Section
A blank slip form on the writer's desk, with a title, instructions and boxes a tool definition §6.2
The instructions printed on the slip form the tool's description §6.2
The boxes on the slip the input_schema §6.2
A filled-in sample slip pinned beside the pile input_examples §6.2
A filled slip handed out of the window a tool_use block §6.3
The writer putting down the pen to wait stop_reason of tool_use §6.3
The number printed on each slip the block's id §6.3
You, carrying slips out and reports back in the agent loop §6.4
The clerk's report, filed under the slip's number a tool_result §6.5
A report saying the errand failed, and why is_error §6.5
Three slips handed out at once parallel tool use §6.6
Your note: "use a slip if you like", "you must", "use this one", "no slips now" tool_choice §6.7
The stencil from §4, laid over the slip, so only valid answers fit strict tool use §6.8
The pile of blank forms the writer rereads before every letter what a tool surface costs §6.9
The clerk checking the customer's ID before fetching their file authorisation in your code §6.10

This section has ten subsections, in five parts:

  1. who does what, and how to describe a tool (§6.1, §6.2);
  2. one round trip, then the loop that repeats it (§6.3, §6.4);
  3. results, failures, and several calls at once (§6.5, §6.6);
  4. steering the model's choice, and guaranteeing its arguments (§6.7, §6.8);
  5. what a whole set of tools costs, and how to design one (§6.9, §6.10).

Four examples call the real API, in §6.3, §6.4, §6.7 and §6.8, so running them needs an API key, and the model may word its reply differently. Every other example is plain Python, and prints the same thing on every machine.

6.1 The Contract: The Model Proposes, Your Code Disposes

The title borrows an old saying. Disposes means decides what actually happens.

Tool use is a contract with three parties. It is worth naming them, because two of the three are yours. In the picture: you print the slip forms, the writer fills one in, and you decide whether the errand runs. The first row mentions JSON Schema, the standard way to describe which fields a piece of JSON must have, which §4 used for structured outputs:

You, declaring
The schema. A name, a description written for a reader who has never seen your system, and a JSON Schema for the arguments. This is the entire interface — the model never sees your implementation, your database, or your error messages except the ones you choose to hand back.
The model, choosing
Whether to call, which to call, and with what arguments. It decides from the conversation and your descriptions. This is the only part you do not control, and improving it is almost entirely a matter of improving the description.
You, executing
The call, the authorisation, and the result. Your loop runs the function — or refuses to. Every check that matters (is this user allowed to read that row? is this amount above the approval threshold?) lives here, because it is the only place that has the request context the model does not.

There is a second question, and it decides how much of the loop you write at all: where the code runs. There are three cases. They behave differently enough that mixing them up is a genuine source of confusion.

User-defined tools are the ordinary case and most of this section. You write the schema and the code. The response contains a tool_use block. You execute it and send back a tool_result. In the picture, you printed the slip form yourself, and your own clerk runs the errand.

Anthropic-schema tools are also executed by you, but the schema is published and not invented by you. The set is:

  • bash, which runs shell commands;
  • the text editor tool, for creating and editing files;
  • the memory tool, for state that outlives a conversation (§9.8);
  • computer use, for screenshot-and-keyboard control of a desktop;
  • browser use, for navigating and interacting with pages in your own browser.

Computer use and browser use are toolsets, not single tools: one entry declares a fixed set of member tools. The text editor tool and the memory tool are ordinary single entries. You declare them by a date-versioned type and no input_schema. Date-versioned means the type's name ends in a date, so a new version gets a new name.

Why prefer one of these over a custom tool that does the same job? Not convenience. These signatures are trained-in: the model met them during its training. So it calls them more reliably, and recovers from their errors more gracefully, than it does with a bespoke equivalent. In the picture, they are the office's standard printed forms, which every writer has filled in a thousand times. §6.10 returns to when that matters.

Server-executed tools (web_search, web_fetch, code_execution and tool_search) run on Anthropic's infrastructure, its own servers. You enable them and read the answer. You never build a tool_result for them. In the picture, the telegram office runs those errands itself, before the letter ever reaches you. §7 is entirely about these, including the one case where the server loop hands control back to you mid-flight.

The distinction that matters for this section: client tools require a loop, server tools do not. A client tool is one your own program runs, as in the first two cases above.

6.2 Defining a Tool

A user-defined tool is a dict with three required keys, plus one optional key that earns its place surprisingly often. A dict is Python's table of names and values, and a key is one of its names. The example below defines a weather tool with name, description and input_schema, then prints what it declared. The last line counts the words in the description, because the description is where the effort goes:

get_weather = {
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": (
        "Get the current weather for a city. Returns temperature in Celsius, "
        "a one-word condition, and the observation time in UTC. Use this when the "
        "user asks about current conditions; it does not provide forecasts, "
        "historical weather, or air quality. If the city is ambiguous, ask the "
        "user to disambiguate rather than guessing a country."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "city": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "City name, optionally with country: 'Lisbon, PT'.",
            },
            "unit": {
                "type": "string",
                "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"],
                "description": "Temperature unit. Defaults to celsius.",
            },
        },
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}

print("name       :", get_weather["name"])
print("required   :", get_weather["input_schema"]["required"])
print("optional   :", sorted(set(get_weather["input_schema"]["properties"])
                             - set(get_weather["input_schema"]["required"])))
print("desc words :", len(get_weather["description"].split()))

name       : get_weather
required   : ['city']
optional   : ['unit']
desc words : 54

Line by line:

  • name is what the model writes when it asks for this tool, and what your code looks up.
  • required lists the one argument the model must always supply: city.
  • optional is worked out by the code: every property, minus the required ones. So unit may be left out.
  • desc words is 54. That is long for one function's description, and it is meant to be.

name must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$. That is a regular expression, a pattern that text either fits or does not (§4.3). Read it as: one to 64 characters, each a letter, a digit, an underscore or a hyphen. No spaces, and no accented letters. The example below checks five names against that pattern:

import re

NAME = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$")

for name in ("get_weather", "github_list-prs", "get weather", "météo", "x" * 65):
    verdict = "ok" if NAME.fullmatch(name) else "rejected"
    print(f"{name[:16]:<18} {len(name):>2} chars  {verdict}")

get_weather        11 chars  ok
github_list-prs    15 chars  ok
get weather        11 chars  rejected
météo               5 chars  rejected
xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx   65 chars  rejected

get_weather and github_list-prs pass. get weather fails on its space, météo on its accented letter, and the last name on its length: it has 65 characters, and only its first 16 are printed.

input_schema is ordinary JSON Schema. Neither is where the difficulty lives.

The tool description is the tool. It is by a wide margin the largest lever on whether the model calls the right thing with the right arguments. In the picture, it is the instructions printed on the slip form, and the writer has nothing else to go on. It is also the part engineers under-write. To the person who built the function, its purpose is obvious. It is not obvious to a reader who has only this paragraph.

Aim for three or four sentences at minimum, and cover four things:

  1. what it does;
  2. when to use it;
  3. when not to;
  4. what it does not return.

Look back at get_weather's description: it covers all four. A tool description written to that shape is longer than feels necessary, and it is still the cheapest accuracy improvement available.

That last one is worth dwelling on. A tool called get_weather that silently returns no forecast will be called for forecasts. The result will not contain one. The model will then do something unhelpful with the gap, most often inventing a forecast. Saying "it does not provide forecasts" costs a handful of tokens and removes an entire failure mode.

The optional fourth key is input_examples. It is an array of example input objects, schema-validated, meaning each example must fit your input_schema. It is for tools whose arguments are complex, nested or format-sensitive. Descriptions come first, and you reach for examples when a sentence cannot convey the shape. In the picture, it is a filled-in sample slip pinned beside the pile of blank ones.

The tool below searches orders. Its placed_between argument is nested: a small object of its own, with a from and a to date. Two examples show the reader its shape:

search_orders = {
    "name": "search_orders",
    "description": (
        "Search orders by any combination of customer, status and date range. "
        "Omitted filters are not applied. Returns at most 50 orders, newest first."
    ),
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "customer_id": {"type": "string"},
            "status": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["placed", "shipped", "cancelled"]},
            "placed_between": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {"from": {"type": "string", "format": "date"},
                               "to": {"type": "string", "format": "date"}},
                "required": ["from", "to"],
            },
        },
    },
    "input_examples": [
        {"customer_id": "c_8814"},
        {"status": "shipped",
         "placed_between": {"from": "2026-08-01", "to": "2026-08-25"}},
    ],
}

for i, ex in enumerate(search_orders["input_examples"], 1):
    print(f"example {i}: {ex}")

example 1: {'customer_id': 'c_8814'}
example 2: {'status': 'shipped', 'placed_between': {'from': '2026-08-01', 'to': '2026-08-25'}}

The loop prints each example on its own line. The first uses a single filter. The second combines a status with a date range, and shows exactly how a date range is written.

One more thing happens when you pass tools, and it is invisible unless you know to look: the API builds a system prompt out of your tool definitions and prepends it to whatever system prompt you supplied. The system prompt is the standing instructions at the top of a request (§2.4), and prepends means puts in front.

So your descriptions are not metadata sitting beside the conversation:

  • They are text in the context window, all the text the model is shown in one request (§1.4).
  • They cost input tokens on every single request.
  • They compete for the model's attention with everything else.

In the picture, the writer rereads every blank slip form on the desk before every letter, and the office bills you for the reading. §6.9 does the arithmetic. It is the reason "just add all forty tools" stops working.

6.3 The Shape of a Tool-Use Turn

Send a request with tools, and one of two things happens. The model may answer with prose, as usual. Or it may stop and ask for a call. The signal that tells you which is stop_reason, the field from §2.6 that says why a reply ended.

The request below gives the model one tool, get_weather, and asks about Lisbon. The loop at the end prints every block of the reply, by its type:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

tools = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Current weather for a city. Returns Celsius and a condition.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"],
    },
}]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the weather in Lisbon?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
for block in response.content:
    print("block type :", block.type)
    if block.type == "text":
        print("  text     :", block.text)
    elif block.type == "tool_use":
        print("  id       :", block.id)
        print("  name     :", block.name)
        print("  input    :", block.input)

stop_reason: tool_use
block type : text
  text     : Let me look that up.
block type : tool_use
  id       : toolu_01Wx9Kq
  name     : get_weather
  input    : {'city': 'Lisbon'}

Line by line:

  • stop_reason: tool_use says the model stopped to ask for a call. It has not finished its answer.
  • The first block is text: the model narrating, "Let me look that up."
  • The second block is tool_use. It carries an id, the tool's name, and the input the model chose: the city, Lisbon.

In the picture, the writer has written one line of the letter, filled in a slip, handed it out of the window, and put down the pen. The id is the number printed on the slip.

Four things in that output are load-bearing: your code breaks if it gets any of them wrong.

stop_reason is "tool_use", and not "end_turn". This is the flag your loop keys on, and it is the only reliable one. The presence of a tool_use block and this stop reason always agree. But reading the stop reason keeps the loop readable, and it handles the other reasons in the same if.

The turn can contain both text and a tool call. Models often narrate before calling. So your loop must iterate over response.content, and not assume content[0] is the call. Assuming index zero is a real bug. It appears the first time the model says "Let me check that for you." before calling.

The example below shows the bug and the fix. It uses a plain list of dicts, shaped like the reply above, so it runs without an API key:

content = [
    {"type": "text", "text": "Let me look that up."},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01", "name": "get_weather",
     "input": {"city": "Lisbon"}},
]

# The bug: assume the first block is the call.
first = content[0]
print("content[0] is a", first["type"], "block")

# The fix: walk every block and pick out the calls.
calls = [block for block in content if block["type"] == "tool_use"]
for call in calls:
    print("call:", call["name"], call["input"], "id", call["id"])

content[0] is a text block
call: get_weather {'city': 'Lisbon'} id toolu_01

The bug reads the first block and finds the text block, not the call. The fix walks every block and keeps the ones whose type is tool_use. It also works when there are two calls, or none.

block.input is already a dict. The SDK parsed it. The SDK is the anthropic library your code imports, and parsed means it turned the JSON text into a Python dict for you. Never string-match on the serialised form, the raw JSON text. Escaping of Unicode and forward slashes varies, and a regex over it will break on a customer whose name contains an apostrophe.

block.id is the correlation key. It is how the result you send back gets matched to the call. Losing it is how you end up with a 400 that says your tool_result has no corresponding tool_use. A 400 is the API's "bad request" error (§2.9). In the picture, a clerk's report with no slip number cannot be filed, because nobody knows which errand it answers.

6.4 The Agent Loop

The figure is the whole of client-side tool use: one while loop, keyed on stop_reason. In the picture, the loop is you, standing at the window. You carry each slip out to a clerk and each report back in, until the writer hands you a finished letter instead of a slip.

Here it is with a real, if small, tool behind it. Read it in four parts:

  1. get_weather is the real function, backed by a table of two cities. It raises a KeyError for a city it does not know.
  2. TOOLS is what the model sees. IMPLEMENTATIONS maps each tool's name to the function that runs it.
  3. The while loop sends the conversation, and stops as soon as stop_reason is anything but tool_use.
  4. Inside the loop, every tool_use block is run, and its result, or its error, is collected into results.

Watch the last line of the output, which counts the messages. It is the puzzle:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

WEATHER = {"Lisbon": (19, "clear"), "Reykjavik": (4, "sleet")}


def get_weather(city):
    if city not in WEATHER:
        raise KeyError(f"no station for {city!r}")
    degrees, condition = WEATHER[city]
    return f"{degrees}C, {condition}"


TOOLS = [{
    "name": "get_weather",
    "description": "Current weather for a city. Returns Celsius and a condition.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["city"]},
}]
IMPLEMENTATIONS = {"get_weather": get_weather}

messages = [{"role": "user",
             "content": "Compare the weather in Lisbon and Reykjavik."}]

turns = 0
while True:
    turns += 1
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    print(f"turn {turns}: stop_reason={response.stop_reason}")

    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break

    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

    results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type != "tool_use":
            continue
        print(f"  calling {block.name}({block.input})")
        try:
            output = IMPLEMENTATIONS[block.name](**block.input)
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": output})
        except Exception as exc:
            results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                            "content": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                            "is_error": True})

    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

final = next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
print("final:", final)
print("messages in the conversation:", len(messages))

turn 1: stop_reason=tool_use
  calling get_weather({'city': 'Lisbon'})
  calling get_weather({'city': 'Reykjavik'})
turn 2: stop_reason=end_turn
final: Lisbon is 19C and clear; Reykjavik is 4C with sleet. Lisbon is 15 degrees warmer.
messages in the conversation: 3

Line by line:

  • turn 1 ends with tool_use. The model asked for two calls in one turn, one per city, and the loop ran both.
  • turn 2 ends with end_turn. The model had both results, and wrote its answer.
  • final is that answer. The model did the comparison itself, 19 minus 4 is 15 degrees, from the results it was given.
  • messages in the conversation: 3 is the puzzle's count.

Here is the puzzle's answer. The model never fetched anything: your loop ran get_weather, twice. And the conversation holds three messages because the loop appended two to your one:

  1. your question, the user message you started with;
  2. the model's turn with its two calls, appended as an assistant message;
  3. the two results, sent back together as one user message.

The final answer is not appended, because the loop breaks first. In the picture, the file holds your letter, the writer's two slips and the clerk's two reports. The finished letter is in your hand.

That loop needs an API key. The one below does not. It replaces the model with fake_model, a plain function that plays the model's part: it asks for both cities the first time, and answers the second time. Everything else is the same loop, written over plain dicts. At the end it prints the conversation it built, one message per line:

# A stand-in for the model: it asks for both cities, then answers.
def fake_model(messages):
    if messages[-1]["role"] == "user" and isinstance(messages[-1]["content"], str):
        return "tool_use", [
            {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_1", "name": "get_weather",
             "input": {"city": "Lisbon"}},
            {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_2", "name": "get_weather",
             "input": {"city": "Reykjavik"}},
        ]
    return "end_turn", [{"type": "text", "text": "Lisbon is warmer."}]


WEATHER = {"Lisbon": "19C, clear", "Reykjavik": "4C, sleet"}

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Compare Lisbon and Reykjavik."}]
while True:
    stop_reason, content = fake_model(messages)
    if stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": content})
    results = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b["id"],
                "content": WEATHER[b["input"]["city"]]}
               for b in content if b["type"] == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

for i, m in enumerate(messages, 1):
    kinds = m["content"] if isinstance(m["content"], str) else \
        ", ".join(b["type"] for b in m["content"])
    print(f"{i}. {m['role']:<9} {kinds}")
print("final answer:", content[0]["text"])

1. user      Compare Lisbon and Reykjavik.
2. assistant tool_use, tool_use
3. user      tool_result, tool_result
final answer: Lisbon is warmer.

The same three messages, now visible: the question, an assistant turn holding two tool_use blocks, and one user message holding two tool_result blocks. Read the structure rather than the weather.

The assistant turn is appended verbatim. response.content goes back as the assistant message, meaning the SDK objects and not a string you reconstructed. Rebuilding it by hand drops the tool call. The next request is then a conversation in which the model asked for nothing, and you answered anyway. In the picture, you file the writer's own slips, not your summary of them.

All results go back in a single user message. That means one message with all of them, and not one message per result: message 3 above holds both. This matters more than it looks. Splitting them is accepted by the API. But it teaches the model, turn after turn, that its parallel calls are being serialised, run one at a time, and it stops making them. §6.6 measures what that costs.

The loop exits on any stop reason that is not tool_use. end_turn is the happy path. max_tokens, stop_sequence and refusal all also land here, and all need handling, which §2.6 and §14.6 cover. A loop written as while response.stop_reason == "tool_use" with no other branch will silently treat a truncated answer as a final one. Truncated means cut off, because the reply ran out of max_tokens.

There is no stop condition. That is the loop's one real defect, and it is deliberate here so you see it plainly. A model that keeps calling tools keeps this loop running until your bill or your patience ends. In the picture, nobody ever tells the writer "that is enough errands for one letter". §11.3 fixes it properly, with three things:

  • an iteration cap, the most rounds the loop may run;
  • a token budget;
  • a rule for what to do when either is hit.

Here is one shortcut worth knowing before you write this loop a second time. The SDK ships a tool runner, client.beta.messages.tool_runner. Given your tools and their implementations, it drives exactly this loop for you, with a max_iterations cap built in. It is the right default for a straightforward loop, and for most others too.

What it does not do is decide your rules. Whoever drives the loop, three things are still yours to write:

  • a gate, a check that can stop a call before it runs;
  • a budget beyond iterations;
  • a trace, a record of every step.

They fit inside the tool runner. A gate can live in the tool function itself, returning "declined" in place of running. And the runner lets you step through the loop one turn at a time, so your code can log each turn, or stop. Write the whole loop by hand only when you want to own all of it, for example to avoid depending on a beta feature, which the runner still is.

§11 builds the gate, the budget and the trace by hand, so you can see each one, and it is why the loop is worth understanding and not merely calling. The tool runner is the right shortcut once you understand what it is doing on your behalf, and the wrong one before.

The conversation grows by two messages per tool round trip, and you resend all of it every time, as §2.3 showed. A round trip is one request and its reply. In the picture, the file gets thicker with every slip and report, and the writer rereads all of it each time. That is the arithmetic that makes §9 necessary.

6.5 Returning Results, and Returning Failures

A tool_result block has three fields that matter:

  • tool_use_id, the number of the call it answers;
  • content, what the tool returned;
  • is_error, which says the call failed.

The last one separates a robust agent from a fragile one.

The instinct when a tool throws, raising an exception, is to catch it, log it, and drop out of the loop. That is almost always wrong. The model is capable of recovering from a failure it is told about. It can:

  • retry with a corrected argument;
  • try a different tool;
  • tell the user what went wrong.

It can do none of those if the failure never reaches it. In the picture, a clerk who fails an errand still brings back a report saying why. A clerk who simply vanishes leaves the writer waiting.

The example below builds three results: one success and two errors. The two errors report the same failure, written two ways. For each result it prints its size and the start of its content:

def render(result):
    """The three shapes a tool result takes, and what each tells the model."""
    return {k: v for k, v in result.items() if v is not None}


ok = render({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01",
             "content": "19C, clear", "is_error": None})

vague = render({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_02",
                "content": "failed", "is_error": True})

useful = render({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_02",
                 "content": "RateLimitError: weather service allows 10 requests "
                            "per minute. Retry after 42 seconds, or call "
                            "get_cached_weather for a reading up to 1 hour old.",
                 "is_error": True})

for label, block in (("success", ok), ("useless error", vague),
                     ("instructive error", useful)):
    print(f"{label:<18} {len(str(block)):>4} chars  is_error={block.get('is_error', False)}")
    print(f"{'':18} {block['content'][:70]}")

success              75 chars  is_error=False
                   19C, clear
useless error        89 chars  is_error=True
                   failed
instructive error   228 chars  is_error=True
                   RateLimitError: weather service allows 10 requests per minute. Retry a

Line by line:

  • success is 75 characters. Its is_error field was None, and render drops a field set to None, so the result has no is_error at all. The .get falls back to False.
  • useless error says only failed.
  • instructive error is 228 characters. Only its first 70 are printed here, but the whole message goes to the model.

Write errors as instructions, not as status. "failed" tells the model nothing it can act on, so it apologises to the user. The third form does three things:

  • it names the constraint: 10 requests per minute;
  • it gives a number: retry after 42 seconds;
  • it offers an alternative: get_cached_weather.

And the model will take the alternative. This is the single cheapest reliability improvement available in tool use, and it costs a sentence. In the picture, a report that says "the archive is shut until three, and the branch office has yesterday's copy" gets the letter finished. A report that says "failed" gets an apology.

Three rules follow from the same principle.

Return a result for every call, including ones you chose not to run. Say you executed a batch sequentially and stopped after a failure. The skipped calls still need tool_result blocks with is_error: true, and a line saying why ("Not executed: the preceding write_file call failed."). A missing result is a protocol error, a break in the API's rules that it rejects. An explained non-execution is information.

The example below runs three file writes in order. The second is refused, so the third is never run, and it still gets a result:

def write_file(path):
    if path.startswith("/etc/"):
        raise PermissionError(f"{path} is outside the workspace")
    return f"wrote {path}"


calls = [("toolu_1", "notes.txt"), ("toolu_2", "/etc/hosts"),
         ("toolu_3", "todo.txt")]

results, failed = [], False
for call_id, path in calls:
    if failed:
        results.append({"tool_use_id": call_id, "is_error": True,
                        "content": "Not executed: the preceding write_file call failed."})
        continue
    try:
        results.append({"tool_use_id": call_id, "content": write_file(path)})
    except PermissionError as exc:
        failed = True
        results.append({"tool_use_id": call_id, "is_error": True,
                        "content": f"PermissionError: {exc}"})

print("calls:", len(calls), " results:", len(results))
for r in results:
    print(r["tool_use_id"], "error" if r.get("is_error") else "ok   ", r["content"])

calls: 3  results: 3
toolu_1 ok    wrote notes.txt
toolu_2 error PermissionError: /etc/hosts is outside the workspace
toolu_3 error Not executed: the preceding write_file call failed.

Three calls, three results. toolu_1 succeeded. toolu_2 was refused, and its error says why. toolu_3 never ran, and its result says so, so the model will not assume todo.txt was written.

Do not leak internals into the error. The content goes into the context window and, through the model's reply, potentially to the user. A stack trace with your table names in it is both a token cost and a disclosure. A stack trace is the list of function calls Python prints when an exception escapes. §14.4 treats this as the injection surface it is, a place where outside text reaches the model.

An invalid tool call is a description bug first. If the model omits a required parameter, the honest fix is a clearer schema and description. Returning "Error: missing required 'city'" does work, because the model retries two or three times with corrections. But you are paying a round trip to compensate for a sentence you did not write. §6.8 removes the failure mode entirely, for the cases where that is worth doing.

6.6 Parallel Tool Use

A single assistant turn can contain several tool_use blocks. You saw it in §6.4, where one turn asked for both cities. This is on by default. It is the difference between an agent that feels responsive and one that does not. In the picture, the writer hands out three slips at once, instead of sending one and waiting for its report before writing the next.

The comparison is not subtle. The cost of each serialised call is a model round trip, and not a function call. A model round trip is a whole request to the API and its reply, and it takes far longer than a lookup.

The example below adds up the time for three lookups, done three ways. The numbers are invented but sized like real ones: 1,400 ms for a model turn, and 180 to 260 ms per tool. ms means milliseconds, thousandths of a second:

LATENCY_MS = {"model_turn": 1400, "search_orders": 220,
              "get_customer": 180, "get_shipment": 260}
CALLS = ["search_orders", "get_customer", "get_shipment"]

# Serial: the model asks for one tool, gets the answer, asks for the next.
serial = 0
for call in CALLS:
    serial += LATENCY_MS["model_turn"] + LATENCY_MS[call]
serial += LATENCY_MS["model_turn"]          # the final answer

# Parallel: one turn proposes all three, you run them concurrently, one turn answers.
parallel = LATENCY_MS["model_turn"] + max(LATENCY_MS[c] for c in CALLS) \
    + LATENCY_MS["model_turn"]

# Parallel calls, but executed one after another by your loop.
parallel_serial_exec = LATENCY_MS["model_turn"] + sum(LATENCY_MS[c] for c in CALLS) \
    + LATENCY_MS["model_turn"]

for name, ms in (("serial (one call per turn)", serial),
                 ("parallel calls, serial execution", parallel_serial_exec),
                 ("parallel calls, concurrent execution", parallel)):
    print(f"{name:<38} {ms:>5} ms  {ms / parallel:>4.1f}x")

serial (one call per turn)              6260 ms   2.0x
parallel calls, serial execution        3460 ms   1.1x
parallel calls, concurrent execution    3060 ms   1.0x

Line by line:

  • Serial takes 6,260 ms: four model turns, 4 × 1,400 = 5,600 ms, plus the three tools, 220 + 180 + 260 = 660 ms.
  • Parallel calls with serial execution take 3,460 ms: two model turns, 2,800 ms, plus the same 660 ms of tools.
  • Parallel calls with concurrent execution take 3,060 ms: two model turns, plus only the slowest tool, 260 ms. Concurrent means the three tools run at the same time.

The saving comes from collapsing model turns, and not from the tools being fast. Even executing the three calls one after another inside your loop captures most of it, because the model round trip dominates. Concurrency in your executor, the part of your loop that runs the functions, is the last increment.

The API does not prescribe an execution order. Running the calls concurrently is your choice. It is usually right for independent, read-only operations, the ones that only look things up. It is the wrong choice for tools with side effects, shared state or ordering requirements. A side effect is a change the call makes in the world, such as writing a file or sending a message. Run those sequentially, and stop at the first failure, as the file-writing example in §6.5 did.

Two of the Anthropic-schema toolsets, computer and browser, are stricter still. When several of their member calls arrive in one turn, they must be run sequentially, in the order given, and abandoned at the first failure. The reason: a click that lands after a page has changed means something different from the click that was requested.

The formatting rules are absolute, and they produce clear errors when broken:

  • one tool_result per tool_use;
  • matched by tool_use_id;
  • all in the same user message;
  • every tool_result block placed before any text content in that message.

The helper below builds that user message for two results and an extra note. The note is ordinary text you want the model to read, so it goes last:

def build_user_turn(calls, outcomes, note=None):
    """tool_result blocks first, then any text. The order is required."""
    blocks = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call_id,
               "content": outcomes[call_id]} for call_id in calls]
    if note:
        blocks.append({"type": "text", "text": note})
    return {"role": "user", "content": blocks}


turn = build_user_turn(
    ["toolu_a", "toolu_b"],
    {"toolu_a": "3 orders", "toolu_b": "customer c_8814, gold tier"},
    note="Prioritise the oldest unshipped order.",
)
for block in turn["content"]:
    print(block["type"], "->", block.get("content", block.get("text")))

tool_result -> 3 orders
tool_result -> customer c_8814, gold tier
text -> Prioritise the oldest unshipped order.

The two tool_result blocks come first, in the order of the calls, and the text comes after them.

If the model has stopped calling tools in parallel, check two things, in this order:

  1. whether your loop has been splitting results across messages;
  2. disable_parallel_tool_use, which lives inside tool_choice and is discussed next.

6.7 Steering the Choice with tool_choice

By default, the model decides whether to call anything at all. tool_choice overrides that, and it has four forms. In the picture, it is a note you pin to the request: "use a slip if you like", "you must send some slip", "send this exact slip", or "no slips this time".

The request below uses the third form. It forces record_sentiment, a tool that is not really an action: it only records a judgement, so forcing it makes the model hand back a typed answer. Sentiment is whether a message reads as positive, neutral or negative, and confidence is a number for how sure the model is:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "record_sentiment",
    "description": "Record the sentiment of a customer message.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "sentiment": {"type": "string",
                          "enum": ["positive", "neutral", "negative"]},
            "confidence": {"type": "number"},
        },
        "required": ["sentiment", "confidence"],
    },
}]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    tools=TOOLS,
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "record_sentiment"},
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "The delivery was three days late and nobody replied."}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
print("sentiment  :", call.input["sentiment"])
print("confidence :", call.input["confidence"])

stop_reason: tool_use
sentiment  : negative
confidence : 0.92

Line by line:

  • stop_reason is tool_use: the model stopped to make the forced call.
  • sentiment is negative, one of the three values the schema's enum, its fixed list of allowed values, permits.
  • confidence is 0.92. Nothing in this schema says it must lie between 0 and 1. The model chose a sensible number, but the schema did not require one.

Here are the four forms side by side:

{"type": "auto"}
The default. The model calls a tool if it judges one useful, otherwise it answers in prose. Right for anything conversational.
{"type": "any"}
Some tool must be called, the model picks which. Useful when every path through the turn should end in a structured action, such as a router that must dispatch to one of several handlers.
{"type": "tool", "name": …}
This exact tool must be called. This is the classifier-and-extractor pattern above: the "tool" is not an action at all, it is a schema, and forcing it turns the model into a typed function. §4 shows the modern alternative and when to prefer it.
{"type": "none"}
No tool may be called on this turn, though the definitions stay in context. Useful for a final "now summarise what you found" turn that must not start new work.

tool_choice also carries disable_parallel_tool_use. It caps how many calls one turn may make:

  • Set with auto or any, it limits the turn to at most one call.
  • Set with a forced tool, it gives you exactly one.

Reach for it when your executor genuinely cannot handle concurrent calls. Be aware that you are paying §6.6's arithmetic to get there: every call becomes its own model turn.

One trap is worth naming: forcing a tool suppresses the model's ability to say "I cannot". A forced record_sentiment on an empty message still records a sentiment. If "no answer" is a legitimate outcome, it has to be representable inside the schema, such as an enum value of "insufficient_evidence", because the forced call removes the model's other way of telling you. In the picture, you told the writer "send this exact slip", so the writer sends it even when there is nothing to put in the boxes, unless one box says "not enough to go on".

6.8 Strict Tool Use

An ordinary tool schema is guidance. The model usually produces conforming arguments, ones that fit the schema. But occasionally it does one of these:

  • omits a required field that looked optional;
  • passes "3", a string, where you asked for a number;
  • invents a property.

Your code then has to validate, checking the arguments itself, and your loop has to round-trip an error.

strict: true on the tool definition removes that class of failure, because inputs are guaranteed to validate against the schema. You met the mechanism in §4.6: the arguments are generated through a grammar built from your schema, so an invalid one cannot be written. In the picture, it is the stencil from §4, laid over the request slip.

The request below declares a refund tool with strict set, and asks for a refund of an order priced in euros:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "create_refund",
    "description": "Issue a refund against an order.",
    "strict": True,
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "order_id": {"type": "string"},
            "amount_cents": {"type": "integer"},
            "reason": {"type": "string",
                       "enum": ["damaged", "late", "duplicate"]},
        },
        "required": ["order_id", "amount_cents", "reason"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
}]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=512,
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Refund order ord_5512 in full — it arrived damaged. "
                          "The order was 42.50 EUR."}],
)

call = next(b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use")
print("input      :", call.input)
print("amount type:", type(call.input["amount_cents"]).__name__)
print("reason ok  :", call.input["reason"] in {"damaged", "late", "duplicate"})

input      : {'order_id': 'ord_5512', 'amount_cents': 4250, 'reason': 'damaged'}
amount type: int
reason ok  : True

Line by line:

  • input holds the three required fields, and nothing else.
  • amount_cents is 4250, an int. The model turned 42.50 EUR into cents, because the schema asked for a whole number of cents.
  • reason is damaged, one of the three allowed values.

There are two requirements, and they are the ones people miss:

  1. strict is a top-level field on the tool definition, alongside name and description. It is not something you put inside tool_choice.
  2. The schema must set additionalProperties: false and list its required fields, because a schema that permits anything cannot guarantee anything.

Use it wherever a bad argument is expensive. Examples are a refund, a write, a deletion and an outbound message. Skip it where the tool is a search whose arguments are advisory, and a slightly odd query is harmless.

It is not free of consequences:

  • Strict tools are incompatible with programmatic tool calling (§7.6), where the model writes code that calls your tools.
  • Constraining generation has a measurable effect on how the model phrases things around the call.

Neither is a reason to avoid it on the tools that change state.

6.9 What a Tool Surface Costs

A tool surface is the whole set of tools one request declares. Tool definitions are context, and that means three things:

  • every request carries all of them;
  • they are billed as input tokens every time;
  • they occupy the window that your conversation, your retrieved documents and your system prompt also want.

Managing tool context means deciding which definitions are present, and what their results leave behind. It is the constraint that decides how big a tool surface can get. Tool context is also the part of the window you control most directly. That is why it is the first place to look when a request is larger than expected. In the picture, it is the pile of blank slip forms on the writer's desk: the writer rereads every one before every letter, and you pay for the reading.

The example below sizes four tool surfaces. It uses a rough rule, about one token per four characters, and two sizes of definition: a simple one of 320 characters and a complex one of 1,150. Then it prices each at 500 requests a day for 30 days:

# Rough but honest sizing: a serialised tool definition costs about a token per
# four characters. Real counts come from count_tokens (see 2.8); this is the
# back-of-envelope that tells you whether to bother.
def approx_tokens(chars):
    return round(chars / 4)


SMALL = 320     # a two-parameter tool with a four-sentence description
LARGE = 1150    # a nested schema, an enum of 20, three input_examples

for n_tools, size, label in ((5, SMALL, "5 simple tools"),
                             (20, SMALL, "20 simple tools"),
                             (20, LARGE, "20 complex tools"),
                             (120, SMALL, "120 simple tools")):
    per_request = approx_tokens(n_tools * size)
    # 500 requests a day, 30 days, at Opus input pricing of $5 per million tokens.
    monthly = per_request * 500 * 30 / 1_000_000 * 5
    share = per_request / 200_000 * 100
    print(f"{label:<18} {per_request:>7,} tokens/request  "
          f"{share:>5.1f}% of a 200k window  ${monthly:>7,.2f}/month")

5 simple tools         400 tokens/request    0.2% of a 200k window  $  30.00/month
20 simple tools      1,600 tokens/request    0.8% of a 200k window  $ 120.00/month
20 complex tools     5,750 tokens/request    2.9% of a 200k window  $ 431.25/month
120 simple tools     9,600 tokens/request    4.8% of a 200k window  $ 720.00/month

Take the first row. Five tools of 320 characters is 1,600 characters, about 400 tokens. At 500 requests a day for 30 days, that is 6,000,000 tokens, and at $5 per million that is $30.00 a month. The other rows scale the same way.

The pricing here is ordinary input-token pricing. There is no separate charge for declaring a tool, so this table is entirely a question of size. Read the two middle rows together: the same twenty tools cost 1,600 or 5,750 tokens, more than three and a half times as much, depending only on how big each definition is. Twenty complex definitions cost about as much as seventy-two simple ones. So "how many tools" is the wrong question, and "how much schema" is the right one.

And note what the table does not show. Even the 120-tool row is under five per cent of a 200k window: 9,600 tokens out of 200,000. Context pressure is rarely the reason a large tool surface fails.

The reason it fails is selection accuracy, how often the model picks the right tool. The model is choosing from a longer list of similar-sounding options. A wrong choice costs a whole round trip, plus whatever the wrong tool did. That cost does not appear in any of these columns, which is exactly why sizing a surface by tokens alone is reassuring and misleading. In the picture, a writer facing 120 blank forms, many with similar titles, grabs the wrong one more often, however cheap the paper is.

The grid below has five levers, and they compose: you can use several together. Four of them shrink the surface or make it cheaper. The fifth, fine-grained tool streaming, instead speeds up one large argument. A few terms first:

  • Tool search lets the model look up a tool's definition only when it needs it. BM25 is a keyword-ranking method, taught in §10.3.
  • Prompt caching lets the API reuse the start of a request it has seen recently, at a lower price (§1.3, §9.3). A stable prefix is a start that does not change between requests.
  • Streaming sends a reply in pieces as it is written (§2.7). Buffering means holding the pieces back until they are complete.
  • Context editing removes old content from a conversation as it grows (§9.6).
Fewer, better tools
Consolidate. Six tools with an action parameter beat eighteen near-identical ones. Always try this first; it is free and it improves selection accuracy rather than merely paying for it.
Tool search
Load definitions on demand. Mark tools defer_loading: true and add a search tool; the model discovers what it needs by regex or BM25 instead of carrying everything. §7.5 builds it. Scales to thousands.
Prompt caching
Stop paying repeatedly for the same definitions. Tools render first in the request, before system and messages, which makes them the ideal stable prefix. §9.3 does this properly, including the trap that a changing tool list invalidates everything after it.
Fine-grained tool streaming
For one large argument. Fine-grained tool streaming sends tool inputs without buffering or JSON validation, so a tool taking a long string starts arriving sooner. It trades the guarantee that the JSON is well formed for latency, so validate what arrives.
Context editing
Clear old tool results, which in a long agent run outweigh the definitions many times over. §9.6.

Note that the second and third options pull in opposite directions, and you should know which you are choosing:

  • Deferred loading keeps tokens out of the request.
  • Caching makes their presence cheap.

For a stable surface of twenty tools used every turn, caching wins. For a surface of four hundred, where any given conversation touches three, search wins. In the picture: if every letter needs the same twenty forms, keep them on the desk and pay the cheap rate for rereading them. If there are four hundred and each letter needs three, keep them in a drawer with an index.

6.10 Designing a Tool Surface

The mechanics above are quickly learned. What separates an agent that works from one that thrashes, lurching from one wrong tool to the next, is the design of the surface. The guidance is unglamorous.

Consolidate related operations. create_pr, review_pr, merge_pr and close_pr should be one pull_request tool with an action enum. A PR, or pull request, is a proposed change to code on a site such as GitHub. Four similar names are four opportunities to pick the wrong one, while one tool with an enum is a choice the schema itself constrains. In the picture, one slip form with four tick boxes beats four forms with nearly the same title.

Namespace by service. Use github_list_prs and slack_send_message, and not list_prs and send_message. The namespace here is the prefix that names the service a tool belongs to. This matters immediately when two services both have a search. And it matters enormously once tool search is involved, because the prefix is what makes a query selective.

Return high-signal results, not payloads. A tool that hands back the whole database row, when the model needs six fields, has spent most of its tokens on internal identifiers the model cannot use. Worse, it buries the useful part. Two rules:

  • Return stable, semantic identifiers, such as a slug or a UUID, and not opaque internal handles. A slug is a short readable name, such as ord_88213. A UUID is a long random identifier that never changes. An opaque handle is a bare number that only means something inside your own database.
  • Return only the fields the model needs to decide what to do next.

The example below compares one order returned both ways: the raw database record, and a shaped result with six fields. It uses §6.9's rough rule of four characters per token:

FULL_RECORD = {
    "id": 88213, "uuid": "c1f2...", "created_at": "2026-08-21T09:14:02.113Z",
    "updated_at": "2026-08-25T11:02:44.882Z", "customer_id": 4471,
    "customer_uuid": "9ab3...", "billing_address_id": 20114,
    "shipping_address_id": 20115, "currency": "EUR", "subtotal_cents": 4250,
    "tax_cents": 978, "shipping_cents": 499, "total_cents": 5727,
    "status": "shipped", "carrier_code": "DHL_EXPRESS",
    "tracking_number": "JJD0099887766", "warehouse_id": 7, "channel": "web",
    "internal_notes": None, "risk_score": 0.02, "fraud_review": False,
}

SHAPED = {
    "order": "ord_88213", "customer": "cus_4471", "status": "shipped",
    "total": "57.27 EUR", "carrier": "DHL_EXPRESS",
    "tracking": "JJD0099887766",
}

for label, payload in (("raw record", FULL_RECORD), ("shaped result", SHAPED)):
    chars = len(str(payload))
    print(f"{label:<15} {len(payload):>2} fields  {chars:>4} chars  "
          f"~{round(chars / 4):>3} tokens")

saved = round((len(str(FULL_RECORD)) - len(str(SHAPED))) / 4)
print(f"\nsaved per call: ~{saved} tokens")
print(f"over a 12-call agent run: ~{saved * 12} tokens")

raw record      21 fields   521 chars  ~130 tokens
shaped result    6 fields   144 chars  ~ 36 tokens

saved per call: ~94 tokens
over a 12-call agent run: ~1128 tokens

Line by line:

  • The raw record has 21 fields, and costs about 130 tokens.
  • The shaped result has 6 fields, and costs about 36.
  • That saves about 94 tokens per call, and 1,128 over an agent run of 12 calls. An agent run is one task worked through the loop from start to finish.

The shaped result is also easier for the model to read: 57.27 EUR instead of four separate amounts in cents, and one customer name instead of two customer numbers.

Prefer the trained-in schema when one exists. If your tool is "run a shell command", use the bash tool, and do not invent execute_command. The bash tool's signature is one the model has seen thousands of successful trajectories through. A trajectory is one run of a task, step by step. If it is "edit this file", use text_editor. The model has seen thousands of successful trajectories through those exact signatures, while a custom equivalent starts from nothing. In the picture, it is the office's standard printed form against one you drew yourself. §11 uses both.

Put the authorisation in the executor, never in the description. Authorisation is the check that this user may do this thing. A description that says "only use this for orders belonging to the current user" is a request, and not a control. The check belongs in the function, where the session is in scope. The session is what your server knows about who is logged in. In the picture, the clerk checks the customer's ID before handing over a file, whatever the slip says.

The example below holds two orders, owned by two customers. The session belongs to cus_A, and the code asks for three orders:

class Forbidden(Exception):
    pass


ORDERS = {"ord_1": {"customer": "cus_A", "total": 4250},
          "ord_2": {"customer": "cus_B", "total": 1195}}


def get_order(order_id, *, session_customer):
    order = ORDERS.get(order_id)
    if order is None:
        raise KeyError(f"no order {order_id!r}")
    if order["customer"] != session_customer:
        raise Forbidden(f"order {order_id} does not belong to this account")
    return order


for requested in ("ord_1", "ord_2", "ord_9"):
    try:
        print(f"{requested}: {get_order(requested, session_customer='cus_A')}")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"{requested}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")

ord_1: {'customer': 'cus_A', 'total': 4250}
ord_2: Forbidden: order ord_2 does not belong to this account
ord_9: KeyError: "no order 'ord_9'"

Line by line:

  • ord_1 belongs to cus_A, so it is returned.
  • ord_2 exists, but belongs to cus_B, so Forbidden is raised.
  • ord_9 does not exist, so KeyError is raised. Its message prints inside an extra pair of quotes, because a KeyError shows its message the way Python writes a string literal.

The model is free to ask for ord_2, and the executor is what makes asking pointless. Treat every argument as untrusted input from a component that has read your users' text, because that is exactly what it is. A user can write anything, and the model may pass some of it on. §14.4 develops this into the full injection model.

Back to the puzzle one last time. The model in §6.4 fetched nothing: it wrote two slips. Your loop ran them, and appended the slips and the reports, and that is where the third message came from. Everything in this section follows from that one fact: the model proposes, and your code decides what happens.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 — Fix a tool definition. The definition below is what a working engineer's first draft usually looks like. Rewrite it, and list the specific failures each change prevents.

tool = {
    "name": "lookup",
    "description": "Looks up a user.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"q": {"type": "string"}},
    },
}
Solution

There are five separate defects, and each maps to a failure you would see in production.

fixed = {
    "name": "directory_find_user",
    "description": (
        "Find a user in the staff directory by email address, employee ID, or "
        "full name. Use this when you need a user's team, manager or office "
        "before taking any other action on their behalf. Returns at most 10 "
        "matches, each with employee ID, full name, team and office. It does "
        "NOT return contact details, salary, or employment history, and it does "
        "not search customers — use crm_find_customer for those. If more than "
        "10 users match, narrow the query rather than paginating."
    ),
    "strict": True,
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "query": {
                "type": "string",
                "description": "Email, employee ID (E-prefixed, e.g. E-4471), "
                               "or full name. Partial names are matched.",
            },
            "field": {
                "type": "string",
                "enum": ["email", "employee_id", "name", "any"],
                "description": "Which field to search. Use 'any' when unsure.",
            },
        },
        "required": ["query", "field"],
        "additionalProperties": False,
    },
    "input_examples": [
        {"query": "ana.silva@example.com", "field": "email"},
        {"query": "E-4471", "field": "employee_id"},
    ],
}

print("name    :", fixed["name"])
print("required:", fixed["input_schema"]["required"])
print("desc has 'does NOT':", "does NOT" in fixed["description"])
print("strict  :", fixed["strict"])

name    : directory_find_user
required: ['query', 'field']
desc has 'does NOT': True
strict  : True
