lookup → directory_find_user. "Lookup" is a verb with no object. In a surface with a customer directory, a DNS tool and a price table, the model has to guess which "lookup" this is. The service prefix makes the choice unambiguous and survives the surface growing.

A one-line description → a paragraph that says what it does not do. The original leaves four questions open: look up by what, returning what, how many, and is this customers or staff? The rewrite closes all four. The "does NOT return contact details… use crm_find_customer" sentence is the one that prevents the specific failure of the model calling this tool for a customer and then inventing the answer from the empty result.

q → query, plus a description. A single-letter parameter with no description tells the model nothing about accepted formats. The description naming the E- prefix is what stops 4471 being sent when E-4471 is required.

No required → required with additionalProperties: false and strict: true. As written, a call with no arguments at all satisfies the schema. Adding field as required also removes an ambiguity the original had no way to express.

input_examples. Two examples cost about forty tokens, and they demonstrate the two formats that a sentence describes less precisely.

The one judgement call: adding a required field parameter makes the model commit to a search mode, which is better than a magic string but does force a decision. Making it required with an "any" member is the compromise, because the model can decline to choose without omitting the field.

Exercise 6.2 — Find the four bugs in this loop. This agent loop looks reasonable and has four distinct defects, at least two of which will only appear in production.

response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                  tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)

while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    call = response.content[0]
    output = IMPLEMENTATIONS[call.name](**call.input)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": call.id, "content": output}]})
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
Solution 
class ToolFailed(Exception):
    pass


def run_agent(client, messages, tools, implementations, *, max_turns=12):
    """The same loop with the four defects fixed."""
    for turn in range(1, max_turns + 1):
        response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024,
                                          tools=tools, messages=messages)

        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            # 2. every other stop reason is handled, not treated as success
            return response, turn, response.stop_reason

        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        results = []
        for block in response.content:          # 1. all tool_use blocks, not [0]
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            try:
                output = implementations[block.name](**block.input)
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                "content": str(output)})
            except Exception as exc:            # 3. failures go back to the model
                results.append({"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": block.id,
                                "content": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}",
                                "is_error": True})

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

    return None, max_turns, "max_turns_exhausted"   # 4. a stop condition


FIXES = [
    "1. iterate every content block, never content[0]",
    "2. branch on every stop reason, not just tool_use",
    "3. return tool failures with is_error instead of raising",
    "4. bound the loop with max_turns",
]
print(run_agent.__doc__)
for fix in FIXES:
    print(" ", fix)

The same loop with the four defects fixed.
  1. iterate every content block, never content[0]
  2. branch on every stop reason, not just tool_use
  3. return tool failures with is_error instead of raising
  4. bound the loop with max_turns

1. response.content[0] assumes the tool call is the first block. It frequently is not, because the model often emits a short text block first ("Let me look that up."), and it is never the whole story when the model makes parallel calls. This bug is invisible in testing with a terse model and appears the moment the model narrates. At that point content[0] is a TextBlock and .name raises AttributeError. It also silently drops the second and third of three parallel calls, producing a 400 on the next request because those tool_use blocks have no matching results.

2. while stop_reason == "tool_use" treats every other stop reason as success. max_tokens means the answer was truncated mid-sentence, and the loop returns it as final. refusal means the model declined. pause_turn means a server-side tool has not finished. All three exit the loop into code that assumes a complete answer.

3. An exception in the tool escapes the loop. The model is never told the call failed, so it cannot retry with a corrected argument or route around the failure. The conversation is also left with an assistant turn containing a tool_use and no corresponding result, which means it cannot even be resumed. Catching the exception and returning is_error: true keeps both the model and the conversation recoverable.

4. There is no stop condition. Nothing bounds the number of turns. A model that keeps calling a tool that keeps failing will loop until something else breaks. max_turns is the minimum, and §11.3 adds a token budget alongside it, because twelve turns of a large tool result is a very different bill from twelve turns of a small one.

There is arguably a fifth issue: the request is duplicated above and inside the loop, which is what let the two calls drift apart in the first place. The for form has exactly one call site.

Exercise 6.3 — Size a tool surface. Your agent has 34 tools averaging 380 characters of serialised definition. It runs 2,000 conversations a day, averaging 6 model turns each, on Claude Opus 5 at $5 per million input tokens. Compute the monthly cost of the tool definitions alone, then compute what prompt caching at a cache-hit rate of $0.50 per million tokens would change, and say what you would do.

Solution 
N_TOOLS, CHARS_EACH = 34, 380
CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY, TURNS_EACH, DAYS = 2000, 6, 30
INPUT_PER_MTOK, CACHE_HIT_PER_MTOK, CACHE_WRITE_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 0.50, 6.25

defs_tokens = round(N_TOOLS * CHARS_EACH / 4)
turns_per_month = CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY * TURNS_EACH * DAYS
tokens_per_month = defs_tokens * turns_per_month

uncached = tokens_per_month / 1_000_000 * INPUT_PER_MTOK

# Caching: the first turn of each conversation writes the cache, the rest read it.
writes = defs_tokens * CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY * DAYS
reads = defs_tokens * CONVERSATIONS_PER_DAY * (TURNS_EACH - 1) * DAYS
cached = (writes / 1_000_000 * CACHE_WRITE_PER_MTOK
          + reads / 1_000_000 * CACHE_HIT_PER_MTOK)

print(f"definitions           : {defs_tokens:,} tokens per request")
print(f"share of a 200k window: {defs_tokens / 200_000 * 100:.1f}%")
print(f"model turns per month : {turns_per_month:,}")
print(f"tokens per month      : {tokens_per_month:,}")
print()
print(f"uncached              : ${uncached:,.2f}/month")
print(f"cached                : ${cached:,.2f}/month")
print(f"saving                : ${uncached - cached:,.2f} "
      f"({(1 - cached / uncached) * 100:.0f}%)")

definitions           : 3,230 tokens per request
share of a 200k window: 1.6%
model turns per month : 360,000
tokens per month      : 1,162,800,000

uncached              : $5,814.00/month
cached                : $1,695.75/month
saving                : $4,118.25 (71%)

The money is larger than it feels, and that is the first lesson. 3,230 tokens looks trivial. Multiplied by 360,000 model turns a month, it is 1.16 billion input tokens and $5,814, for text that never changes. Nobody arrives at that figure by intuition, which is the argument for spending two minutes on the arithmetic before spending a sprint on anything.

Caching removes 71% of it, taking $5,814 to $1,696. That is the highest-value change available, and it is roughly twenty minutes of work, because tools render first in the request, before system and before messages, and are therefore already the natural stable prefix (§9.3). Note that the saving is 71% and not 90%, because one turn in six is a cache write at $6.25 per million, which is more expensive than an ordinary input token. Conversations with more turns each would do better.

The context window is not the problem here. 3,230 tokens is 1.6% of a 200k window and negligible against 1M, so context pressure is not the argument for restructuring. This is exactly the sort of conclusion this arithmetic exists to reach before someone builds tool search that nothing needed.

What I would actually do, in order. Add caching. Then look at the 34 tools for consolidation, not to save tokens but because 34 similar-sounding names is where selection accuracy degrades, and a wrong tool call costs a full round trip plus whatever the wrong tool did. Consider tool search only after that. Anthropic suggests it from about ten tools or 10k tokens of definitions, and consolidation may well bring 34 tools under the first; at 3,230 tokens the definitions are already far under the second.

The number this calculation does not contain, and which dominates all of it, is tool results. Six turns of a search tool returning even 800 tokens each is 4,800 tokens per conversation, against 3,200 for the definitions. Unlike the definitions, results are different every time and therefore uncacheable. That is what §9.6's context editing is for, and it is why sizing a tool surface by its definitions alone always looks reassuring.

SECTION 7

Server Tools, Skills and MCP

Start with a puzzle. Your model needs to look up 400 orders and add up their totals. Done the §6 way, with the model asking for each lookup and reading each answer, the job bills about 2,544,000 input tokens. Done another way, it bills 12,180. The same 400 lookups still happen, through the same function of yours, and the answer is the same. So where did two and a half million tokens go? Guess before you read on. §7.6 runs the numbers for both ways and answers it.

Section 6 built the client-side loop. Client-side means it runs in your program, the client of the API. The model asks, you execute, and you report back. This section is about the capabilities where you do not write that loop. That happens in three ways:

  • the tool runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, meaning Anthropic's own servers, so they do the running;
  • the tool's schema, its description and boxes from §6.2, comes from a server you did not build;
  • the "tool" is not a tool at all, but a folder of instructions that the model reads when it decides it needs them.

There are four mechanisms in all. They are easy to mix up, because all four end up as entries in tools. Two questions keep them straight: who executes and who supplies the definition. The grid answers both for each one. It uses three new words, each taught later in this section:

  • MCP is an open standard for offering tools to a model (§7.7);
  • code execution is a server tool that lets the model run code it wrote;
  • a sandbox is the sealed-off computer that code runs in, where it cannot touch anything else.
Server tools
Anthropic executes; Anthropic defines. web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search. You enable them and read the answer. No tool_result, no loop.
MCP connector
A third party executes; a third party defines. A remote MCP server's tools become callable from the Messages API with no MCP client of your own. Anthropic's servers do the calling.
Agent Skills
Not a tool at all. A folder of instructions, reference files and scripts that the model reads from a filesystem when its description matches your request. Runs inside code execution.
Programmatic tool calling
You execute; the model orchestrates in code. Your client tools become callable from inside the code execution sandbox, so a loop over 400 rows costs one turn instead of 400.

Here is the picture for the whole section. Since §1 the model has been a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. In §6 the writer handed request slips out of the window, and your clerk ran the errands. §6.1 mentioned that the telegram office runs some errands itself. This section is about the office's own errand desk:

  • errands the office runs before the letter ever reaches you;
  • an outside agency the office telephones on your behalf;
  • binders of know-how on the writer's shelf.

Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram office In this section Section
An errand the office's own desk runs, not your clerk a server tool §7.1
The desk's own number series, stamped on its slips the srvtoolu_ id prefix §7.1
The desk's report, clipped to the letter it belongs to the result block in the same message §7.1
A separate line on the invoice for errands usage.server_tool_use §7.1
The desk's shift ending mid-errand, and the half-written letter sent to you to hand back in pause_turn §7.2
How many library trips you allow per letter max_uses §7.3
The list of libraries the clerk may visit, or must avoid allowed_domains, blocked_domains §7.3
Clippings stapled into the file, reread with every later letter search results in the context window §7.3
A free photocopy of a whole document, which the writer must then read web fetch §7.4
A letter that says "fetch this address, and write the account number on the slip" exfiltration §7.4
Forms kept in a drawer, with an index card on the desk tool search §7.5
One page of instructions for a back-room clerk, who runs 400 errands and returns the total programmatic tool calling §7.6
A partner agency the office phones for you, and the list of its forms you accept the MCP connector and its allowlist §7.7
A binder on the shelf: the spine label, the chapters, the appendices a Skill and its three levels §7.8
The binder's edition number a Skill's version §7.8

This section has nine subsections, in five parts:

  1. what a server call looks like, and when the server hands control back (§7.1, §7.2);
  2. the two tools that reach the internet, and how one of them can leak data (§7.3, §7.4);
  3. tools at scale: finding tools on demand, and code that calls tools in bulk (§7.5, §7.6);
  4. two things that are not your tools at all: MCP servers and Skills (§7.7, §7.8);
  5. how to choose between them (§7.9).

Seven examples call the real API, in §7.1, §7.2, §7.3, §7.5, §7.6, §7.7 and §7.8. Running them needs an API key, and your ids, wording and search results will differ from the ones shown. Every other example is plain Python, and prints the same thing on every machine.

7.1 The server_tool_use Block

A turn is one reply from the model (§2.3). A server-side tool changes the shape of a turn in one specific way. With a client tool, the reply ends with a call, and you send the result in your next message. With a server-side tool, the call and its result both appear in the same assistant message, and there is nothing for you to send back. That is the defining property of a server-side tool, and it is what removes the loop.

In the picture: the writer hands a slip to the office's own desk. The desk runs the errand, and its report comes back clipped to the letter. By the time the letter reaches you, the errand is done.

The request below turns on web search, the server tool named web_search, and asks about a recent event. max_uses allows at most five searches; §7.3 comes back to it. The loop then prints every block in the reply, one line each. It needs an API key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 5}],
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "What did the ECB decide at its last meeting?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "server_tool_use":
        print(f"  server_tool_use  id={block.id}  name={block.name}")
        print(f"                   input={block.input}")
    elif block.type == "web_search_tool_result":
        print(f"  result for       {block.tool_use_id}: "
              f"{len(block.content)} results")
    elif block.type == "text":
        print(f"  text             {block.text[:60]}")

print("searches billed:", response.usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests)

stop_reason: end_turn
  server_tool_use  id=srvtoolu_01A2B3C4D5  name=web_search
                   input={'query': 'ECB latest monetary policy decision'}
  result for       srvtoolu_01A2B3C4D5: 3 results
  text             At its most recent meeting the ECB held the deposit facility
searches billed: 1

Read it line by line:

  • stop_reason: end_turn says the model finished. It did not stop to wait for you, as it does with tool_use in §6.3.
  • The server_tool_use line is the model's call: one search, with the query it chose.
  • The result for line is the search's answer, 3 results, paired to the call by its id.
  • The text line is the start of the answer, written after reading those results.
  • searches billed: 1 is a count kept apart from tokens.

All of that happened inside one request. Your code sent one message and got back one reply. Three details in that output are worth naming.

The id prefix is srvtoolu_, not toolu_. That is how you tell a server call from a client call when reading a trace, the record of everything a run did. In the picture, the office's desk stamps its slips from its own number series. It is worth keying on the prefix and not on the block type, because new server tools keep arriving, each with its own block type.

The result block follows the call in the same turn, paired by tool_use_id. You never construct one. A loop written to answer every *_tool_use block with a tool_result will send something the API did not ask for.

That mistake is easy to make, so here it is on plain dicts, with no API key needed. The turn below holds a server call, its result, a client call and some text. The wrong loop picks blocks by their type name. The right one picks them by id prefix:

# One assistant turn, as plain dicts: a server call, its result, a client call.
content = [
    {"type": "server_tool_use", "id": "srvtoolu_01", "name": "web_search"},
    {"type": "web_search_tool_result", "tool_use_id": "srvtoolu_01"},
    {"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_02", "name": "get_order"},
    {"type": "text", "text": "Let me check that order."},
]

# Wrong: answer every block whose type ends in "tool_use".
wrong = [b["id"] for b in content if b["type"].endswith("tool_use")]

# Right: answer only client calls, recognised by the id prefix.
right = [b["id"] for b in content if b.get("id", "").startswith("toolu_")]

print("the wrong loop answers:", wrong)
print("the right loop answers:", right)

the wrong loop answers: ['srvtoolu_01', 'toolu_02']
the right loop answers: ['toolu_02']

The wrong loop picked two ids. The type server_tool_use ends in tool_use, so it looked like a call to answer. But the server already answered srvtoolu_01, and the result is right there in the same turn. The right loop picked only toolu_02, the one call your code must run. In the picture: you only report back on slips from your own clerk's number series.

usage.server_tool_use is a separate meter. Usage is the part of the response that counts what you are billed for. Web search is billed at $10 per 1,000 searches on top of tokens, and failed searches are not billed. At that price one search costs one cent, so the request above cost one cent in searching, plus its tokens. Web fetch is free beyond tokens, and so is code execution when it is paired with search or fetch. §15 puts these in one cost model. In the picture, errands get their own line on the invoice, apart from the words.

The figure puts the two shapes side by side. The top row is §6's loop. The bottom row is a server tool, with the one exit you must still handle, which §7.2 covers:

7.2 pause_turn: The Server Loop Handing Control Back

The server runs its own agentic loop, the same ask, run and report cycle as §6.4, entirely inside one request. It searches, reads what it found, and decides whether to search again. That loop has an iteration cap: a most-rounds limit, as §6.4's loop should have had. When it hits the cap, you get a stop reason you must handle, pause_turn.

In the picture, the office's desk works a fixed shift on each letter. If the shift ends mid-errand, the desk sends you the half-written letter, with every clipping gathered so far. It waits for you to hand it back in.

The request below asks a question that needs many searches, and allows up to ten. The loop sends it. While the reply is pause_turn, it appends the reply and sends again, up to four requests in all. It needs an API key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 10}]
messages = [{"role": "user",
             "content": "Compare the last three ECB and Fed rate decisions."}]

for attempt in range(1, 5):
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=2048,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    print(f"request {attempt}: stop_reason={response.stop_reason}")
    if response.stop_reason != "pause_turn":
        break
    # Send the paused turn straight back, unmodified, and it continues.
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
else:
    raise RuntimeError("still pausing after 4 requests")

print("final:", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

request 1: stop_reason=pause_turn
request 2: stop_reason=end_turn
final: The ECB cut once and held twice; the Fed held across all three meetings.

Line by line: request 1 ended with pause_turn, so the loop appended the reply to messages and sent it again. Request 2 ended with end_turn, so the loop stopped and printed the answer. Nothing in the loop told the model what it had already found. The appended reply carried that.

A paused turn is resumed by appending it and re-sending. You do not start over, and you do not summarise what happened. The assistant content carries the partial work, and stripping it throws away every search already paid for. Send the same tools as well: a paused turn can end on a server call that has not run yet, and the continuation needs that tool to run it. In the picture, you hand back the half-written letter with its clippings, not a note saying "carry on".

Bound the continuations. A continuation is one more request to resume a paused turn. The loop above gives up after four requests. Without a bound, you have re-created §6.4's unbounded loop in a place where each iteration is more expensive, because every continuation resends a conversation that now contains search results.

You can watch both cases without an API key. Below, fake_create plays the server. It pauses as many times as you tell it, then finishes. run is the loop from above, written over plain dicts, with the cap as a parameter. It prints how many messages each request sends:

# A stand-in for the API: the server pauses `pauses` times, then finishes.
def fake_create(messages, pauses):
    done = sum(1 for m in messages if m["role"] == "assistant")
    if done < pauses:
        return "pause_turn", [{"type": "text", "text": f"part {done + 1}"}]
    return "end_turn", [{"type": "text", "text": "Done."}]


def run(pauses, max_requests=4):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Compare three rate decisions."}]
    for attempt in range(1, max_requests + 1):
        stop_reason, content = fake_create(messages, pauses)
        print(f"  request {attempt}: {stop_reason:<10} messages sent: {len(messages)}")
        if stop_reason != "pause_turn":
            return content[0]["text"]
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": content})
    raise RuntimeError(f"still pausing after {max_requests} requests")


print("a server that pauses twice:")
print("  final:", run(pauses=2))
print("a server that never finishes:")
try:
    run(pauses=99)
except RuntimeError as error:
    print("  gave up:", error)

a server that pauses twice:
  request 1: pause_turn messages sent: 1
  request 2: pause_turn messages sent: 2
  request 3: end_turn   messages sent: 3
  final: Done.
a server that never finishes:
  request 1: pause_turn messages sent: 1
  request 2: pause_turn messages sent: 2
  request 3: pause_turn messages sent: 3
  request 4: pause_turn messages sent: 4
  gave up: still pausing after 4 requests

Read the two runs:

  • The first server pauses twice. Each pause adds one assistant message, so the requests send 1, 2 and 3 messages. The third one gets end_turn.
  • The second server never finishes. The loop sends four requests, each bigger than the last, then raises an error instead of carrying on.

That growing count is what the bound protects you from. With a real server, those messages carry search results, and every request resends all of them.

One further server tool is worth knowing about even though it is used differently from the rest. The advisor tool pairs a fast executor model with a higher-intelligence advisor that supplies strategic guidance mid-generation, while the executor is still writing. The executor is the model doing the work. The advisor tool is aimed at long-horizon agentic workloads, tasks that run for many steps, where the executor benefits from a second opinion without paying the larger model's price for every token. In the picture, it is a junior writer who can knock on a senior writer's door mid-letter.

There is a second way control comes back, and it is easy to miss. If the model calls a server tool and one of your client tools in the same turn, you get stop_reason: "tool_use" and a server_tool_use block without its result. Return your client tool_result blocks as usual, and the API runs the server tool afterwards. So a turn can contain a server call you must not answer and a client call you must. This is where §7.1's prefix test earns its place: answer the toolu_ call, and leave the srvtoolu_ one alone.

7.3 Web Search

Web search is the most-used server tool. It is also the one whose configuration matters most, because its defaults are permissive by design. Left alone, it may search as often as it likes, anywhere on the web. In the picture, that is a clerk sent to "the library", with no list of libraries and no limit on trips.

The request below sets three things:

  • max_uses allows at most 3 searches;
  • allowed_domains limits the search to two sites, the European Central Bank's and the US Federal Reserve's;
  • user_location says roughly where the user is, so results suit someone in Lisbon.

It needs an API key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[{
        "type": "web_search_20250305",
        "name": "web_search",
        "max_uses": 3,
        "allowed_domains": ["ecb.europa.eu", "federalreserve.gov"],
        "user_location": {"type": "approximate", "city": "Lisbon",
                          "country": "PT", "timezone": "Europe/Lisbon"},
    }],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the current ECB deposit rate?"}],
)

print("stop_reason :", response.stop_reason)
print("searches    :", response.usage.server_tool_use.web_search_requests)
print("answer      :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason : end_turn
searches    : 1
answer      : According to the ECB press release, the deposit facility rate was left unchanged at this meeting.

The answer cites the ECB's own press release, because allowed_domains left the search nowhere else to look. One search was enough.

max_uses is the only hard constraint on how much searching happens. Everything else, such as "search more readily" or "prefer answering directly", is steering through the system prompt (§2.4), which is guidance. A simple factual question uses one to three searches, and a comparative research question can use ten or more, each billed. Exceeding max_uses produces a max_uses_exceeded error in the result block and not a failed request. In the picture, the clerk who runs out of trips comes back with a note saying so, and the writer finishes the letter with what it has.

allowed_domains and blocked_domains are mutually exclusive. You can say "only these libraries" or "never these libraries", not both. Sending both is a 400, the API's "bad request" error (§2.9). Entries are bare domains with an optional path (example.com, example.com/blog) and no scheme, so a value of https://example.com is not what the API expects. The scheme is the https:// at the front of a web address. Two more rules from the same docs:

  • a domain covers its subdomains, so example.com also covers docs.example.com;
  • paths work for web search only. Web fetch matches on the domain alone, so an entry with a path never matches a fetch.

Those rules are easy to get wrong before a request ever leaves your machine. Here is a small check of our own, written from the first two rules. It is not the API's validator, just a way to catch the two mistakes before you pay for a request:

# Our own check, written from the two rules above. It is not the API's validator.
def check_domains(tool):
    if "allowed_domains" in tool and "blocked_domains" in tool:
        return "rejected: both lists in one tool"
    for domain in tool.get("allowed_domains", []) + tool.get("blocked_domains", []):
        if "://" in domain:
            return f"rejected: {domain!r} has a scheme"
    return "ok"


TRIES = [
    {"allowed_domains": ["ecb.europa.eu", "federalreserve.gov"]},
    {"allowed_domains": ["example.com/blog"]},
    {"allowed_domains": ["https://example.com"]},
    {"allowed_domains": ["ecb.europa.eu"], "blocked_domains": ["spam.example"]},
]
for tool in TRIES:
    print(check_domains(tool))

ok
ok
rejected: 'https://example.com' has a scheme
rejected: both lists in one tool

The first two lists pass: two bare domains, then a domain with a path. The third has a scheme. The fourth uses both lists in one tool, which the API rejects with a 400.

Search results enter the context window and stay there. The context window is everything the model reads on a request (§1.4). Search results are input tokens on this turn and on every later turn of the conversation, which is §9's arithmetic applied to content you did not write. This is the strongest argument for max_uses, because it bounds tokens and not just search fees. In the picture, every clipping is stapled into the file, and the writer rereads the whole file before every later letter.

That last problem has a purpose-built answer. Dynamic filtering, available on web_search_20260209 and later, has the model write and run code that filters results before they reach the context window, so only the relevant part is loaded. It is the same idea as §7.6's programmatic tool calling, and it uses the same machinery. In the picture, a clerk reads the clippings first, and only the useful paragraphs reach the writer's desk.

7.4 Web Fetch, and the Exfiltration Problem

Web fetch retrieves a specific URL, one web address, and puts the page in the conversation. It costs nothing beyond tokens, which makes its real cost easy to underestimate. A research paper PDF is around 125,000 tokens, and it lands in your context window. In the picture, the office photocopies the document for free. The cost is the writer reading every page, again, before every later letter.

The block below prices three typical sizes of page, using the sizes Anthropic's docs give. It assumes $5.00 per million input tokens, and shows each page once and over ten turns:

CONTENT_SIZES = [("average web page", 10, 2_500),
                 ("large documentation page", 100, 25_000),
                 ("research paper PDF", 500, 125_000)]
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00

print(f"{'content':<26}{'size':>8}{'tokens':>10}{'cost once':>11}"
      f"{'over 10 turns':>15}")
for label, kilobytes, tokens in CONTENT_SIZES:
    once = tokens / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK
    print(f"{label:<26}{str(kilobytes) + ' kB':>8}{tokens:>10,}"
          f"{'$%.3f' % once:>11}{'$%.2f' % (once * 10):>15}")

print("\nthe fetch itself is free; the context it fills is not")

content                       size    tokens  cost once  over 10 turns
average web page             10 kB     2,500     $0.013          $0.12
large documentation page    100 kB    25,000     $0.125          $1.25
research paper PDF          500 kB   125,000     $0.625          $6.25

the fetch itself is free; the context it fills is not

Line by line: each row is one kind of page. A kB is a kilobyte, about a thousand characters of text. The tokens column is what the page puts in the context window. cost once is those tokens at $5.00 per million, on the turn the page arrives. over 10 turns is the same page resent ten times, because it stays in the conversation. Remember the PDF row: one free fetch, $0.625 on the turn it arrives, and $6.25 over ten turns. The figure draws the same three rows to scale:

max_content_tokens caps this, and on anything user-facing it should be set. It is a limit on how many tokens of a fetched page are kept. User-facing means a user's request decides what gets fetched, so you cannot know the size in advance.

The other consideration is security, and it is not hypothetical. Two words first. Untrusted input is any text your system did not write and cannot vouch for: a web page, an email, a document a user uploaded. Exfiltration means carrying data out of a system to someone who should not have it. Web fetch in an environment where the model reads untrusted input alongside sensitive data is a data-exfiltration channel.

The attack is simple. Text the model reads contains an instruction to fetch https://attacker.example/?data=<the secret>, and the fetch itself is the leak. No reply needs to reach the attacker: the address of the request carries the secret, and the attacker's server only has to record the addresses it was asked for. In the picture, a letter arrives saying "please fetch this address, and write the account number on the slip". A clerk who runs that errand has delivered the account number, whatever the errand brings back.

The platform mitigates the worst version, because the model may not construct URLs dynamically. It may only fetch a URL that already appeared in the conversation:

  • in a user message;
  • in a result from one of your client tools;
  • in an earlier search or fetch result.

It also refuses a URL that seems to carry a credential, such as an API key, unless that credential appears in the system prompt or a user message. But that is a mitigation and not a fix, since a search result is itself content the model did not verify. Three controls are yours:

Do not enable it
The only complete answer when the same conversation holds untrusted text and data that must not leave. Consider whether fetch is doing enough work to justify the channel.
allowed_domains
Restrict to hosts you trust. An allowlist turns the exfiltration channel into one that only reaches places you chose, which for most internal tools is sufficient.
max_uses
Bound the number of requests. Limits both the token bill and how much can be exfiltrated per conversation.

A fourth, newer control narrows the list of sources above. url_sources can stop a source from counting, for example the results of a client tool that echoes text the model wrote.

The allowed_domains row is enforced by the platform for web fetch. The moment you write a fetch tool of your own (§6), the same check becomes yours, and its obvious version has a hole. Below, naive asks whether a URL mentions a trusted domain anywhere. careful takes the URL apart with urlsplit, from Python's standard library. It asks whether the host, the server name between :// and the next /, is a trusted domain or a subdomain of one, which is the same rule the API's lists use:

from urllib.parse import urlsplit

ALLOWED = ["ecb.europa.eu", "federalreserve.gov"]


def naive(url):
    # "Does the URL mention a trusted domain anywhere?"
    return any(domain in url for domain in ALLOWED)


def careful(url):
    # "Is the host a trusted domain, or a subdomain of one?"
    host = urlsplit(url).hostname or ""
    return any(host == d or host.endswith("." + d) for d in ALLOWED)


URLS = ["https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/",
        "https://federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm",
        "https://ecb.europa.eu.attacker.example/?d=SECRET",
        "https://attacker.example/?q=federalreserve.gov"]

print(f"{'url':<50}{'naive':>7}{'careful':>9}")
for url in URLS:
    print(f"{url:<50}{str(naive(url)):>7}{str(careful(url)):>9}")

url                                                 naive  careful
https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/                     True     True
https://federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy.htm        True     True
https://ecb.europa.eu.attacker.example/?d=SECRET     True    False
https://attacker.example/?q=federalreserve.gov       True    False

Line by line:

  • The first two rows are real ECB and Fed addresses, and both checks pass them.
  • The third starts its host with a trusted name, but the host really belongs to attacker.example. Everything before that is a subdomain the attacker controls.
  • The fourth names a trusted domain only in the query string, the part after ?.

The naive check passes all four, so it would have made both bad requests. Compare hosts, never substrings. Keep the domains in your lists plain ASCII too: a name with one look-alike letter from another alphabet is a different domain.

§14.4 develops the general form of this argument: give each part of a system only the access it needs. The point to carry here is that a tool that makes outbound network requests is an exfiltration primitive, whoever executes it, and it should be reasoned about as one. A primitive is a basic building block that an attack can be built from.

7.5 Tool Search: Scaling Past a Few Dozen Tools

§6.9 established that tool definitions are context you pay for on every request, and that selection accuracy degrades as the surface grows. Selection accuracy is how often the model picks the right tool, and the surface is the whole set of tools you offer. Tool search fixes both by not loading most of them. In §6.9's picture, you keep the forms in a drawer, with an index card on the desk. The writer reads the index, asks for the forms this letter needs, and never rereads the rest.

The request below offers three tools:

  • the search tool itself, in its regex variant, so the model searches with a regular expression, a pattern for matching text (§4.3);
  • two ordinary tools named in §6.10's style, each marked defer_loading: True, meaning "do not load this until it is found".

The loop prints what the model searched for, what it discovered, and what it called. It needs an API key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[
        {"type": "tool_search_tool_regex_20251119", "name": "tool_search_tool_regex"},
        {"name": "github_list_prs",
         "description": "List open pull requests for a repository.",
         "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                          "properties": {"repo": {"type": "string"}},
                          "required": ["repo"]},
         "defer_loading": True},
        {"name": "slack_send_message",
         "description": "Post a message to a Slack channel.",
         "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                          "properties": {"channel": {"type": "string"},
                                         "text": {"type": "string"}},
                          "required": ["channel", "text"]},
         "defer_loading": True},
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What PRs are open on acme/api?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
for block in response.content:
    if block.type == "server_tool_use":
        print("  searched for:", block.input)
    elif block.type == "tool_search_tool_result":
        for ref in block.content.tool_references:
            print("  discovered  :", ref.tool_name)
    elif block.type == "tool_use":
        print("  called      :", block.name, block.input)

stop_reason: tool_use
  searched for: {'pattern': 'github_.*pr'}
  discovered  : github_list_prs
  called      : github_list_prs {'repo': 'acme/api'}

Line by line:

  • searched for shows the pattern the model wrote, github_.*pr: "github_, then anything, then pr".
  • discovered is the one tool that matched. Its full definition was loaded only now.
  • called is the model using it, with the repository from the question.
  • stop_reason: tool_use appears because github_list_prs is an ordinary client tool. You run it and send a tool_result, exactly as in §6. Only the search was done by the server.

The mechanism is this: you send every tool definition, marking with defer_loading: true the ones that should not be loaded up front. The model's context initially holds only the search tool and any non-deferred tools. When it needs something, it searches. The API returns tool_reference blocks (up to five by default) and expands them into full definitions automatically. At least one tool must stay non-deferred, and it is normally the search tool itself. In the picture, the drawer holds every form, but the desk holds only the index card, plus any forms you always want at hand.

There are two variants, and the choice is not arbitrary. Both search tool names, descriptions and argument names. They differ in how the model asks:

  • Regex (tool_search_tool_regex_20251119) has the model construct patterns, which rewards the service-prefix naming convention from §6.10. For example, github_ matches everything GitHub in one query.
  • BM25 (tool_search_tool_bm25_20251119) takes natural-language queries and ranks tools by how well the words match (§10.3 teaches BM25). That rewards descriptions written for a reader and not for a matcher.

If your tools are consistently namespaced, regex is sharper. If they are well described but inconsistently named, BM25 is.

How much does it save? The block below estimates it. Its numbers are set at the top:

  • an average tool definition of 353 characters, measured over a real seven-tool surface;
  • a search tool of 420 characters;
  • 2 tools discovered in a typical conversation;
  • about 1.4 seconds for the extra step a search adds.

approx_tokens uses the rough rule of four characters per token. The block prints eager loading, every definition sent up front, against search, for five sizes of surface:

AVG_TOOL_CHARS = 353       # measured over a real 7-tool surface
SEARCH_TOOL_CHARS = 420
TYPICAL_DISCOVERY = 2      # tools a given conversation actually needs
EXTRA_STEP_MS = 1_400     # the model writes a search and reads it


def approx_tokens(chars):
    return round(chars / 4)


searched = approx_tokens(SEARCH_TOOL_CHARS + TYPICAL_DISCOVERY * AVG_TOOL_CHARS)

print(f"{'tools':>7}{'eager':>10}{'with search':>14}{'saved':>10}")
for n in (7, 20, 40, 100, 400):
    eager = approx_tokens(n * AVG_TOOL_CHARS)
    print(f"{n:>7}{eager:>10,}{searched:>14,}{eager - searched:>+10,}")

print()
print(f"the search column never moves: {searched:,} tokens at every scale")
print(f"what it costs instead: one extra step (~{EXTRA_STEP_MS} ms)")
print("before the first real tool call; the cached prefix is unaffected,")
print("because deferred tools are kept out of it (see 9.3)")

  tools     eager   with search     saved
      7       618           282      +336
     20     1,765           282    +1,483
     40     3,530           282    +3,248
    100     8,825           282    +8,543
    400    35,300           282   +35,018

the search column never moves: 282 tokens at every scale
what it costs instead: one extra step (~1400 ms)
before the first real tool call; the cached prefix is unaffected,
because deferred tools are kept out of it (see 9.3)

Line by line:

  • The eager column grows with the number of tools: 7 tools are 618 tokens, 400 tools are 35,300.
  • The with search column is the search tool plus the two tools found: (420 + 2 × 353) ÷ 4, which rounds to 282.
  • saved is the difference.

The flatness is the property, not the saving. The search column is the same 282 tokens whether the surface holds seven tools or four hundred, because the model only ever loads what it discovered. Eager loading grows linearly and is untenable well before the four-hundred mark.

So why did §6.9 say that for twenty tools used on every turn, caching wins, when the table shows search ahead on tokens even at seven? Because tokens are not all it costs. It costs an extra step before the first real tool call: the model must write a search and read what came back before it can call anything. That is around 1.4 seconds of latency, waiting time, on every conversation that needs a tool it has not already found. If every request uses every tool, each conversation pays that step and saves little.

It does not cost your prompt cache. The API keeps deferred tools out of the cached prefix entirely, and adds a discovered definition later, inside the conversation. So the start of the request stays the same however the search goes (§9.3 explains why that start matters).

At twenty tools the trade is real: 1,483 tokens saved against 1.4 seconds of waiting, and which matters more depends on your product. Anthropic's guidance is to consider tool search from about ten tools, or about 10k tokens of definitions, and to keep your three to five most-used tools non-deferred, so they need no search. At four hundred tools, 35,000 tokens a request is not something an extra step can outweigh.

7.6 Programmatic Tool Calling

This one solves a problem that looks like a context problem and is really a turn problem. Suppose the model needs to call get_order for 400 order ids and sum the totals. With ordinary tool use that is 400 tool calls, each returning a result into the context window, across many model turns.

Programmatic tool calling lets the model write code that calls your tools, and the code is executed inside the code execution sandbox (an isolated environment). The loop runs there, and only the final answer comes back to the model.

In the picture: instead of handing out 400 slips, a few at a time, the writer writes one page of instructions. "For each order on this list, fetch it, and add up the totals." A clerk in the back room follows it. Your clerk still runs each errand, all 400 of them. But the reports go to the back room, and only the total reaches the writer's desk.

Here is the request, wrapped in the loop it needs. The tool list holds code execution and one ordinary tool, get_order, here a stub that returns the same record every time. A comment marks the line that makes it work. It needs an API key:

import json

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [
    {"type": "code_execution_20260120", "name": "code_execution"},
    {"name": "get_order",
     "description": "Fetch one order by id. Returns total_cents and status.",
     "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                      "properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
                      "required": ["order_id"]},
     # This is what makes the tool callable from inside code execution.
     "allowed_callers": ["code_execution_20260120"]},
]


def get_order(order_id):
    # A stand-in for your real lookup: every order is 4,281 cents.
    return json.dumps({"order_id": order_id, "total_cents": 4281, "status": "paid"})


messages = [{"role": "user",
             "content": "Total orders ord_0001 to ord_0400 and give me the mean."}]
response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=4096,
                                  tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
results_sent = 0
while response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    # The sandbox's code is paused, waiting for these results.
    calls = [b for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": get_order(**b.input)}
        for b in calls]})
    results_sent += len(calls)
    response = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=4096,
                                      tools=TOOLS, messages=messages,
                                      container=response.container.id)

print("tool results sent:", results_sent)
print("stop_reason      :", response.stop_reason)
print("answer           :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

tool results sent: 400
stop_reason      : end_turn
answer           : The 400 orders total 1,712,400 cents; the mean is 42.81 EUR.

This is a loop, and here is why. Each time the model's code calls get_order, the code pauses inside the sandbox. The API returns stop_reason: "tool_use" with a tool_use block, just as in §6. That block also carries a caller field, which says the call came from code execution and not from the model directly. Your loop runs the function and sends back the results. Three details differ from §6.4:

  • the user message carrying the results may hold only tool_result blocks;
  • the request passes container, the id of the paused sandbox, so the code can resume;
  • it sends the same tools as before.

The code may ask for several orders at once, so one pause can carry many calls. The model is not asked to read any of the results. It writes the code at the start, and reads the code's printed summary at the end. In between, your loop and the sandbox trade results without the model. That is how the output above can say 400 results were sent and still be cheap.

allowed_callers: ["code_execution_20260120"] is the whole switch. Without it the tool is callable only directly by the model, and with it the sandbox may call it too.

Now the puzzle from the start of this section. The block below does the arithmetic for both ways of running the 400 lookups. Its numbers are set at the top:

  • 220 tokens for each order record;
  • a 6,000-token conversation to start from;
  • 1.4 seconds per model turn;
  • for ordinary tool use, a generous 8 calls per turn.

For programmatic calling it assumes a 180-token summary, and the conversation sent twice: once to write the code, once to read the summary:

N_CALLS = 400
RESULT_TOKENS = 220          # one order record coming back
BASE_CONTEXT = 6_000
MODEL_TURN_MS = 1_400

# Ordinary tool use: results accumulate, and the conversation is resent each turn.
CALLS_PER_TURN = 8           # generous parallelism
turns = N_CALLS // CALLS_PER_TURN
ordinary_context = BASE_CONTEXT + N_CALLS * RESULT_TOKENS
ordinary_billed = sum(BASE_CONTEXT + t * CALLS_PER_TURN * RESULT_TOKENS
                      for t in range(1, turns + 1))

# Programmatic: the loop runs in the sandbox; one summary returns.
ptc_context = BASE_CONTEXT + 180
ptc_billed = BASE_CONTEXT * 2 + 180

print(f"{'':22}{'model turns':>12}{'peak context':>14}{'input billed':>14}")
print(f"{'ordinary tool use':<22}{turns:>12}{ordinary_context:>14,}"
      f"{ordinary_billed:>14,}")
print(f"{'programmatic':<22}{2:>12}{ptc_context:>14,}{ptc_billed:>14,}")
print()
print(f"latency from model turns: {turns * MODEL_TURN_MS / 1000:>6.1f}s  ->"
      f"{2 * MODEL_TURN_MS / 1000:>6.1f}s")
print(f"input tokens billed     : {ordinary_billed / ptc_billed:>6.0f}x fewer")

                       model turns  peak context  input billed
ordinary tool use               50        94,000     2,544,000
programmatic                     2         6,180        12,180

latency from model turns:   70.0s  ->   2.8s
input tokens billed     :    209x fewer

Line by line:

  • Ordinary tool use takes 400 ÷ 8 = 50 turns. Its peak context is 6,000 + 400 × 220 = 94,000 tokens.
  • It bills 2,544,000 input tokens, because every turn resends the whole conversation so far. Turn 1 sends 6,000 + 8 × 220 = 7,760 tokens, turn 50 sends 94,000, and the block adds up all fifty.
  • Programmatic calling takes 2 turns. Its peak is 6,000 + 180 = 6,180, and it bills 6,000 × 2 + 180 = 12,180.
  • In model time, 50 × 1.4 = 70.0 seconds becomes 2 × 1.4 = 2.8, and 2,544,000 ÷ 12,180 is about 209.

Here is the puzzle's answer. The two and a half million tokens were never the lookups. They were the conversation being resent. In ordinary tool use, every result lands in the context window and is reread on every later turn. With programmatic tool calling, the 400 results stay in the sandbox. Your function still ran 400 times. The model just never read the results one by one. In the picture, the back-room clerk reads 400 reports, and the writer reads one total.

The 209 is this example's arithmetic for the best case: one loop of identical lookups. Anthropic reports a smaller measured saving on mixed, realistic work, about 38% fewer billed input tokens on a 75-tool benchmark. The figure shows this example's two bills to scale:

There are two constraints before you reach for it. It requires the code execution tool, which brings that tool's billing and its sandbox. And it is incompatible with strict: true (§6.8), so a tool you want schema-guaranteed cannot also be programmatically callable, and you have to decide which property matters more for that tool. In the picture, §4's stencil fits over a slip the writer fills in. It cannot be laid over a slip that code in the back room fills in.

7.7 The MCP Connector

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for exposing tools to a model. An open standard is a published set of rules that anyone may build to, the way anyone may build a web browser. MCP has two sides:

  • a server offers tools;
  • a client connects to the server and calls them.

Its usual shape is a client you run that speaks to a remote MCP server, one running elsewhere on the network. The MCP connector removes the client: you name a remote MCP server in mcp_servers, and Anthropic's infrastructure connects to it and calls its tools. In the picture, a partner agency prints its own forms and runs its own clerks. The telegram office phones the agency for you, and you never deal with it directly.

The request below connects to an issue tracker's MCP server and allows two of its tools. Three of its words are new:

  • authorization_token is the key the server expects, here a placeholder. OAuth is the common standard for issuing such keys.
  • betas switches on a feature that is still in beta: released for use, but still allowed to change.
  • client.beta.messages.create is the SDK's door to beta features.

It needs an API key and a real server:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    betas=["mcp-client-2025-11-20"],
    mcp_servers=[{
        "type": "url",
        "url": "https://mcp.example.com/sse",
        "name": "issue-tracker",
        "authorization_token": "OAUTH_TOKEN_HERE",
    }],
    tools=[{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "issue-tracker",
            "default_config": {"enabled": False},
            "configs": {"search_issues": {"enabled": True},
                        "get_issue": {"enabled": True}}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is blocking the release?"}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("answer     :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason: end_turn
answer     : Two issues are blocking: ENG-441 (auth migration) and ENG-455 (flaky deploy).

There are two components, and conflating them is the usual first mistake.

  • mcp_servers declares the connection: URL, name and auth.
  • A mcp_toolset entry in tools declares which of that server's tools are enabled. Its allowlist takes two settings. default_config with "enabled": False switches every tool off, and configs switches the named tools back on.

A server declared but never referenced by a toolset contributes nothing. In the picture, you have the agency's phone number, but you have not said which of its forms you accept.

There are two limitations to design around.

Only tool calls are supported. The MCP specification also covers resources, prompts and sampling, other things a server can offer besides tools, but the connector implements the tools portion. If your integration depends on MCP resources, the connector is not the mechanism.

A remote MCP server must be reachable over HTTP, using Streamable HTTP or SSE. HTTP is the protocol web pages travel over, and SSE and Streamable HTTP are two ways of sending a reply over it in pieces. A local STDIO server cannot be connected this way. STDIO means standard input and output: the server runs on your own machine, and a program talks to it by writing to its input and reading its output. That is how most MCP servers are developed and how Claude Code runs them, so the difference catches people moving a working local setup into an API integration.

And here is the consideration that outranks both: an MCP server is third-party code defining tools whose descriptions enter your model's context. A compromised or hostile server can describe a tool in terms designed to make the model call it with data from your conversation. In the picture, the agency writes the printed instructions on its own forms, and the writer reads them as trustingly as yours. The allowlist is the control. Enumerate what you permit and do not accept whatever the server offers. With every tool off by default, a server that grows a new tool tomorrow does not silently acquire a place in your prompt.

7.8 Agent Skills

A Skill is not a tool. It is a directory of instructions, reference files and executable scripts that the model reads from a filesystem when it decides the task calls for it. A directory is a folder, and a filesystem is the set of folders and files on a computer. The mechanism that makes this efficient has a name worth knowing: progressive disclosure, which means the model sees a short description first and loads more only when it needs it.

In the picture, a Skill is a binder on the writer's shelf. The writer can always read the spine label. The writer opens the binder only when a letter calls for it. The appendices at the back are read only when the chapter points to them.

The grid gives the three levels. YAML frontmatter is a few lines of name: value settings at the top of the file, and SKILL.md is the file every Skill starts from:

Level 1 — metadata
Always loaded, about 100 tokens per Skill. Just name and description from the YAML frontmatter. This is what the model matches your request against.
Level 2 — instructions
Loaded when the Skill triggers, under 5k tokens. The body of SKILL.md: workflows, conventions, gotchas.
Level 3 — resources
Nothing until read. Bundled files the instructions point at. Reference files cost tokens when opened; scripts run through bash, so only their output enters context, never their source.

The block below prices five Skills at each level. Its sizes are examples chosen within the grid's limits, in tokens. It then totals three cases: metadata only, one Skill triggered, and everything loaded at once:

SKILLS = [("pdf-processing", 104, 3_900, 12_000),
          ("brand-voice", 92, 2_100, 4_500),
          ("xlsx", 118, 4_400, 26_000),
          ("incident-review", 88, 3_200, 8_800),
          ("sql-conventions", 96, 2_800, 15_000)]

always = sum(meta for _, meta, _, _ in SKILLS)
if_all_loaded = sum(meta + body + res for _, meta, body, res in SKILLS)
one_triggered = always + SKILLS[0][2]        # metadata for all, body for one

print(f"{'skill':<18}{'metadata':>10}{'SKILL.md':>10}{'resources':>11}")
for name, meta, body, res in SKILLS:
    print(f"{name:<18}{meta:>10}{body:>10,}{res:>11,}")

print()
print(f"always in context (5 skills)      : {always:>7,} tokens")
print(f"one skill triggered, body loaded  : {one_triggered:>7,} tokens")
print(f"if everything were loaded eagerly : {if_all_loaded:>7,} tokens")
print(f"ratio                             : {if_all_loaded / always:>7.0f}x")

skill               metadata  SKILL.md  resources
pdf-processing           104     3,900     12,000
brand-voice               92     2,100      4,500
xlsx                     118     4,400     26,000
incident-review           88     3,200      8,800
sql-conventions           96     2,800     15,000

always in context (5 skills)      :     498 tokens
one skill triggered, body loaded  :   4,398 tokens
if everything were loaded eagerly :  83,198 tokens
ratio                             :     167x

Line by line:

  • The table lists each Skill's three levels. The metadata column is about 100 tokens each, and the bodies are all under 5,000.
  • always in context adds the five metadata entries: 104 + 92 + 118 + 88 + 96 = 498.
  • one skill triggered adds pdf-processing's body to that: 498 + 3,900 = 4,398.
  • if everything were loaded eagerly adds every column of every row, 83,198, which is 167 times the metadata alone.

Progressive disclosure is what lets you install many Skills, and the metadata cost is the whole of the argument. Five Skills cost about half a thousand tokens until one of them is needed. It is also why the description is the most important line in a Skill. It is the only thing the model sees when deciding whether to look further, so it must say what the Skill does and when to use it, and not just what it is about. In the picture, a spine label that says "Finance" gets the binder opened at the wrong time. "How to close the month's accounts; use when asked to reconcile" gets it opened at the right one.

In the API, Skills run inside code execution and are named in the container parameter. The container is the sandbox from §7.6. The request below asks for Anthropic's own pptx Skill, which makes PowerPoint decks. It needs an API key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    container={"skills": [{"type": "anthropic", "skill_id": "pptx",
                           "version": "latest"}]},
    tools=[{"type": "code_execution_20250825", "name": "code_execution"}],
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Make a five-slide deck on our Q3 incident trends."}],
)

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("answer     :", next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))

stop_reason: end_turn
answer     : I have built a five-slide deck covering incident volume, mean time to recovery and the top three causes.

Skills require the code execution tool, because the filesystem they live on is that sandbox. You can use up to 20 Skills per request. The shape is identical for Anthropic-provided Skills (pptx, xlsx, docx, pdf) and custom ones you upload. type says which kind it is: anthropic or custom.

Pin the version in production. In production means in the real system your users rely on. "version": "latest" is convenient, and it means the Skill's instructions can change underneath a prompt you evaluated last month. Anthropic's Skills also have dated versions, such as 20251013, and a dated version does not change. §13's regression suite cannot protect you from a dependency that updates itself. A regression suite compares your system against its own past behaviour, and it has no way to attribute a change to a Skill that silently updated. In the picture, you would not judge a writer's letters this month against last month's if someone had swapped the binder for a new edition in between.

The figure sums up the three levels, with the totals from the block above:

7.9 Choosing Between Them

These mechanisms overlap enough that the choice is genuinely unclear in places. The question that resolves most cases is: what is the thing you actually have? In the picture: is it an errand only your clerk can run, one the office runs, an agency's form, or a binder of know-how?

A function in your code
A client tool (§6). Add allowed_callers if it will be called in bulk; add strict if a bad argument is expensive. You cannot have both.
A capability Anthropic runs
A server tool. Bound it with max_uses and, where it reaches the network, with allowed_domains.
A service with an MCP server
The MCP connector, with every tool you allow enabled by name. Saves you writing and maintaining an integration.
Knowledge, not an action
A Skill. "How we write incident reviews", "our SQL conventions", "the steps for a release". If the answer is a procedure rather than a call, a Skill is the shape.
Too many tools to load
Tool search, from about ten tools or 10k tokens of definitions. Consolidate first (§6.10).

The distinction people most often get wrong is the fourth. A Skill is for knowledge, and a tool is for action. "Generate a PowerPoint" feels like a tool and is a Skill, because what the model needs is not a function to call but a procedure to follow plus a library to use. Conversely, "look up an order" feels like it could be documented as knowledge and is a tool, because it requires reaching a system only your code can reach.

Back to the picture one last time. Your clerk runs the errands only you can run (§6). The office's desk runs search, fetch, code and tool lookups, and pauses when its shift ends. A partner agency runs its own forms, if you allow them. Binders on the shelf teach the writer how things are done here. In every case, you still decide what the office may do on your behalf.

Exercises

Exercise 7.1 — Bound a research agent. You are building an agent that answers questions about competitors using web search and web fetch. It handles 500 questions a day. Configure the tools, and compute the monthly cost of the server-tool fees alone.

Solution 
QUESTIONS_PER_DAY, DAYS = 500, 30
SEARCHES_PER_QUESTION = 4        # comparative questions, measured not guessed
FETCHES_PER_QUESTION = 2
SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000 = 10.00
FETCH_TOKENS_EACH = 25_000       # a large documentation page
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00

searches = QUESTIONS_PER_DAY * SEARCHES_PER_QUESTION * DAYS
search_fees = searches / 1000 * SEARCH_FEE_PER_1000

fetch_tokens = QUESTIONS_PER_DAY * FETCHES_PER_QUESTION * DAYS * FETCH_TOKENS_EACH
fetch_token_cost = fetch_tokens / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK

print(f"searches per month     : {searches:>12,}")
print(f"search fees            : {'$%.2f' % search_fees:>12}")
print(f"fetched tokens         : {fetch_tokens:>12,}")
print(f"cost of fetched tokens : {'$%.2f' % fetch_token_cost:>12}")
print(f"total                  : {'$%.2f' % (search_fees + fetch_token_cost):>12}")
print()
capped = QUESTIONS_PER_DAY * FETCHES_PER_QUESTION * DAYS * 4_000
print(f"with max_content_tokens=4000, fetched tokens: {capped:>10,}")
print(f"cost                                        : "
      f"{'$%.2f' % (capped / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>10}")
print(f"saving from one parameter                   : "
      f"{'$%.2f' % (fetch_token_cost - capped / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>10}")

searches per month     :       60,000
search fees            :      $600.00
fetched tokens         :  750,000,000
cost of fetched tokens :     $3750.00
total                  :     $4350.00

with max_content_tokens=4000, fetched tokens: 120,000,000
cost                                        :    $600.00
saving from one parameter                   :   $3150.00

The configuration.

TOOLS = [
    {"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search",
     "max_uses": 6,
     "blocked_domains": ["competitor-forum.example"]},
    {"type": "web_fetch_20250910", "name": "web_fetch",
     "max_uses": 3,
     "max_content_tokens": 4000},
]

The free tool is the expensive one, and that is the finding. Web search charges $10 per thousand searches and comes to $600 a month here. Web fetch charges nothing, and costs $3,750, more than six times as much, because 25,000 tokens of fetched page is 25,000 input tokens on that turn and on every turn after it. A cost model built from the published fee schedule alone would have got this exactly backwards.

max_content_tokens is the single highest-value parameter in the configuration. Capping fetched content at 4,000 tokens removes most of that spend for one line. The judgement call is what it costs you in answer quality, which is a §13 question and not a guess. Run the eval at 4,000, at 10,000 and uncapped, and buy the smallest cap that holds your accuracy.

Why blocked_domains and not allowed_domains here. Competitor research is open-ended, so an allowlist would have to enumerate the web. That makes this one of the few cases where a denylist is right. It also means the exfiltration argument in §7.4 applies with full force, so this agent must not be given access to anything confidential in the same conversation.

What I would add that the arithmetic does not show. A max_uses of 6 on search against a measured average of 4 leaves headroom for genuinely comparative questions while capping the tail. Measure the distribution before setting it. The mean is not the number that matters, and the p95 (the value that 95% of requests stay under) is.

Exercise 7.2 — Skill, tool, or MCP? Classify each and say why: (a) "format a number as currency in the user's locale"; (b) "look up a customer's subscription tier"; (c) "our team's code review checklist"; (d) "create and share a Linear issue"; (e) "convert this spreadsheet to a chart deck".

Solution 
ANSWERS = [
    ("a  format currency", "neither",
     "Deterministic, pure, no external state — write it in your own code and "
     "never involve the model. A tool call costs a round trip to do what a "
     "library does in microseconds."),
    ("b  look up subscription tier", "client tool",
     "Requires reaching a system only your code can reach, and the answer is "
     "an action's result rather than a procedure. Narrow schema, strict:true."),
    ("c  code review checklist", "Skill",
     "Knowledge, not action. Nothing to execute; the model needs a procedure "
     "to follow. Level-2 instructions, loaded when a review is happening."),
    ("d  create and share a Linear issue", "MCP connector",
     "A third party already publishes the integration. Writing and maintaining "
     "your own Linear tools is work the connector removes."),
    ("e  spreadsheet to chart deck", "Skill (+ code execution)",
     "Feels like a tool and is not: what is needed is a procedure plus "
     "libraries, running on a filesystem. This is exactly what pptx/xlsx are."),
]

for task, verdict, why in ANSWERS:
    print(f"{task:<36} -> {verdict}")
    print(f"{'':36}    {why}")

a  format currency                   -> neither
                                        Deterministic, pure, no external state — write it in your own code and never involve the model. A tool call costs a round trip to do what a library does in microseconds.
b  look up subscription tier         -> client tool
                                        Requires reaching a system only your code can reach, and the answer is an action's result rather than a procedure. Narrow schema, strict:true.
c  code review checklist             -> Skill
                                        Knowledge, not action. Nothing to execute; the model needs a procedure to follow. Level-2 instructions, loaded when a review is happening.
d  create and share a Linear issue   -> MCP connector
                                        A third party already publishes the integration. Writing and maintaining your own Linear tools is work the connector removes.
e  spreadsheet to chart deck         -> Skill (+ code execution)
                                        Feels like a tool and is not: what is needed is a procedure plus libraries, running on a filesystem. This is exactly what pptx/xlsx are.

(a) is the trap, and it is the most useful one in the list. "Format currency" is a perfectly plausible tool definition, and building it means every formatted number costs a model round trip and can be got wrong. If a task is deterministic and local, it does not belong to the model at all. The general rule is this: before asking which mechanism, ask whether the model should be involved.

(b) is a client tool and nothing else can be. No server tool reaches your subscription table, no MCP server exists for it, and no amount of instruction lets the model know the answer. This is the ordinary case, and it is most of production traffic.

(c) is the clearest Skill. There is nothing to execute. What the model lacks is your team's conventions: what you check, in what order, and what you always miss. Note that this could be a system prompt instead. The reason to prefer a Skill is §7.8's arithmetic: as knowledge it is only loaded when a review is actually happening, whereas a system prompt is present on every request forever.

(d) is MCP because the work is already done. You could write three client tools against Linear's REST API. The connector is the same capability without the maintenance, and its allowlist (default_config off, configs enabling exactly create_issue and add_comment) keeps out the rest of the server's surface.

(e) is the one that most often gets built wrong. The instinct is a make_presentation(data) tool, which means writing and maintaining slide-generation code and a schema rich enough to express a deck. The Skill approach gives the model the procedure and the library and lets it write the code in the sandbox. That is far more flexible, and it is already built.

The pattern. Ask what is missing. Missing reach into a system is a tool. Missing knowledge of how you do things is a Skill. Missing an integration someone else maintains is MCP. Missing nothing is a function call in your own code.

Exercise 7.3 — When does programmatic tool calling pay? Your agent calls get_customer in a loop. Find the number of calls at which programmatic tool calling beats ordinary parallel tool use, and name what the arithmetic leaves out.

Solution 
RESULT_TOKENS = 220
BASE_CONTEXT = 6_000
CALLS_PER_TURN = 8
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00
SANDBOX_OVERHEAD_TOKENS = 900      # the code the model writes, plus its output


def ordinary(n_calls):
    """Results accumulate in context, and the whole conversation is resent."""
    turns = max(1, -(-n_calls // CALLS_PER_TURN))
    return sum(BASE_CONTEXT + t * CALLS_PER_TURN * RESULT_TOKENS
               for t in range(1, turns + 1)), turns


def programmatic(n_calls):
    """One turn to write the code, one to read the summary."""
    return BASE_CONTEXT * 2 + SANDBOX_OVERHEAD_TOKENS, 2


print(f"{'calls':>7}{'ordinary tokens':>18}{'turns':>7}"
      f"{'ptc tokens':>13}{'turns':>7}{'winner':>12}")
crossover = None
for n in (2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 400):
    o_tokens, o_turns = ordinary(n)
    p_tokens, p_turns = programmatic(n)
    winner = "programmatic" if p_tokens < o_tokens else "ordinary"
    if crossover is None and p_tokens < o_tokens:
        crossover = n
    print(f"{n:>7}{o_tokens:>18,}{o_turns:>7}{p_tokens:>13,}{p_turns:>7}"
          f"  {winner:<12}")

print(f"\ncrossover is somewhere between "
      f"{[x for x in (2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 400) if x < crossover][-1]} "
      f"and {crossover} calls")
print(f"at 400 calls: {ordinary(400)[0] / programmatic(400)[0]:.0f}x fewer "
      f"input tokens, {ordinary(400)[1]} turns -> 2")

  calls   ordinary tokens  turns   ptc tokens  turns      winner
      2             7,760      1       12,900      2  ordinary    
      5             7,760      1       12,900      2  ordinary    
     10            17,280      2       12,900      2  programmatic
     20            28,560      3       12,900      2  programmatic
     50            91,280      7       12,900      2  programmatic
    100           238,160     13       12,900      2  programmatic
    400         2,544,000     50       12,900      2  programmatic

crossover is somewhere between 5 and 10 calls
at 400 calls: 197x fewer input tokens, 50 turns -> 2

On tokens alone the crossover is startlingly low, between five and ten calls. The reason is §9.1's quadratic growth. Ordinary tool use does not merely accumulate results. It resends everything accumulated so far on every turn, so doubling the calls more than doubles the bill. By four hundred calls the gap is roughly two hundredfold.

Three things the arithmetic leaves out, and all three matter.

Programmatic tool calling requires code execution, which has its own billing. It is free when paired with web search or fetch, and otherwise billed by container time with a five-minute minimum. For a handful of calls, that minimum alone can dominate everything computed above, which pushes the real crossover higher than the token model suggests.

It is incompatible with strict: true. If get_customer is a read, that costs nothing. If the tool being looped over writes anything, you are choosing between schema guarantees and bulk efficiency, and for a write tool the guarantee usually wins.

The failure modes differ. With ordinary tool use, each call's result passes through the model, so a malformed record gets noticed. Inside the sandbox the loop either handles the error or throws, and what returns is a summary, so a systematic problem in row 200 can be silently averaged into an answer. That is an argument for having the generated code report counts and anomalies, and for §13.10's required-call assertions covering bulk operations too.

What I would actually do. Below roughly fifty calls, use ordinary parallel tool use, because it is simpler, more observable, and needs no extra tool. Above a few hundred, use programmatic calling. In between, measure, because the container minimum makes the token model optimistic.

SECTION 8

Multimodal, Files and Citations

Start with a puzzle. A field technician photographs utility meters with a phone and sends each photo to an assistant in its own message, asking what the meter reads. Every photo is the same size, 4032 × 3024 pixels, which is the phone camera's default. The first twenty messages work. The twenty-first is rejected with an error about "many-image requests". Nothing about photo 21 is different from photo 20. So what changed? Guess before you read on. §8.1 runs the whole conversation and answers it.

Everything so far has been text in and text out. This section is about the other things a request can carry:

  • images, such as photos, screenshots and scanned pages;
  • PDFs, the document format most reports, contracts and invoices arrive in;
  • uploaded files, which you send to Anthropic once and then refer to by an id.

It is also about the mechanism that makes an answer drawn from them checkable. That mechanism is citations: pointers from each sentence of the answer back to the exact passage of your document it came from.

One idea underneath all of it explains most of the costs and limits. Images are converted to tokens, and PDFs are processed as images. A token is the unit the model reads and bills in (§1.2). So a page is not a cheap attachment. It is a few thousand tokens that occupy your context window and your bill. The context window is the most a single request can hold (§1.4). Every design decision here follows from that.
