Here is the picture for the whole section. Since §1 the model has been a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. Until now every telegram held only words. This section is about enclosures: photographs and documents sent along with the telegram, and the receipts the writer pins to the reply. Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram office In this section Section
A photograph sent along with the telegram an image block §8.1
Wiring a photo down the line as text characters, a third longer than the photo a base64 source §8.1
Telling the office where a photo hangs on a public noticeboard a url source §8.1
A cloakroom ticket for a parcel you left at the office earlier a file source and its file_id §8.1, §8.4
The rule that a file with more than twenty photos must use smaller prints, counting the copies from earlier letters the stricter limit above 20 images §8.1
A grid of squares laid over each photo, one word charged per square visual tokens: 28 × 28 patches §8.2
A photo too big for the office's frame, shrunk until it fits downscaling §8.2
A note on the photo: "send it back rather than shrink it" "oversized_image": "error" §8.2
A blank border added so the last row of squares is whole padding §8.2
A document where every page is photographed and also typed out a PDF document block §8.3
The cloakroom itself, shared by everyone in the building the Files API and its workspace scope §8.4
A quotation slip pinned to a sentence of the reply: the exact words and where they sit a citation §8.5
A slip reading "from character 50 up to, but not including, 81" exclusive end indices §8.5
A sentence of the reply with no slip on it an uncited claim §8.5

This section has six subsections, in three parts:

  1. images: how to send them, and what they cost (§8.1, §8.2);
  2. documents: PDFs, and the Files API that stores them (§8.3, §8.4);
  3. checking and designing: citations, and how to put a request together (§8.5, §8.6).

Three examples call the real API, in §8.3, §8.4 and §8.5. Running them needs an API key and your own files, and your ids, wording and token counts will differ from the ones shown. Every other example is plain Python, and prints the same thing on every machine.

8.1 Images

An image block is a content block (§2.5) inside a user message. An image block can get its data from three sources:

  • base64: the bytes of the image, written out as text inside the request itself;
  • url: an address on the web, which the API fetches the image from;
  • file: the file_id of an image you uploaded earlier with the Files API (§8.4).

The model sees the same image whichever source you pick. So the choice between them is about payload size and not capability. The payload is the request body itself, the bytes your program sends over the network. On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud only base64 is available today.

The example below builds one block of each kind, without calling the API, and prints how long each block is when written out as text. The image is a PNG one pixel in size, so even its base64 version is small here:

import base64

PIXEL = base64.b64decode(
    "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mP8"
    "z8BQDwAEhQGAhKmMIQAAAABJRU5ErkJggg==")

by_base64 = {
    "type": "image",
    "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "image/png",
               "data": base64.standard_b64encode(PIXEL).decode()},
}
by_url = {
    "type": "image",
    "source": {"type": "url", "url": "https://example.com/diagram.png"},
}
by_file = {
    "type": "image",
    "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": "file_011CQ8s7Xk2b"},
}

for label, block in (("base64", by_base64), ("url", by_url), ("file", by_file)):
    payload = len(str(block))
    print(f"{label:<8} source type={block['source']['type']:<8} "
          f"block size {payload:>4} chars")

print()
print("base64 grows with the image; url and file_id do not")
print(f"a 4 MB photo base64-encodes to about "
      f"{round(4 * 1024 * 1024 * 4 / 3 / 1024):,} kB of request body")

base64   source type=base64   block size  182 chars
url      source type=url      block size   86 chars
file     source type=file     block size   77 chars

base64 grows with the image; url and file_id do not
a 4 MB photo base64-encodes to about 5,461 kB of request body

Reading the output:

  • The base64 block is the longest, at 182 characters, even for a single pixel, because the image itself travels inside it.
  • The url and file blocks are 86 and 77 characters, and they stay that size however large the image is.
  • The last line scales the first one up: a 4 MB photo becomes about 5,461 kB of request body.

In the picture: base64 is wiring the photograph down the telegraph line as text characters. It always works, but text is a third longer than the photo, and the office has a limit on how much one telegram may carry.

Base64 is the simplest and the one that fails first. Base64 is a way of writing binary data as plain text. Binary data is anything that is not text, such as the bytes of a photo. The encoding writes every 3 bytes as 4 characters, so it inflates the data by about a third. The request size limit is 32 MB for standard endpoints. Send several photos and you are there.

How many photos is "several"? The example below encodes real bytes and checks them against two limits from the grid further down: 10 MB per image after encoding, and 32 MB for the whole request:

import base64

MB = 1024 * 1024
REQUEST_LIMIT = 32 * MB          # standard endpoints
IMAGE_LIMIT = 10 * MB            # per image, base64-encoded, Claude API

for raw_mb in (1, 3, 7.5, 8):
    raw = bytes(int(raw_mb * MB))
    encoded = len(base64.standard_b64encode(raw))
    verdict = "ok" if encoded <= IMAGE_LIMIT else "over the 10 MB image limit"
    print(f"{raw_mb:>4} MB photo -> {encoded / MB:6.2f} MB as base64  {verdict}")

print()
photo = len(base64.standard_b64encode(bytes(3 * MB)))
print(f"3 MB photos that fit in one 32 MB request: {REQUEST_LIMIT // photo}")

   1 MB photo ->   1.33 MB as base64  ok
   3 MB photo ->   4.00 MB as base64  ok
 7.5 MB photo ->  10.00 MB as base64  ok
   8 MB photo ->  10.67 MB as base64  over the 10 MB image limit

3 MB photos that fit in one 32 MB request: 8

Reading it:

  • A 3 MB photo becomes exactly 4.00 MB of base64.
  • 7.5 MB is the largest photo that fits the 10 MB image limit. An 8 MB photo goes over it, although the file on your disk is under 10 MB, because the limit counts the encoded size.
  • Only 8 photos of 3 MB fit in one request. The grid allows 100 or more images per request, so the size of the request runs out long before the count does.

Formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP. Animations are not supported, and only the first frame is used, silently. Silently means with no error and no warning: an animated GIF is accepted, and the model sees one still picture.

One capability worth naming, because it removes a design decision, is that multilingual input and output need no configuration. Text in any supported language goes in the same blocks as English, whether it is a French support ticket, a Japanese product description or a document that mixes scripts. The model answers in the language of the request unless told otherwise. What does change is the token count (§1.2). Non-Latin scripts, such as Japanese, Arabic or Hindi, run considerably denser: the same message needs more tokens. So a multilingual workload budgeted on English prose is under-budgeted.

The limits worth knowing before you design around them are in the grid below. "A 200k window" means a context window of 200,000 tokens:

100 images per request
On models with a 200k window; 600 on models with a larger one. Request size usually binds first.
10 MB per image
Base64-encoded, on the Claude API. 5 MB on Bedrock and Google Cloud.
8000 × 8000 px
Maximum dimensions. Larger is rejected.
Over 20 images
A stricter per-image dimension limit applies to every image block in the request. Keep each under 2000 px, or keep the request to 20 blocks or fewer.

That last row is the one that surprises people, because the count includes images from earlier turns that you resend, and images nested inside tool_result content, such as screenshots returned to the computer use tool. Both need a word of explanation:

  • Each request carries the whole conversation again, because the API keeps nothing between requests (§2.3). So a photo sent in turn 1 is still inside the request of turn 21.
  • Computer use is a tool that lets the model operate a computer: it asks for a screenshot, reads it and asks for a click. Your program returns each screenshot inside a tool_result (§6.5).

An agent driving computer use accumulates screenshots turn after turn, which is how a conversation crosses the threshold without any single request looking large. On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud, document blocks such as PDFs count toward the threshold as well. Above it, an image over the stricter limit is rejected with an error that states the limit in pixels. To stay under it on every platform, keep each image at 2000 px or less on both sides, or keep the request to 20 image and document blocks or fewer.

Now the puzzle. The example below replays the technician's conversation through a stand-in for that rule. It is a toy, not the API's own check: it uses 2000 px, the safe value from the docs, where the real limit is the number the error message states. The image_blocks function also looks inside tool_result blocks, because nested images count too:

LIMIT_PX = 2000     # the safe edge the docs give for requests over 20 images


def image_blocks(content):
    """Every image block in a content list, including ones nested in tool results."""
    for block in content:
        if block["type"] == "image":
            yield block
        elif block["type"] == "tool_result":
            yield from image_blocks(block["content"])


def check(messages):
    images = [b for m in messages if isinstance(m["content"], list)
              for b in image_blocks(m["content"])]
    if len(images) <= 20:
        return f"{len(images):>2} images: ok"
    too_big = [b for b in images if max(b["size"]) > LIMIT_PX]
    if too_big:
        return f"{len(images):>2} images: rejected, {len(too_big)} over {LIMIT_PX} px"
    return f"{len(images):>2} images: ok"


photo = {"type": "image", "size": (4032, 3024)}     # a phone camera's default
messages = []
for turn in range(1, 23):
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [
        photo, {"type": "text", "text": f"Meter {turn}: what does it read?"}]})
    if turn in (1, 20, 21, 22):
        print(f"turn {turn:>2}: {check(messages)}")
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": "(a reading)"})

print()
small = {"type": "image", "size": (2000, 1500)}
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [small]} for _ in range(21)]
print("21 photos resized to 2000 px:", check(messages))

turn  1:  1 images: ok
turn 20: 20 images: ok
turn 21: 21 images: rejected, 21 over 2000 px
turn 22: 22 images: rejected, 22 over 2000 px

21 photos resized to 2000 px: 21 images: ok

Reading the output, turn by turn:

  • Turn 1 sends one image, and turn 20 sends twenty. Up to twenty images, a 4032-pixel photo is accepted, and the API shrinks it itself (§8.2).
  • Turn 21 sends 21 images, because the request carries every earlier photo again. Above twenty the stricter limit applies to every image in the request. All 21 photos are over it, not only the new one.
  • The last line sends the same 21 photos resized to 2000 px, and they pass.

That is the puzzle's answer. Photo 21 was no different from photo 20. The request was different: it was the first one carrying more than twenty images, and the rule judges the whole request. In the picture: the office has a rule for thick files, where more than twenty photos means every print must be small. Your file includes a copy of every photo from your earlier letters, because you resend the whole conversation each time.

8.2 What an Image Costs

The model does not read an image pixel by pixel. It cuts the image into squares of 28 × 28 pixels, called patches, and each patch becomes one visual token. So the cost is ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉. The ⌈ ⌉ brackets mean "round up": a strip 10 pixels wide at the edge still costs a whole patch. You can compute this exactly before you send anything.

There is a ceiling. Each model has a largest image it reads at full size, set by two limits: the longest edge in pixels, and the number of visual tokens. Models fall into two tiers:

  • the standard tier: 1,568 px on the longest edge, and 1,568 visual tokens;
  • the high-resolution tier, Claude 4.7 and later models: 2,576 px and 4,784 visual tokens.

An image over either limit is downscaled, made smaller, to the largest size that fits both limits. The aspect ratio, the proportion of width to height, stays the same.

For nearly every photo and screenshot the token limit decides the final size, not the edge limit. That is easy to get wrong. Scaling a 1920 × 1080 screenshot down to the 1,568 px edge gives 1568 × 882, and that costs 56 × 32 = 1,792 tokens, which is over the budget. The function resized_size below is the rule Anthropic documents. It uses a binary search: it tries the width halfway between one that fits and one that does not, keeps the half where the answer must lie, and repeats until one pixel separates the two. The table shows what each tier makes of five common sizes, and the last two lines price two of them on Opus 5, at $5 per million input tokens:

import math

TIERS = {"standard": (1568, 1568), "high-resolution": (2576, 4784)}


def visual_tokens(width, height):
    return math.ceil(width / 28) * math.ceil(height / 28)


def resized_size(width, height, tier):
    """The size the image is scaled to before padding (Anthropic's documented rule)."""
    max_edge, max_tokens = TIERS[tier]

    def fits(w, h):
        return (math.ceil(w / 28) * 28 <= max_edge
                and math.ceil(h / 28) * 28 <= max_edge
                and visual_tokens(w, h) <= max_tokens)

    if fits(width, height):
        return width, height
    if height > width:
        h, w = resized_size(height, width, tier)
        return w, h
    aspect = width / height
    lo, hi = 1, width                 # lo always fits; hi never does
    while lo + 1 < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if fits(mid, max(round(mid / aspect), 1)):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo, max(round(lo / aspect), 1)


SIZES = [(200, 200), (1000, 1000), (1920, 1080), (2000, 1500), (3840, 2160)]
print(f"{'image':<14}{'standard px':>14}{'tokens':>8}"
      f"{'high-res px':>14}{'tokens':>8}")
for width, height in SIZES:
    sw, sh = resized_size(width, height, "standard")
    hw, hh = resized_size(width, height, "high-resolution")
    print(f"{f'{width}x{height}':<14}{f'{sw}x{sh}':>14}{visual_tokens(sw, sh):>8}"
          f"{f'{hw}x{hh}':>14}{visual_tokens(hw, hh):>8}")

print()
OPUS_PER_MTOK = 5.00
for label, tokens in (("1000x1000 on Opus 5", 1296), ("4K on Opus 5", 4784)):
    print(f"{label:<24}{tokens:>6} tokens  "
          f"${tokens / 1e6 * OPUS_PER_MTOK * 1000:>6.2f} per thousand images")

image            standard px  tokens   high-res px  tokens
200x200              200x200      64       200x200      64
1000x1000          1000x1000    1296     1000x1000    1296
1920x1080           1456x819    1560     1920x1080    2691
2000x1500           1270x952    1564     2000x1500    3888
3840x2160           1456x819    1560     2576x1449    4784

1000x1000 on Opus 5       1296 tokens  $  6.48 per thousand images
4K on Opus 5              4784 tokens  $ 23.92 per thousand images

Reading the table, row by row:

  • 200 × 200 and 1000 × 1000 fit both tiers unchanged. 1000 / 28 rounds up to 36, and 36 × 36 = 1,296 tokens.
  • 1920 × 1080 shrinks to 1456 × 819 on the standard tier, which is 52 × 30 = 1,560 tokens. On the high-resolution tier it is left alone, at 69 × 39 = 2,691 tokens.
  • 2000 × 1500 shrinks to 1270 × 952 on the standard tier, 46 × 34 = 1,564 tokens. Anthropic's own table of examples prints 1269 × 952 for this size, one pixel narrower than its reference code gives; the cost is 1,564 tokens either way.
  • 3840 × 2160, a 4K screenshot, has the same proportions as 1920 × 1080, so the standard tier gives it the same 1456 × 819. The high-resolution tier gives 2576 × 1449, which is 92 × 52 = 4,784 tokens, exactly its ceiling.
  • The prices: 1,296 tokens × $5 per million × 1,000 images = $6.48, and 4,784 tokens give $23.92.

In the picture: the office lays a grid of squares over each photograph and charges one word per square. A photo too big for the office's frame is shrunk until it fits.

High resolution is automatic on Claude 4.7 and later. There is no header and no opt-in, and it costs up to roughly three times the visual tokens of the standard tier for the same image: 4,784 against 1,560 for the 4K screenshot above. That is a good trade for computer use, screenshot understanding and dense documents, and a poor one for a photo you only need described.

Downscale before uploading when you do not need the fidelity. Fidelity is how much fine detail survives. Downscaling reduces tokens, latency and request size at once. Latency is the time you wait for the answer. It is the single most effective lever here. It also simplifies any coordinate work, because the model reports coordinates relative to the image after resizing.

Coordinates need a moment of their own. Ask the model where something is, such as "where is the Submit button?", and it answers in pixels, counted from the top-left corner: x to the right, y downward. Those pixels belong to the image the model saw, and two things separate that image from yours:

  • the resize, from §8.2's rule;
  • the padding: after any resize, every image is padded on its bottom and right edges up to the next multiple of 28 pixels. The padding is blank. The model sees it, but the content only ever fills the unpadded part.

So a coordinate is rescaled by the resized size, never the padded size. The example below takes a page scanned at 130 dpi, dots per inch. That page is 1075 × 1520 pixels: both sides are under 1,568, but it costs 39 × 55 = 2,145 tokens, so the standard tier resizes it. The example then maps a point the model reports back onto your page, both ways:

import math

def resized_size(width, height, max_edge=1568, max_tokens=1568):
    def fits(w, h):
        return (math.ceil(w / 28) * 28 <= max_edge
                and math.ceil(h / 28) * 28 <= max_edge
                and math.ceil(w / 28) * math.ceil(h / 28) <= max_tokens)
    if fits(width, height):
        return width, height
    if height > width:
        h, w = resized_size(height, width, max_edge, max_tokens)
        return w, h
    aspect = width / height
    lo, hi = 1, width
    while lo + 1 < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if fits(mid, max(round(mid / aspect), 1)):
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo, max(round(lo / aspect), 1)


page = (1075, 1520)                     # an A4 page scanned at 130 dpi
seen = resized_size(*page)
padded = tuple(math.ceil(n / 28) * 28 for n in seen)
print("your page     :", page)
print("model sees    :", seen)
print("after padding :", padded)

x, y = 462, 653.5                       # a point the model reports
right = (x / seen[0] * page[0], y / seen[1] * page[1])
wrong = (x / padded[0] * page[0], y / padded[1] * page[1])
print("rescaled by what it sees :", tuple(round(v, 1) for v in right))
print("rescaled by padded size  :", tuple(round(v, 1) for v in wrong))

your page     : (1075, 1520)
model sees    : (924, 1307)
after padding : (924, 1316)
rescaled by what it sees : (537.5, 760.0)
rescaled by padded size  : (537.5, 754.8)

Reading it:

  • The model sees 924 × 1307, and padding takes that to 924 × 1316, which is 47 × 28.
  • Rescaled by the size the model saw, the point lands at (537.5, 760.0). That is exactly half of 1075 and half of 1520: the centre of your page.
  • Rescaled by the padded size, y becomes 754.8, five pixels too high. Every coordinate shifts this way, and the error grows toward the bottom of the page.

In the picture: the office's frame only holds whole squares, so a blank border fills out the last row. Measure the photo, not the border.

The simplest fix is to resize the image yourself, to the size resized_size returns, before you send it. Then the image you have is the image the model sees, and its coordinates need no conversion. A high-resolution model does not resize that scan at all, because 2,145 tokens is inside its budget of 4,784.

Two smaller notes have real consequences:

  • Compressing to JPEG or WebP reduces latency by shrinking the request. But this kind of compression throws detail away, and heavy compression makes small text unreadable, so check what you are actually sending.
  • An oversized image is silently downscaled by default. To make it fail loudly instead, set the image block's transformations field to {"oversized_image": "error"}. The request is then rejected with a 400 that names the image's size and the largest size that fits. That is what you want in a coordinate workflow, because a new image source, or a switch to a model on the other tier, would otherwise shift every coordinate with no error at all.

One exception runs the other way. A screenshot returned to the computer use tool in a tool_result is never downscaled: if it is over the model's limits, the API rejects it. Resize those yourself before returning them. In the picture: some photos carry a note saying "if this does not fit the frame, send it back; do not shrink it", and the computer use desk applies that note to every screenshot.

8.3 PDFs

A PDF is a document block, and it is processed by the same vision path, the part of the model that reads images: each page is rendered as an image and also extracted as text. Rendered means drawn as a picture, like a screenshot of the page. Extracted means the text stored inside the file is read out. So the model gets every page twice. A document block carries:

  • a source, which takes the same three kinds as an image block: base64, url or file;
  • an optional title;
  • an optional context, a note about the document that the model reads but never cites;
  • an optional citations setting, which §8.5 is about.

The request below sends a board pack, the report a company's directors read before a meeting, by its file_id, with citations turned on. It prints the answer and the pages each citation covers. It needs an API key and a file you uploaded:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document",
         "source": {"type": "file", "file_id": "file_011CQ8s7Xk2b"},
         "title": "Q3 board pack",
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "What was the reported churn rate?"},
    ]}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    print("answer:", block.text)
    for citation in (block.citations or []):
        pages = range(citation.start_page_number,     # the end page is
                      citation.end_page_number)       # exclusive, like range
        print(f"  pages {list(pages)}: {citation.cited_text!r}")

print("input tokens:", response.usage.input_tokens)

answer: Reported churn was 3.1% for the quarter.
  pages [14]: 'Quarterly churn: 3.1% (down from 3.6%).'
input tokens: 48210

Reading the output:

  • The answer is one sentence, and it came back with one citation. Its cited_text is the passage word for word.
  • The citation's fields said page 14 to page 15, and the code printed [14]. That is not a typo. The end page is exclusive: the range runs up to it but does not include it, exactly like Python's range. §8.5 comes back to this rule.
  • 48,210 input tokens is the whole board pack, every page as text and as an image, inside the context window.

PDF support is available on every active model, and it needs no beta header. A beta header is an extra HTTP header that switches on a feature still being tested. The requirements for PDF support are worth memorising because they are the ones you hit:

32 MB per request
The whole payload, not just the PDF.
600 pages
Per request — but 100 when the request's context window is under 1M tokens.
1,500–3,000 text tokens/page
Typical, depending on density. Each page's image is billed on top, by §8.2's arithmetic. No PDF surcharge; standard token pricing.
No encryption
Standard PDFs only. Password-protected files are rejected.

The third row needs care. The docs give 1,500–3,000 tokens per page for the text of a page. Every page is also an image, and that image costs tokens too, by the same arithmetic as any other image. So the figures below are a floor, not an estimate. count_tokens (§2.8) on a few real pages gives the true number.

The example below sizes three documents with the text figures only, against a 200,000-token window and $5 per million input tokens:

PAGES_PER_DOC = [("a 4-page invoice", 4), ("a 40-page contract", 40),
                 ("a 300-page annual report", 300)]
TOKENS_PER_PAGE_LOW, TOKENS_PER_PAGE_HIGH = 1_500, 3_000
WINDOW, INPUT_PER_MTOK = 200_000, 5.00

print(f"{'document':<28}{'pages':>7}{'tokens (low-high)':>22}"
      f"{'% of 200k window':>19}{'cost':>9}")
for name, pages in PAGES_PER_DOC:
    low, high = pages * TOKENS_PER_PAGE_LOW, pages * TOKENS_PER_PAGE_HIGH
    share = high / WINDOW
    print(f"{name:<28}{pages:>7}{f'{low:,}-{high:,}':>22}"
          f"{share:>18.0%}{'$%.3f' % (high / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>9}")

print()
print("the 300-page report does not fit a 200k window at all —")
print("the PAGE limit is 600, and the window binds long before that")

document                      pages     tokens (low-high)   % of 200k window     cost
a 4-page invoice                  4          6,000-12,000                6%   $0.060
a 40-page contract               40        60,000-120,000               60%   $0.600
a 300-page annual report        300       450,000-900,000              450%   $4.500

the 300-page report does not fit a 200k window at all —
the PAGE limit is 600, and the window binds long before that

Reading it:

  • The 4-page invoice takes at most 12,000 tokens, 6% of the window, for 6 cents.
  • The 40-page contract takes up to 60% of the window before you have asked anything.
  • The 300-page report needs up to four and a half windows of text alone, before a single image token is counted.

Note the cited_text field on each citation. It carries the passage verbatim, word for word, so a check can compare cited_text against the source and not trust the page number alone (§8.5).

The page limit is almost never what stops you. A dense document fills the context window well before 600 pages, and the failure looks like a context error and not a document error. Split long documents into sections, or retrieve the relevant pages (§10) and do not send the whole thing. To retrieve is to search the document first and send only the parts that match the question.

Because PDF support runs on the vision path, it inherits every vision limitation, and §8.6 lists them. Accuracy degrades on low-quality scans, and the model should not be relied on for perfect precision without review. Two more consequences belong to PDFs alone:

  • Pages are turned into images on Anthropic's servers, at sizes you do not control. So coordinates the model gives for a PDF page cannot be mapped back onto the page reliably. To locate things on a page, turn the pages into images yourself and use §8.2's rule.
  • A scanned PDF that has no text inside it, only pictures of pages, can be read but cannot be cited. Citations point into extracted text (§8.5).

In the picture: a PDF is a document where every page is photographed and also typed out, and both copies go into the envelope.

8.4 The Files API

The Files API is a storage service. You upload a file once, get back an id, the file_id, and refer to the file by it in later requests. That keeps request payloads small and avoids re-sending the same bytes on every turn of a conversation. It needs no beta header, and the SDK call is client.files.upload. The example below uploads a PDF and prints what comes back. It needs an API key, and the bytes in it stand in for a real file:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

uploaded = client.files.upload(
    file=("board-pack.pdf", b"%PDF-1.7 ...", "application/pdf"),
)

print("id           :", uploaded.id)
print("filename     :", uploaded.filename)
print("size (bytes) :", uploaded.size_bytes)
print("mime type    :", uploaded.mime_type)
print("downloadable :", uploaded.downloadable)

id           : file_011CQ8s7Xk2b
filename     : board-pack.pdf
size (bytes) : 2418877
mime type    : application/pdf
downloadable : False

Reading the output:

  • id is what you put in later requests.
  • The size is 2,418,877 bytes, about 2.3 MB.
  • downloadable is False. A file you upload cannot be downloaded again through the API. Only files that the code execution tool or a Skill created (§7.8) can be.

The file_id then goes in a source of type "file", in an image block or a document block depending on what it is. Plain-text files go in a document block too. Formats a document block cannot read, such as spreadsheets, go to the code execution tool instead, the server tool that runs code in a sandbox (defined in §7's opening), in a container_upload block.

For an image, the file_id goes inside an image block's source, and for a PDF, inside a document block's. What this buys you is worth being precise about, because it is not a token saving. The content still enters the context window and is still billed as input tokens every turn. What you save is request payload, meaning the bytes crossing the wire. The upload is also done once and not per request. For a conversation that refers to the same 30-page PDF over ten turns, the bytes cross the wire once instead of ten times, and the token cost is the same either way.

The example below counts both for §8.3's board pack over ten turns. It uses the board pack's size from the upload above and its 48,210 tokens from §8.3's run:

import base64

PDF_BYTES = 2_418_877            # the board pack from the upload below
PDF_TOKENS = 48_210              # what one turn bills for it (§8.3's run)
TURNS = 10

as_base64 = len(base64.standard_b64encode(bytes(PDF_BYTES)))
as_file_id = len('{"type": "file", "file_id": "file_011CQ8s7Xk2b"}')

for name, per_turn in (("base64", as_base64), ("file_id", as_file_id)):
    sent = per_turn * TURNS
    print(f"{name:<8} bytes sent over {TURNS} turns: {sent:>12,}   "
          f"input tokens: {PDF_TOKENS * TURNS:,}")

base64   bytes sent over 10 turns:   32,251,720   input tokens: 482,100
file_id  bytes sent over 10 turns:          480   input tokens: 482,100

Reading it:

  • Base64 sends 32,251,720 bytes over ten turns, about 3.2 MB in every request.
  • The file_id reference is 48 characters a turn, 480 in all.
  • Input tokens are 482,100 on both lines. The bill does not move. Prompt caching (§9.3) is what makes resent tokens cheaper; the Files API does not.

In the picture: the Files API is the office cloakroom. You leave the parcel once and write the ticket number on each telegram. The writer still opens the parcel and reads all of it, every time.

The cloakroom has rules worth knowing before you build on it:

  • A file belongs to the whole workspace, not to one user, conversation or session. A workspace is a group inside your Anthropic organisation, with its own API keys. Any key with access to that workspace can use any file in it. So never accept a file_id from your users: someone who sends another person's id would read that person's document. Keep the record of which user owns which file in your own application. An application that serves many separate customers can give each customer a workspace of its own.
  • A file can be up to 500 MB, and an organisation can store 1 TB in all.
  • Uploading, listing, downloading and deleting are free. The content is billed as input tokens whenever a request uses it.
  • A file cannot be changed after upload. To change one, upload a new file and delete the old one.

Files persist until you delete them, or until an expiry you set at upload with expires_in_seconds, from one hour to 90 days. That is a data-retention surface, meaning one more place where customer data is kept: an uploaded customer document sits in your workspace until something removes it. Delete what you no longer need, and treat the file store the way you treat any other repository of customer content.

8.5 Citations

Citations turn an answer into something your code can check. Enable them on a document or search result, and each text block comes back with the exact passages it drew on.

Here is how it works. The API splits a plain-text or PDF document into sentences, which it calls chunks. The model then writes its answer as several text blocks instead of one. Each block that used a source carries a list of citations, and each citation names the chunk it points at. The request below gives the model a three-sentence refund policy as a plain-text document and asks two questions about it. It prints each text block with its citations. It needs an API key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

POLICY = ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery. "
          "Perishable goods are excluded. "
          "Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.")

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "document",
         "source": {"type": "text", "media_type": "text/plain", "data": POLICY},
         "title": "Refund policy",
         "citations": {"enabled": True}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "How long do refunds take, and are there exclusions?"},
    ]}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    marks = len(block.citations or [])
    print(f"[{marks} citation(s)] {block.text}")
    for citation in (block.citations or []):
        print(f"    chars {citation.start_char_index}-{citation.end_char_index}: "
              f"{citation.cited_text!r}")

[0 citation(s)] Here is what the policy says. 
[1 citation(s)] Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days, 
    chars 81-135: 'Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.'
[1 citation(s)] and perishable goods are excluded.
    chars 50-81: 'Perishable goods are excluded.'

Reading the output, block by block:

  • The answer came back as three text blocks, not one. The first is connective prose, words that link the answer together, and it cites nothing.
  • The second block cites characters 81 to 135, the policy's third sentence, word for word.
  • The third block cites characters 50 to 81, "Perishable goods are excluded." That span is 31 characters long for a sentence of 30, because a span includes the space after its sentence, while cited_text shows the sentence trimmed.
  • The policy's first sentence, about 30 days, is not cited anywhere, because the answer did not use it.

In the picture: the writer pins a quotation slip to each sentence of the reply, with the exact words and where they sit in your document.

The granularity is character indices into your source. Granularity is how finely a citation points. A character index is a position in the text, counted from 0. That is what makes the check mechanical and not a matter of judgement. You can verify that the cited span exists, that it says what the sentence claims, and, the useful one, that a sentence has no citation at all.

The indices follow one rule that catches people out. The start counts from 0 and the end is exclusive, exactly like a Python slice: source[50:81]. Page numbers count from 1, and their end is exclusive too. The check below compares one citation against the source, first the right way and then with the classic off-by-one mistake:

SOURCE = ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery. "
          "Perishable goods are excluded. "
          "Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.")

# One citation as the API returns it (§8.5's second sentence).
citation = {"start_char_index": 50, "end_char_index": 81,
            "cited_text": "Perishable goods are excluded."}


def span_matches(source, c):
    """End is exclusive, like a slice; the span keeps the sentence's trailing space."""
    span = source[c["start_char_index"]:c["end_char_index"]]
    return span.strip() == c["cited_text"]


def span_matches_inclusive(source, c):
    """The off-by-one: treating the end index as the last character."""
    span = source[c["start_char_index"]:c["end_char_index"] + 1]
    return span.strip() == c["cited_text"]


print("source length          :", len(SOURCE))
print("the exact slice        :", repr(SOURCE[50:81]))
print("exclusive end (right)  :", span_matches(SOURCE, citation))
print("inclusive end (wrong)  :", span_matches_inclusive(SOURCE, citation))
print("what the wrong one read:", repr(SOURCE[50:82]))

pages = {"start_page_number": 14, "end_page_number": 15}
covered = list(range(pages["start_page_number"], pages["end_page_number"]))
print("pages covered by 14, 15:", covered)

source length          : 135
the exact slice        : 'Perishable goods are excluded. '
exclusive end (right)  : True
inclusive end (wrong)  : False
what the wrong one read: 'Perishable goods are excluded. A'
pages covered by 14, 15: [14]

Reading it:

  • The slice 50:81 gives the sentence plus its trailing space. After strip(), which removes spaces at either end, it matches cited_text.
  • Treating 81 as the last character reads one too many, the "A" that starts the next sentence. The match fails, and a grader written that way flags a correct citation as bad.
  • Pages 14 and 15 cover page 14 only, which is how §8.3's citation printed [14].

In the picture: the slip reads "from character 50 up to, but not including, 81".

Three practical points.

Citations are off by default and enabled per block. Within one request, all search results must agree on the setting (§10.7), while documents are configured individually.

A text block with no citations is a claim resting on nothing in your sources. §10.7 builds the grader, and this is where the data for it comes from. It is the cheapest faithfulness check available, and it needs no judge. Faithfulness means the answer says only what the sources support. A judge is a second model call that grades the answer (§13.5).

Not every uncited sentence is a defect. Connective prose such as "Here is what I found" legitimately cites nothing. The check to build is not "every block has a citation" but "every block making a factual claim has one". That is why §13.4's graders combine the citation check with a rubric, a written list of what a good answer must do, and do not replace one with the other.

Two more facts shape designs:

  • Citations cost little. Turning them on adds a few input tokens, for the extra instructions and the chunking. The cited_text field does not count toward output tokens, and it does not count toward input tokens either when you send the answer back in a later turn.
  • Citations and structured outputs (§4) cannot be used together. A request that enables citations on any document or search result and also sets output_config.format is rejected with a 400, because citation blocks cannot be woven into an answer that must match a strict JSON schema. If you need both, get the cited answer first, then extract fields from it in a second call (prompt chaining, §3.8). In the picture: the writer cannot fill in your printed reply card (§4) and pin slips to its sentences at the same time, because the card has no room for slips.

8.6 Designing a Multimodal Request

Putting it together, here are the decisions worth making deliberately. The table below lists five common situations, the source to use for each, and why. It is plain Python that prints the table:

SCENARIOS = [
    # (scenario, source, why)
    ("one screenshot, one turn", "base64",
     "simplest; payload is small and nothing is reused"),
    ("a 30-page PDF across 10 turns", "Files API",
     "upload once; the tokens recur either way but the bytes do not"),
    ("40 product photos to classify", "Files API + batch",
     "over the 20-image threshold, so resize to 2000px as well"),
    ("an image the user linked to", "url",
     "no upload, no payload — but the URL must stay reachable"),
    ("screenshots in an agent loop", "base64, resized",
     "they accumulate in context and count toward the 20-image threshold"),
]

print(f"{'scenario':<32}{'source':<22}{'why'}")
for scenario, source, why in SCENARIOS:
    print(f"{scenario:<32}{source:<22}{why}")

print()
print("the recurring trap: images from EARLIER turns still count")

scenario                        source                why
one screenshot, one turn        base64                simplest; payload is small and nothing is reused
a 30-page PDF across 10 turns   Files API             upload once; the tokens recur either way but the bytes do not
40 product photos to classify   Files API + batch     over the 20-image threshold, so resize to 2000px as well
an image the user linked to     url                   no upload, no payload — but the URL must stay reachable
screenshots in an agent loop    base64, resized       they accumulate in context and count toward the 20-image threshold

the recurring trap: images from EARLIER turns still count

Reading the table, row by row:

  • One screenshot, used once: base64. Nothing is reused, so storing a file buys nothing.
  • A 30-page PDF across ten turns: the Files API. As §8.4's example showed, the tokens recur either way but the bytes do not.
  • 40 product photos: the Files API, and the Batch API (§15.2), which runs requests later at half price. 40 photos are over the 20-image threshold of §8.1, so resize each one to 2000 px as well.
  • An image the user linked to: a url source. There is nothing to upload, but the URL must still work when the API fetches it.
  • Screenshots in an agent loop: base64, resized. They pile up in the conversation and count toward the 20-image threshold, and a computer use screenshot over the model's limits is rejected rather than shrunk (§8.2).

The last line of the output is the puzzle from the start of this section, in one sentence.

And here are the limitations to design around and not discover:

  • The model will not identify people in images and refuses to.
  • Counting objects is approximate, especially when there are many small ones.
  • Coordinate output is approximate.
  • Images that are blurry, rotated or smaller than 200 pixels are misread more often.
  • It cannot tell whether an image is AI-generated, and will be confidently wrong if asked.
  • It is not a diagnostic tool for medical imaging, such as CT or MRI scans.
  • It does not read an image's metadata, such as the date or camera settings a photo file carries.

Each of these is a place where an application built on the assumption of precision will fail in a way its tests did not catch. So if your product depends on one of them, that is the case §13.3 needs in its edge-case bucket.

Back to the technician's meter photos. The twenty-first message failed because a request carries the whole conversation, and the image rules judge the whole request: above twenty images, every image must meet the stricter limit, including the ones sent in earlier turns. Resizing each photo to 2000 px, which §8.2's arithmetic says costs no more than the original on either tier, fixes it. In the picture, that is the office counting every photo in your file, the old copies included. The rest of the section was the other enclosures: the grid of squares that prices a photo, the documents photographed and typed out, the cloakroom ticket that saves bytes but not words, and the quotation slips that let your code check the reply.

Exercises

Exercise 8.1 — Size a document pipeline. You process 2,000 scanned invoices a day, averaging 3 pages each, extracting line items as structured output. Compute the token cost, decide base64 versus Files API, and say what you would change to halve the bill.

Solution 
INVOICES_PER_DAY, PAGES_EACH, DAYS = 2_000, 3, 30
TOKENS_PER_PAGE = 2_200          # scans are dense; measure, do not assume
OUTPUT_TOKENS = 320              # a structured line-item extraction
IN_PER_MTOK, OUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 25.00
HAIKU_IN, HAIKU_OUT = 1.00, 5.00
BATCH_DISCOUNT = 0.50

pages = INVOICES_PER_DAY * PAGES_EACH * DAYS
input_tokens = pages * TOKENS_PER_PAGE
output_tokens = INVOICES_PER_DAY * DAYS * OUTPUT_TOKENS

opus = input_tokens / 1e6 * IN_PER_MTOK + output_tokens / 1e6 * OUT_PER_MTOK
haiku = input_tokens / 1e6 * HAIKU_IN + output_tokens / 1e6 * HAIKU_OUT

print(f"pages per month     : {pages:>12,}")
print(f"input tokens        : {input_tokens:>12,}")
print(f"output tokens       : {output_tokens:>12,}")
print()
print(f"{'configuration':<34}{'$/month':>12}{'vs baseline':>13}")
for label, cost in (("Opus 5, real time", opus),
                    ("Opus 5, Batch API", opus * BATCH_DISCOUNT),
                    ("Haiku 4.5, real time", haiku),
                    ("Haiku 4.5, Batch API", haiku * BATCH_DISCOUNT)):
    print(f"{label:<34}{'$' + format(cost, ',.0f'):>12}{cost / opus:>12.0%}")

print()
print(f"input is {input_tokens / (input_tokens + output_tokens):.0%} of all tokens:")
print("this is an INPUT-bound workload, so page count is the lever")

pages per month     :      180,000
input tokens        :  396,000,000
output tokens       :   19,200,000

configuration                          $/month  vs baseline
Opus 5, real time                       $2,460        100%
Opus 5, Batch API                       $1,230         50%
Haiku 4.5, real time                      $492         20%
Haiku 4.5, Batch API                      $246         10%

input is 95% of all tokens:
this is an INPUT-bound workload, so page count is the lever

Use the Files API, and be clear that it is not a cost decision. Base64 inflates the payload by a third, and a three-page scan is easily several megabytes, so at 2,000 a day you will meet the 32 MB request limit on the fat ones. But the token cost is identical either way, because the pages still enter the window. The Files API buys reliability and smaller requests, and not a smaller bill.

Batch processing halves it, and this workload is the ideal candidate. Invoices are not latency-sensitive, because nobody is waiting. That is a 50% saving for a scheduling change, and it is the first thing I would do.

Then reconsider the model. This is a structured-extraction task against a schema (§4), which is close to the definition of what a small model handles well. Haiku is a fifth of the price, and combined with batching it is a tenth of the baseline. The prerequisite is §13's eval: run both models over a few hundred labelled invoices and compare field-level accuracy. If Haiku holds, the saving is enormous. If it does not, you have learned that at the cost of an afternoon and not a quarter.

And the lever the arithmetic points at. Input is the overwhelming majority of tokens, so anything that reduces pages reduces the bill proportionally. Two things are worth checking. One is whether every page needs to go to the model at all, since a cover sheet and a terms-and-conditions page carry no line items. The other is whether the scans are being downscaled before upload. A 300 dpi scan of an A4 page is far past what is needed to read a table, and §8.2's arithmetic applies directly.

What I would measure first. The 2,200-tokens-per-page figure is an assumption, and everything above scales with it. count_tokens on a representative sample of real invoices costs nothing and turns this estimate into a number.

Exercise 8.2 — Build the citation check. Write a grader that flags unsupported claims in a cited answer, and say what it cannot catch.

Solution 
SOURCE = ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery. Perishable goods "
          "are excluded. Approved refunds are processed within 5 business days.")

# What the API returns: text blocks, each with zero or more citations.
BLOCKS = [
    ("Here is what the policy says.", []),
    ("Refunds are available within 30 days of delivery.",
     [(0, 49)]),
    ("Perishable goods are excluded.", [(50, 80)]),
    ("Processing takes 5 business days once approved.", [(81, 135)]),
    ("Most customers see the credit within a week.", []),
    ("Refunds are available within 60 days.", [(0, 49)]),
]

CLAIM_MARKERS = ("day", "week", "%", "excluded", "processed", "available")


def looks_factual(text):
    return any(marker in text.lower() for marker in CLAIM_MARKERS)


def grade(blocks, source):
    findings = []
    for text, spans in blocks:
        if not looks_factual(text):
            continue                      # connective prose cites nothing
        if not spans:
            findings.append(("UNCITED", text))
            continue
        for start, end in spans:
            cited = source[start:end]
            if cited not in source:
                findings.append(("BAD-SPAN", text))
    return findings


for kind, text in grade(BLOCKS, SOURCE):
    print(f"{kind:<10}{text}")

print()
total = sum(looks_factual(t) for t, _ in BLOCKS)
print(f"{total} factual claims, {len(grade(BLOCKS, SOURCE))} flagged")
print()
print("what it CANNOT catch:")
for miss in ("a claim that cites a real span which does not support it",
             "'60 days' citing the sentence that says 30 — the span is valid",
             "an omission: something true the answer left out"):
    print(f"  · {miss}")

UNCITED   Most customers see the credit within a week.

5 factual claims, 1 flagged

what it CANNOT catch:
  · a claim that cites a real span which does not support it
  · '60 days' citing the sentence that says 30 — the span is valid
  · an omission: something true the answer left out

What it catches is real and cheap. An uncited factual claim, such as "Most customers see the credit within a week", is flagged with no model call, no judge and no rubric. In a RAG system that is the most common hallucination shape, because the model is filling a gap the sources left.

What it misses is the more interesting half, and the last row is the demonstration. "Refunds are available within 60 days" cites character span 0–49, which is a genuine span of the source saying 30 days. The citation is structurally valid and semantically wrong. No span check can see that, because the mechanism only proves where the model looked and not that the sentence follows from it.

So the citation check is a filter, not a verifier, and it works together with §14's layers in the same way. Structural checks are free and catch the cheap failures at volume. A judge (§13.5) with a rubric that asks "is this claim supported by the cited text?" catches the expensive ones. You can afford to run it only on the blocks that carry citations, because the uncited ones were already caught for nothing.

The looks_factual heuristic is the weakest part, and I would replace it. Keyword matching to decide which sentences are claims will both over-fire and under-fire. It is here because it is honest about the shape of the problem. In production, the better design is to require citations on every block and treat the connective-prose exception as a rubric question for the judge.

One thing this cannot address at all: omission. An answer that cites everything it says and leaves out the exclusion for perishable goods scores perfectly. Faithfulness and completeness are different criteria, and §13.2's multidimensional table is where they get measured separately.

SECTION 9

Context Engineering

Start with a puzzle. A support assistant answers staff questions from a forty-page handbook. The team reads that prompt caching makes repeated text cheap, switches it on, and sends two questions a minute apart. The handbook is identical in both requests. Both responses report the same thing: 9,840 tokens written to the cache and 0 read from it. Nothing errors, both answers are fine, and the bill for those two requests is 25% higher than it was with caching off. So what is different between the two requests? Guess before you read on. §9.3 runs a small model of the cache that answers it, and §9.5 names the culprit for real.

To see why that can happen, you need one fact from §1. The model is stateless, which means it remembers nothing between requests. Every request carries the entire world it will see, and you resend that world on every turn. Section 6 built a loop that grows the conversation by two messages per tool call and then sends all of it again. This section is about three things:

  • what that resending costs, in money and in waiting time;
  • what a long, cluttered conversation does to the quality of the answers;
  • the four mechanisms the API gives you for controlling it.

The word engineering is doing real work in the title. Prompt engineering (§3) is about what you say. Context engineering is about what is present. The context is everything a single request puts in front of the model, and the context window is the most it can hold (§1.4). Context engineering decides:

  • what stays in the window;
  • what gets cached, so it is cheap to send again;
  • what gets cleared, because it is no longer useful;
  • what gets summarised, so it takes less room;
  • what lives outside the window entirely and is fetched back on demand.

In production systems, meaning the ones real users depend on, this is where the money is and where the latency is. Latency is how long a user waits for an answer. It is also, and people discover this last, where a surprising amount of the accuracy is. A window stuffed with stale tool output is a window in which the relevant sentence is harder to find.

Here is the picture for the whole section. Since §1 the model has been a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. The office charges by the word, and the writer keeps no copies. So every telegram you send has to carry the whole correspondence again, from the first letter. This section is about managing the file you resend: keeping it cheap, keeping it short, and keeping the important parts somewhere safe. Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram office In this section Section
The writer keeps no copies, so every telegram carries the whole file again resending the conversation on every turn §9.1
The office's free desk that counts the words of a draft before you send it the token counting endpoint §9.2
A printing plate of your standard opening pages, kept at the office the prompt cache §9.3
A plate fits only a letter whose opening is the same, word for word, up to where the plate ends the prefix rule §9.3
Making a plate costs a little more than one printing; printing from it costs a tenth cache write 1.25×, cache read 0.1× §9.3
A pencil mark on the draft: "make a plate up to here" a cache breakpoint §9.4
How long the office keeps a plate: five minutes, or an hour for a higher fee the cache TTL §9.4
The clock time typed at the top of page one a timestamp in the system prompt §9.5
Old enclosures taken out of the file, each replaced by a slip saying "removed" context editing §9.6
The writer's own short summary replacing the oldest pages compaction §9.7
A notebook in your own filing cabinet that the writer may ask to read or write the memory tool §9.8
A lock that keeps the writer to one drawer of that cabinet path confinement §9.8

This section has nine subsections, in four parts:

  1. what context costs, and how to measure it before you send it (§9.1, §9.2);
  2. caching the part that never changes (§9.3, §9.4, §9.5);
  3. shrinking the part that grows, by clearing or by summarising (§9.6, §9.7);
  4. keeping things outside the window, and choosing between all four mechanisms (§9.8, §9.9).

Six examples call the real API, one in each of §9.2 to §9.7. Running them needs an API key, and your token counts and wording will differ from the ones shown. Every other example is plain Python, and prints the same thing on every machine.

9.1 The Bill You Pay Every Turn

Start with the arithmetic, because it is unintuitive and it decides everything else.

The example below models a ten-turn conversation with an agent. Each turn adds a user question, one tool result and the model's answer, and then the whole history is sent again. The prices are Claude Opus 5's: $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, often written $5/MTok and $25/MTok. The table it prints shows five of the ten turns:

SYSTEM_TOKENS = 1_200         # instructions, stable
TOOLS_TOKENS = 3_200          # 34 definitions, stable
USER_TOKENS = 60              # one question
ASSISTANT_TOKENS = 220        # one answer
TOOL_RESULT_TOKENS = 900      # one search result coming back

INPUT_PER_MTOK, OUTPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00, 25.00

print(f"{'turn':>4} {'input tokens':>13} {'cumulative in':>14} "
      f"{'cost this turn':>15} {'cumulative':>11}")
history = SYSTEM_TOKENS + TOOLS_TOKENS
cumulative_in = 0
cumulative_cost = 0.0
for turn in range(1, 11):
    history += USER_TOKENS + TOOL_RESULT_TOKENS + ASSISTANT_TOKENS
    cumulative_in += history
    cost = (history / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK
            + ASSISTANT_TOKENS / 1e6 * OUTPUT_PER_MTOK)
    cumulative_cost += cost
    if turn in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10):
        print(f"{turn:>4} {history:>13,} {cumulative_in:>14,} "
              f"{'$%.4f' % cost:>15} {'$%.4f' % cumulative_cost:>11}")

linear = 10 * (SYSTEM_TOKENS + TOOLS_TOKENS + USER_TOKENS
               + TOOL_RESULT_TOKENS + ASSISTANT_TOKENS)
print(f"\nif each turn were independent: {linear:,} input tokens")
print(f"because the conversation is resent: {cumulative_in:,} input tokens")
print(f"ratio: {cumulative_in / linear:.2f}x")

turn  input tokens  cumulative in  cost this turn  cumulative
   1         5,580          5,580         $0.0334     $0.0334
   2         6,760         12,340         $0.0393     $0.0727
   3         7,940         20,280         $0.0452     $0.1179
   5        10,300         39,700         $0.0570     $0.2260
  10        16,200        108,900         $0.0865     $0.5995

if each turn were independent: 55,800 input tokens
because the conversation is resent: 108,900 input tokens
ratio: 1.95x

Line by line, here is what the table says:

  • Turn 1 sends 5,580 input tokens. That is the stable part, 1,200 tokens of system prompt plus 3,200 of tool definitions, plus this turn's 60 + 900 + 220 tokens. At $5 per million that is $0.0279 of input, and the 220-token answer adds $0.0055 of output, so the turn costs $0.0334.
  • Turn 2 sends 6,760. That is turn 1's 5,580 again, plus 1,180 new tokens. Nothing from turn 1 was dropped, because the writer keeps no copies.
  • Turn 10 sends 16,200 by itself, and the ten turns together have sent 108,900 input tokens.
  • The last three lines compare that with an imaginary world in which each turn stood alone at 5,580 tokens: 55,800 in all.

A conversation costs a quadratic in its length, not a linear amount. Quadratic means the total grows roughly with the square of the number of turns, the way the area of a square grows with its side. Turn ten pays for turns one through nine again. That is why ten turns cost 108,900 input tokens and not the 55,800 they would cost if each stood alone, which is 1.95× already, and the multiplier keeps climbing. At twenty turns it is higher still, because every new turn re-pays for a longer history. This is the single most important cost fact about the API, and it is invisible if you only ever test with two-turn conversations.

In the telegram office, this is the file growing. Every telegram carries every earlier letter, every enclosure and every reply, and the office counts all of it again.

Three consequences follow, and each one gets a subsection below.

The stable part is resent unchanged every time, which means it can be cached and should be (§9.3). System prompts and tool definitions are the same bytes on turn ten as on turn one. So paying full price for them ten times is a choice and not a requirement.

The volatile part grows without bound, and most of the growth is tool results: 900 tokens each here, against 220 for the model's own answers. Volatile means it changes from turn to turn. Those results were useful when the model read them and are mostly dead weight afterwards. §9.6 clears them.

Eventually the window fills. A 1M-token window is large, but an agent doing real work reaches it, and quality degrades before capacity does. §9.7 summarises the old part instead of truncating it, meaning cutting off the oldest part and throwing it away.

9.2 Counting Before You Send

Guessing token counts is how people end up debugging a 400 in production. A 400 is the HTTP status the API returns for a request it refuses (§2.9), and a request that does not fit the window is one of them. In the telegram office, there is a free desk that counts the words of a draft before you send it. The API has the same thing: an endpoint for counting, it is free, and it accepts the same request shape you were going to send.

The example below counts a small request with one tool and a system prompt. It calls the real API, so it needs a key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

TOOLS = [{
    "name": "search_docs",
    "description": "Full-text search over the internal handbook.",
    "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                     "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
                     "required": ["query"]},
}]

count = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    system="You are a concise internal support assistant.",
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I request unpaid leave?"}],
)

print("input tokens:", count.input_tokens)

input tokens: 168

Note what is being counted. tools and system are included, because they are part of the prompt. This is how you discover that a tool surface you thought was small is not. The tool surface is the set of tool definitions you send (§6.9).

Four details about the counting endpoint itself are worth knowing:

  • The count is an estimate. The docs say the real request may differ "by a small amount". Treat it as a measurement for decisions, not as an invoice.
  • It has its own rate limit, separate from sending messages, so counting does not eat into the budget you send messages from.
  • It refuses a few things the Messages API accepts: server tools such as web search (§7), the MCP connector, and image or document blocks that use a url or file source. To count an image or a PDF, send it as base64.
  • It ignores caching. A count tells you how big the request is, not how much of it would be read from the cache.

Two facts about counting shape design decisions elsewhere in the course.

Tokens are not words and not characters. English prose runs roughly four characters per token, but code, JSON, non-Latin scripts and long identifiers all run denser. The ~chars/4 estimates used for back-of-envelope work in §6.9 are fine for deciding whether to investigate, and useless for deciding whether a request fits.

The tokeniser changed. The tokeniser is the part that cuts text into tokens (§1.2). Claude 4.7 and later use a newer tokeniser that produces roughly 30% more tokens for the same text than the one Sonnet 4.6 and earlier use. That is not a price rise, because per-token prices differ too. But it does mean that a token budget measured on an older model does not transfer. It also means that any hard-coded "this fits in 8,000 tokens" assertion inherited from an older codebase should be re-measured and not trusted.

Here is that last point as arithmetic. The 30% is the docs' rough figure, and the real increase depends on the text, so this is an illustration and not a conversion formula:

BUDGET = 8_000                  # "this prompt fits in 8,000 tokens"
measured_on_old_model = 7_200   # counted once, on a model before Claude Opus 4.7

for model, factor in (("older tokeniser", 1.00), ("newer tokeniser", 1.30)):
    tokens = round(measured_on_old_model * factor)
    verdict = "fits" if tokens <= BUDGET else "does NOT fit"
    print(f"{model}: about {tokens:,} tokens -> {verdict}")

older tokeniser: about 7,200 tokens -> fits
newer tokeniser: about 9,360 tokens -> does NOT fit

The prompt did not change, and the budget did not change. Only the model did, and a prompt that fitted with 800 tokens to spare is now 1,360 tokens over. The fix is not to multiply by 1.3. It is to count again, with the model you will actually send, because the endpoint counts with that model's tokeniser.

9.3 Prompt Caching: The Prefix Rule

Caching is the highest-value change available in most LLM applications, and it hinges on one rule that is easy to state and easy to violate by accident.

In the telegram office, caching is a printing plate. Your standard opening pages, the instructions and the handbook, are the same on every telegram. So the office can set them in type once, keep the plate, and print from it next time instead of counting the words again. But a plate is a fixed thing. It fits only a letter whose opening is the same, word for word, up to the place where the plate ends.

The cache is a prefix match. A prefix is the beginning of something, up to some point. The request is rendered in a fixed order (tools, then system, then messages), and a cache entry covers everything from the start up to a designated breakpoint. Any byte that changes anywhere in that prefix invalidates the entry and everything after it. To invalidate an entry means it no longer matches, so the next request writes a new one instead of reading the old one.

1. tools
Rendered first, so cached first. Change one tool description and every cache below it dies — tools, system and messages alike. A tool description is the highest-leverage text in the request in both directions: it decides tool selection (§6.2) and it gates the entire cache.
2. system
Second. A timestamp in the system prompt is the classic silent cache killer: it invalidates system and messages on every single request while looking completely harmless.
3. messages
Last, and the part that grows. In a conversation the breakpoint moves forward through this as turns accumulate.

Here is the rule as a toy you can run. It does not call the API. It keeps a set of every prefix it has seen, renders each request in the API's order, and either reads the prefix from its "cache" or writes it there. Only the tools and the system prompt form the prefix here, as if the breakpoint sat at the end of the system prompt, so the user's question after it never affects the lookup:

cache = set()       # the prefixes the office has kept a plate of


def send(tools, system, question):
    """A toy of the prefix rule. The real API is not called."""
    prefix = tools + "\n" + system           # rendered in order: tools, then system
    size = len(prefix.split())               # the toy counts one token per word
    if prefix in cache:
        return f"read  {size} tokens from the cache"
    cache.add(prefix)
    return f"write {size} tokens to the cache"


TOOLS = "search_docs: full-text search over the staff handbook"
HANDBOOK = "Staff may request unpaid leave in writing. " * 40

print("1:", send(TOOLS, HANDBOOK, "How do I request unpaid leave?"))
print("2:", send(TOOLS, HANDBOOK, "Can I take leave in December?"))
print("3:", send(TOOLS, "Today is 2026-10-21 09:14:03. " + HANDBOOK, "How do I request unpaid leave?"))
print("4:", send(TOOLS, "Today is 2026-10-21 09:15:41. " + HANDBOOK, "Can I take leave in December?"))
print("5:", send(TOOLS, HANDBOOK, "Today is 2026-10-21 09:16:20. Can I carry leave over?"))

1: write 287 tokens to the cache
2: read  287 tokens from the cache
3: write 291 tokens to the cache
4: write 291 tokens to the cache
5: read  287 tokens from the cache

Line by line:

  • Request 1 writes. The cache is empty, so the 287-word prefix (the tool line plus the handbook) is stored.
  • Request 2 reads. The question is different, but the question comes after the breakpoint. Everything before it is byte for byte the same, so the stored prefix matches.
  • Requests 3 and 4 both write. Someone added "Today is" and the current time to the top of the system prompt. The two times differ by 98 seconds, so the two prefixes differ, and neither matches anything stored. Each request pays for a write and gets no read.
  • Request 5 reads again. The time is still there, but it moved into the question, after the breakpoint. The prefix is back to the 287 words that request 1 stored.

That is the opening puzzle. The team's system prompt began with the current time, to the second. Every request had a new prefix, so every request wrote the cache and none read it. A write costs more than a normal input token, as the next part shows, so caching made the bill worse. §9.5 lists this and the other usual invalidators.

The pricing is what makes it worth arranging your request around. A cache write costs 1.25× a normal input token, and a cache read costs 0.1×. In the telegram office, making the plate costs a little more than printing the pages once, and every later printing from the plate costs a tenth.

Those two numbers are Claude Opus 5's, the model this course pins. The read price is model-specific: on Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 a read costs 0.05× the input price, and on Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 it costs 0.025×. Writes cost the same 1.25× everywhere. So the arithmetic below is, if anything, cautious for the newest models.

The example below compares the same 20,000-token prefix sent with and without caching, for different numbers of reuses. The unit is the "base input token", one normal input token, so the comparison works at any price. The break-even comes quickly:

BASE, WRITE_MULT, READ_MULT = 1.0, 1.25, 0.10

def cost(prefix_tokens, reads, cached):
    """Total cost in 'base input token' units for one write plus `reads` reuses."""
    if not cached:
        return prefix_tokens * BASE * (reads + 1)
    return prefix_tokens * WRITE_MULT + prefix_tokens * READ_MULT * reads


PREFIX = 20_000
print(f"{'reuses':>7} {'uncached':>10} {'cached':>10} {'saving':>8}")
for reads in (0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 50):
    a, b = cost(PREFIX, reads, False), cost(PREFIX, reads, True)
    print(f"{reads:>7} {a:>10,.0f} {b:>10,.0f} {(1 - b / a) * 100:>7.0f}%")

print("\nbreak-even is the first reuse: a single write costs "
      f"{WRITE_MULT}x, so one read at {READ_MULT}x already beats {2 * BASE}x.")

reuses   uncached     cached   saving
      0     20,000     25,000     -25%
      1     40,000     27,000      32%
      2     60,000     29,000      52%
      3     80,000     31,000      61%
      5    120,000     35,000      71%
     10    220,000     45,000      80%
     50  1,020,000    125,000      88%

break-even is the first reuse: a single write costs 1.25x, so one read at 0.1x already beats 2.0x.

Line by line:

  • 0 reuses: 20,000 against 25,000. The prefix is sent once. Uncached, that costs its size. Cached, it costs 1.25 times its size, and nobody ever reads it. That is the opening puzzle's bill: every request wrote and none read, so every request paid this row's 25% extra.
  • 1 reuse: 40,000 against 27,000. Uncached, you pay the full prefix twice. Cached, you pay one write (25,000) and one read at a tenth (2,000). You are already 32% ahead.
  • 10 reuses: 220,000 against 45,000, an 80% saving.
  • 50 reuses: 88%. The saving creeps towards 90% and never reaches it, because each read still costs a tenth.

Move the sliders in the figure below to try your own prefix size and reuse count:

One reuse pays for the write, and the first row is the only losing one. A prefix used exactly once costs 25% more cached than uncached, because you paid the write multiplier for a cache nobody read. Reuse it once and you are 32% ahead, and ten times and you are 80% ahead. Almost every real application has a repeated prefix, so there is essentially no scenario where caching is the wrong call, as long as the prefix really does repeat.

Here is the first real cached request. A support assistant answers from a handbook, and the handbook is the part that repeats. So the request puts cache_control on the system block that holds it. That marker says "make a plate up to the end of this block". It calls the real API, so it needs a key, and HANDBOOK stands in for forty pages of real text:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

HANDBOOK = "…forty pages of policy text…"

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[{"type": "text", "text": f"Answer only from this handbook.\n\n{HANDBOOK}",
             "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "How do I request unpaid leave?"}],
)

u = response.usage
print("written to cache:", u.cache_creation_input_tokens)
print("read from cache :", u.cache_read_input_tokens)
print("uncached input  :", u.input_tokens)
print("total input     :", u.cache_creation_input_tokens
      + u.cache_read_input_tokens + u.input_tokens)

written to cache: 9840
read from cache : 0
uncached input  : 14
total input     : 9854

Line by line:

  • written to cache: 9840. The instructions and the handbook, everything up to and including the marked block, were stored. This is the first request, so there was nothing to read.
  • read from cache : 0. The same reason: nothing was stored before this request.
  • uncached input : 14. The question. It comes after the marked block, so it is neither written nor read. It is billed at the normal price.
  • total input : 9854. All three added together. Hold on to that sum, because the paragraph after next explains why you need it.

These are the opening puzzle's numbers. A second request with the same handbook and a different question should report 0 written and 9840 read. The team's requests reported 9840 written twice, and §9.5 shows the exact difference.

There is an even simpler form, and it is the one most people meet first. Automatic caching, which is that top-level cache_control, places the breakpoint at the last cacheable block for you and moves it forward as the conversation grows. Automatic caching consumes one of the four breakpoint slots, so it works alongside explicit ones and does not replace them.

Be precise about what "the last cacheable block" means, because it decides when automatic caching helps. It is the last block of the request, which is usually the newest message. Two rules from the docs then explain everything:

  • A cache entry is written only at a breakpoint. Nothing is stored for any earlier position.
  • A read can only find an entry that an earlier request wrote. The lookup walks backwards from your breakpoint, looking for a stored prefix. It does not discover stable text by itself.

In one growing conversation, that is exactly right. Turn 1's entry ends at turn 1's message. Turn 2 sends turn 1 again plus one new message, so walking back one step finds turn 1's entry. For a chat or an agent loop, automatic caching is the right answer and the whole of your caching implementation.

For separate requests that share only a prefix, it is wrong. Request 1's entry ends at question 1. Request 2 has a different question, so no stored entry matches any position it can see, and the handbook is written again. In the telegram office, the plate always ends at the pencil mark. Automatic caching puts the mark after your newest page, so the plate includes this telegram's question. A letter continuing the same correspondence starts with those same pages, and the plate fits. A fresh letter with a different question does not. The docs' rule covers both cases: put the breakpoint on the last block that stays identical across requests. That is what the handbook example does.

Read the usage fields carefully, because their meaning is not the obvious one. input_tokens counts only the tokens after the last breakpoint, and not the total. The total is the sum of all three. A team tracking spend from input_tokens alone after enabling caching will see their numbers apparently collapse and conclude something is broken. In the handbook example, input_tokens is 14 out of 9,854.

9.4 Placing Breakpoints by Hand

Explicit breakpoints, meaning cache_control on individual blocks, earn their complexity when different parts of your prompt change at different rates. You get four cache breakpoint slots, and the automatic breakpoint consumes one of the four if you use both. A cache breakpoint marks where a cached prefix ends, so its placement is the only decision that matters. In the telegram office, it is the pencil mark that says "make a plate up to here", and you may make up to four marks on one draft.

The design question is always the same: order your content from least to most volatile, and put the breakpoint at the boundary. Least volatile means it changes least often. So text that changes every quarter goes before text that changes every session, and that goes before text that changes every request.

The example below has three system blocks: a one-line role, a long policy that changes every quarter, and one customer's account details. It marks the policy and the account separately, with different lifetimes. It calls the real API, so it needs a key:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

POLICY = "…forty pages that change quarterly…"
ACCOUNT = "…this customer's plan, tier and open tickets…"

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[
        {"type": "text", "text": "You are a support assistant."},
        {"type": "text", "text": POLICY,
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}},
        {"type": "text", "text": ACCOUNT,
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Can I downgrade mid-cycle?"}],
)

print("stop_reason :", response.stop_reason)
print("cache writes:", response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)

stop_reason : end_turn
cache writes: 11420

The output says the request finished normally (end_turn) and wrote 11,420 tokens to the cache, covering both marked blocks and everything before them.

There are two breakpoints here, with two lifetimes. A lifetime, or TTL, is how long the office keeps the plate after it is last used. The policy is shared by every conversation in the system and changes quarterly, so it takes the 1-hour cache. The account block is shared by one customer's session, so it takes the default 5 minutes. The 1-hour cache costs 2× base input to write, against the 5-minute cache's 1.25×. So it pays for itself the moment it avoids one extra write: one 2× write is cheaper than two 1.25× writes.

Here is a constraint that will bite if you do not know it: entries with a longer TTL (time to live) must appear before shorter ones. A 1-hour breakpoint after a 5-minute breakpoint is rejected.

The example below checks three layouts against three of the rules in this subsection: at most four breakpoints, longer TTLs first, and a minimum prefix size (explained next). It is a toy written from the docs, not the API's own validator, and it counts tokens you give it rather than measuring them:

MIN_PREFIX = 512                 # Claude Opus 5's minimum cacheable prefix
LONGER = {"1h": 2, "5m": 1}      # a bigger number is a longer lifetime


def check(blocks):
    """A toy of three documented rules. It is not the API's own validator."""
    problems = []
