IDF stands for inverse document frequency: a score that is high for a word found in few documents and low for one found in many. err_4471 and perishable each appear in one of five documents and score 1.386. refund appears in two and scores 0.875. the appears in three and scores 0.539.

Now the three queries one at a time, because each teaches something different.

ERR_4471 is where keyword search wins outright. It appears in one document, its IDF (a score that rewards rare words) is high, and it ranks first with certainty. Now compare an embedding. An embedding of that string is a point in space near other alphanumeric noise, and semantic similarity has nothing useful to say about it. ERR_4471 has no meaning to capture; it is just a label. Every corpus has terms like this, and they are disproportionately what people search for:

  • SKUs, the stock codes a shop gives each product;
  • error codes;
  • function names;
  • customer identifiers.

The refund query shows the classic keyword-search defect, and it is worth catching here. This is the answer to the opening puzzle. d1 begins "Refunds are issued…" and scores exactly zero, because this tokeniser produces refunds and the query produces refund, and those are different strings. To a computer comparing text, refund and refunds are as different as refund and banana. Real keyword search applies a stemmer, which reduces words to a common root, so that both become refund. In the archive picture, it is a book index that files refunds, refunded and refunding under one entry.

Here is the smallest possible stemmer, so you can watch it fix the puzzle and then watch it make mistakes. It drops one trailing s from words longer than three letters, unless the word ends in ss:

import re


def tokenise(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9_]+", text.lower())


def stem(word):
    """A deliberately crude stemmer: drop one trailing 's'."""
    if len(word) > 3 and word.endswith("s") and not word.endswith("ss"):
        return word[:-1]
    return word


doc = "Refunds are issued within 30 days of delivery to the original card."
query = "refund"

plain_doc, plain_query = tokenise(doc), tokenise(query)
stemmed_doc = [stem(w) for w in plain_doc]
stemmed_query = [stem(w) for w in plain_query]

print("without a stemmer:", plain_doc[:3], "contains 'refund'?",
      plain_query[0] in plain_doc)
print("with a stemmer   :", stemmed_doc[:3], "contains 'refund'?",
      stemmed_query[0] in stemmed_doc)
print()
for word in ("days", "process", "is", "news", "analysis"):
    print(f"  {word:<10} -> {stem(word)}")

without a stemmer: ['refunds', 'are', 'issued'] contains 'refund'? False
with a stemmer   : ['refund', 'are', 'issued'] contains 'refund'? True

  days       -> day
  process    -> process
  is         -> is
  news       -> new
  analysis   -> analysi

Read it line by line:

  • Without a stemmer, the document's first word is refunds, and the query word refund is not in the document.
  • With a stemmer, the first word becomes refund, and the match is found. d1 would now score above zero.
  • The last five lines show why real stemmers are not this simple. days becomes day, which is right. process is protected by the ss rule, and is by the length rule. But news becomes new, which is a different word, and analysis becomes analysi, which is not a word at all.

Real search engines use stemmers with hundreds of rules, built for each language. The best known is the Porter stemmer for English. PostgreSQL's built-in full-text search applies one for you, and the SQL course's full-text search lessons show it turning foxes into fox. You should not write your own. The point of the toy is the failure it prevents. Leave the stemmer out and your search silently misses every plural, every tense and every inflected form, which in an English corpus is a large fraction of everything. It is also a good illustration of why hybrid search (§10.5) is worth having, because a vector retriever has no such blind spot. An embedding of refunds and an embedding of refund land almost on top of each other.

"can I return a cake" is where it loses, and the last row shows why. Not one word of the query appears in the document about perishable goods. A cake is perishable, and you know that; keyword search does not. It only knows which strings appear where, so it cannot bridge cake to perishable. That is the gap embeddings fill.

10.4 Embeddings and Semantic Search

Keyword search matches words. Semantic search matches meanings. To do that, it turns text into numbers in a special way.

An embedding maps text to a vector (a list of numbers) such that similar meanings land near each other. In the archive picture, it is shelving papers by topic: refund policies on one shelf, server outages on another, so that papers about similar things sit close together. A real embedding has hundreds or thousands of numbers, one per dimension. You cannot picture a thousand dimensions, but you can picture two or three, and the arithmetic is the same.

Once every text is a vector, "how similar are these two texts?" becomes "how close are these two vectors?". The usual measure is the cosine similarity, which is the cosine of the angle between two vectors. Think of each vector as an arrow from the origin:

  • arrows pointing the same way have an angle of 0°, and a cosine of 1.0: the meanings match;
  • arrows at right angles have a cosine of 0.0: the texts are unrelated. The mathematical word for "at right angles" is orthogonal.

So similarity is 1.0 for identical directions and 0.0 for orthogonal (unrelated) ones.

Where do you get embeddings? Not from Anthropic. Anthropic does not offer an embedding model. The Claude API has no embeddings endpoint, and any example claiming otherwise is wrong. Claude's documentation points to one provider, Voyage AI, which is now part of MongoDB, and says plainly that you should assess several vendors before choosing. Here is what Voyage offers today:

  • General models: voyage-4-large (best quality), voyage-4 (balanced) and voyage-4-lite (lowest latency and cost). Each takes up to 32,000 tokens of input and returns 1024 dimensions by default, with 256, 512 and 2048 also available.
  • Domain-specific models: voyage-code-4 for code, voyage-finance-2 for finance, and voyage-law-2 for law. The law model takes 16,000 tokens of input.
  • One setting to always pass: input_type, set to "query" for a question and "document" for a chunk. The model embeds the two slightly differently, which improves retrieval, and the docs say not to leave it out.

Choosing a provider is a real decision with real lock-in. Vectors from one model cannot be compared with vectors from another, so switching models means re-embedding the whole corpus, and re-embedding a large corpus is expensive. It deserves more thought than the default.

The mechanics are worth building once, because the arithmetic explains several practical constraints. The block below uses toy 4-dimensional vectors, placed by hand so the geometry is easy to follow. It ranks every vector against the query "return an item" with a bar for each score. Then it works out how much storage 500,000 chunks need at four common sizes, at 4 bytes per number:

import math

# Toy 4-dimensional "embeddings", hand-placed so the geometry is visible.
VECTORS = {
    "refund policy":    [0.90, 0.10, 0.05, 0.20],
    "return an item":   [0.85, 0.15, 0.10, 0.25],
    "perishable goods": [0.60, 0.55, 0.10, 0.15],
    "server latency":   [0.05, 0.10, 0.95, 0.30],
    "payment gateway":  [0.30, 0.20, 0.40, 0.80],
}


def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    return dot / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b)))


query = VECTORS["return an item"]
ranked = sorted(((cosine(query, v), name) for name, v in VECTORS.items()),
                reverse=True)
print("query: 'return an item'")
for score, name in ranked:
    bar = "#" * round(score * 40)
    print(f"  {score:>6.3f}  {name:<18} {bar}")

print()
DIMENSIONS = [(256, 4), (512, 4), (1024, 4), (2048, 4)]
CHUNKS = 500_000
print(f"{'dims':>6}{'bytes/vector':>14}{'500k chunks':>14}")
for dims, bytes_per in DIMENSIONS:
    per_vector = dims * bytes_per
    print(f"{dims:>6}{per_vector:>14,}{per_vector * CHUNKS / 1e9:>12.2f} GB")

query: 'return an item'
   1.000  return an item     ########################################
   0.994  refund policy      ########################################
   0.849  perishable goods   ##################################
   0.602  payment gateway    ########################
   0.251  server latency     ##########

  dims  bytes/vector   500k chunks
   256         1,024        0.51 GB
   512         2,048        1.02 GB
  1024         4,096        2.05 GB
  2048         8,192        4.10 GB

Read it line by line:

  • return an item scores 1.000 against itself, which is what an identical direction looks like.
  • refund policy scores 0.994. Its numbers are close to the query's in every position, so the arrows point almost the same way. These two share no words at all, yet they are nearly identical by meaning. That is exactly the bridge keyword search could not build.
  • perishable goods scores 0.849: related, less close.
  • payment gateway at 0.602 and server latency at 0.251 trail off, because their large numbers sit in different positions.
  • The storage table doubles with every row. 256 dimensions at 4 bytes each is 1,024 bytes per vector and 0.51 GB for 500,000 chunks. At 2048 dimensions it is 8,192 bytes and 4.10 GB.

There are three facts that follow from the geometry.

Cosine similarity is bounded and comparable within one model, and meaningless across models. Bounded means it always lands between fixed limits, so 0.83 always means the same thing for one model. But a score of 0.83 from one embedding model and 0.83 from another are not the same quantity, because each model lays out its own space. Similarity thresholds must be tuned per model and re-tuned when you change it.

One shortcut is worth knowing here. Voyage's embeddings come normalised: every vector has length 1. For vectors of length 1, cosine similarity equals the plain dot product (multiply the numbers position by position and add them up), which is cheaper to compute. The block below proves it on the two closest vectors from above:

import math


def norm(v):
    return math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v))


def cosine(a, b):
    return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / (norm(a) * norm(b))


def normalise(v):
    n = norm(v)
    return [x / n for x in v]


a = [0.90, 0.10, 0.05, 0.20]     # "refund policy" from the block above
b = [0.85, 0.15, 0.10, 0.25]     # "return an item"

ua, ub = normalise(a), normalise(b)
print(f"cosine of the raw vectors       : {cosine(a, b):.6f}")
print(f"dot product of the unit vectors : {sum(x * y for x, y in zip(ua, ub)):.6f}")
print(f"lengths after normalising       : {norm(ua):.6f} {norm(ub):.6f}")
print()

DIMS, CHUNKS = 1024, 500_000
print(f"{'stored as':<18}{'bytes/vector':>14}{'500k chunks':>14}")
for label, bytes_per_vector in (("float (4 bytes)", DIMS * 4),
                                ("int8 (1 byte)", DIMS * 1),
                                ("binary (1 bit)", DIMS // 8)):
    print(f"{label:<18}{bytes_per_vector:>14,}"
          f"{bytes_per_vector * CHUNKS / 1e9:>11.3f} GB")

cosine of the raw vectors       : 0.994404
dot product of the unit vectors : 0.994404
lengths after normalising       : 1.000000 1.000000

stored as           bytes/vector   500k chunks
float (4 bytes)            4,096      2.048 GB
int8 (1 byte)              1,024      0.512 GB
binary (1 bit)               128      0.064 GB

The first two lines agree to six decimal places, and the third line shows that normalising really made both lengths 1. That is why vector databases often offer "dot product" as the distance setting: for normalised vectors it gives the same ranking, faster.

Dimension is a cost knob with a quality trade-off. Storing 500,000 chunks at 1024 dimensions is a couple of gigabytes. At 256 it is a quarter of that, and search is proportionally faster. Models that support several output dimensions let you pick the point on that curve and do not force one on you. Fewer dimensions usually lose a little quality, so measure the loss with §10.8's recall@k before you take the saving.

The second half of the block above shows a second knob: how many bytes each number gets. That is called quantization, and Voyage supports it through an output_dtype setting. A float is 4 bytes and the default. An int8 is 1 byte, four times smaller. A binary value is a single bit, 32 times smaller, so 500,000 vectors fit in 64 MB. Each step down keeps less detail, which is the same quality trade, measured the same way.

Nothing here is exact search. The toy ranking above compared the query with every vector. That is fine for five vectors and far too slow for fifty million. At production scale, a vector database stores these vectors and searches them with an approximate nearest-neighbour index, which trades recall for speed. Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) means "find vectors that are probably the closest, without checking them all". In the archive picture, it is a clerk who walks to the most likely shelf and searches only there.

The block below builds the simplest version of that idea. It files eight 2-dimensional points into two buckets, each point under whichever "centre" it is nearest. A query then searches only the bucket whose centre is nearest to it, and the block compares that answer with an exact search:

import math

# Eight 2-dimensional "embeddings", so the geometry fits in your head.
POINTS = {
    "p1": (0.10, 0.90), "p2": (0.20, 0.80), "p3": (0.45, 0.55),
    "p4": (0.90, 0.10), "p5": (0.80, 0.30), "p6": (0.55, 0.48),
    "p7": (0.30, 0.70), "p8": (0.70, 0.20),
}
# An approximate index files every point under its nearest "centre"
# once, at build time, and at query time searches only one bucket.
CENTRES = {"north-west": (0.2, 0.8), "south-east": (0.8, 0.2)}


def dist(a, b):
    return math.dist(a, b)


buckets = {name: [] for name in CENTRES}
for pid, p in POINTS.items():
    nearest = min(CENTRES, key=lambda c: dist(p, CENTRES[c]))
    buckets[nearest].append(pid)

query = (0.50, 0.50)
exact = min(POINTS, key=lambda pid: dist(query, POINTS[pid]))
bucket = min(CENTRES, key=lambda c: dist(query, CENTRES[c]))
approx = min(buckets[bucket], key=lambda pid: dist(query, POINTS[pid]))

print("buckets       :", buckets)
print("query         :", query, "-> searches bucket", repr(bucket))
print(f"exact nearest : {exact}  distance {dist(query, POINTS[exact]):.3f}  "
      f"(compared all {len(POINTS)} points)")
print(f"approx nearest: {approx}  distance {dist(query, POINTS[approx]):.3f}  "
      f"(compared {len(buckets[bucket])} points)")
print("missed the best match:", approx != exact)

buckets       : {'north-west': ['p1', 'p2', 'p3', 'p7'], 'south-east': ['p4', 'p5', 'p6', 'p8']}
query         : (0.5, 0.5) -> searches bucket 'north-west'
exact nearest : p6  distance 0.054  (compared all 8 points)
approx nearest: p3  distance 0.071  (compared 4 points)
missed the best match: True

Read it line by line:

  • The buckets put four points in the north-west and four in the south-east.
  • The query (0.5, 0.5) sits almost exactly between the two centres. It is a fraction closer to the north-west centre, so that is the only bucket it searches.
  • The exact search checked all 8 points and found p6, at distance 0.054.
  • The approximate search checked only 4 and returned p3, at 0.071. p6 was filed in the other bucket, so it was never looked at.

Half the work, and the wrong answer. Real ANN indexes, with names like HNSW and IVF, are far cleverer than two buckets, and settings such as how many buckets or neighbours to search let you buy back accuracy with time. That trade is a knob on the vector database, and a badly tuned index silently fails to return documents that exist. That failure mode looks exactly like the model being unhelpful.

10.5 Hybrid Search

You now have two retrievers, and each is good at what the other is bad at:

  • keyword search wins on rare terms, like ERR_4471;
  • semantic search wins on paraphrase, the same meaning in different words, like cake and perishable.

Real queries contain both. "Why did ERR_4471 stop my refund?" has a rare code and an ordinary question in one sentence. So run both, and fuse the results.

Fusing is harder than it sounds, because the two scores are on unrelated scales. A BM25 score of 1.4 and a cosine of 0.83 cannot be added or compared. So the standard fusion method is reciprocal rank fusion, which combines rankings and not scores. That is the point, since the two scores are not on a comparable scale. In the archive picture, you ask two clerks for their lists, ignore how confident each one sounds, and combine the lists by position alone.

The formula is short. A document ranked r-th in one list earns 1/(k + r) points from that list, and its points from every list are added up. k is a constant, usually 60, explained below the figure. The block below fuses one keyword ranking and one vector ranking of five documents, then prints where each document came in each list and its fused score:

BM25_RANKING = ["d3", "d1", "d5", "d2", "d4"]        # rare terms, exact matches
VECTOR_RANKING = ["d2", "d1", "d4", "d5", "d3"]      # paraphrase, meaning


def rrf(rankings, k=60):
    """Reciprocal rank fusion: sum 1/(k + rank) across every ranking."""
    scores = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[doc] = scores.get(doc, 0.0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])


fused = rrf([BM25_RANKING, VECTOR_RANKING])
print("bm25   :", BM25_RANKING)
print("vector :", VECTOR_RANKING)
print("fused  :", [doc for doc, _ in fused])
print()
for doc, score in fused:
    b = BM25_RANKING.index(doc) + 1
    v = VECTOR_RANKING.index(doc) + 1
    print(f"  {doc}  bm25 #{b}  vector #{v}  fused {score:.5f}")

print()
print("d1 is second in both and wins: agreement beats a single first place")

bm25   : ['d3', 'd1', 'd5', 'd2', 'd4']
vector : ['d2', 'd1', 'd4', 'd5', 'd3']
fused  : ['d1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd5', 'd4']

  d1  bm25 #2  vector #2  fused 0.03226
  d2  bm25 #4  vector #1  fused 0.03202
  d3  bm25 #1  vector #5  fused 0.03178
  d5  bm25 #3  vector #4  fused 0.03150
  d4  bm25 #5  vector #3  fused 0.03126

d1 is second in both and wins: agreement beats a single first place

Read it line by line:

  • The two input rankings disagree completely at the top. Keyword search puts d3 first; vector search puts d2 first.
  • The fused order starts with d1, which was first in neither list.
  • The score lines show why. d1 is second in both, so it earns 1/62 twice: 0.03226 in total. d2 is first in one list and fourth in the other, 1/61 + 1/64, which is 0.03202. d3 is first in one and last in the other, and gets 0.03178.

The figure draws the same fusion: the two rankings, and the fused order they produce.

Fusion rewards agreement. d1 is not first in either ranking and comes out on top, because both retrievers rank it highly, which is a better signal than one retriever being confident. d3 and d2 are each first in one ranking and low in the other, and they land below it. Two clerks who each put a paper second are more convincing together than one clerk who is sure and another who barely listed it.

The k constant (conventionally 60) damps the influence of top ranks. Lower it and first places dominate, and raise it and the fusion flattens toward counting appearances. You can watch both happen by fusing the same two rankings with three values of k:

BM25_RANKING = ["d3", "d1", "d5", "d2", "d4"]
VECTOR_RANKING = ["d2", "d1", "d4", "d5", "d3"]


def rrf(rankings, k=60):
    scores = {}
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[doc] = scores.get(doc, 0.0) + 1 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])


for k in (0, 60, 1000):
    fused = rrf([BM25_RANKING, VECTOR_RANKING], k=k)
    print(f"k={k:<5} fused order {[doc for doc, _ in fused]}  "
          f"top score {fused[0][1]:.4f}")

k=0     fused order ['d2', 'd3', 'd1', 'd5', 'd4']  top score 1.2500
k=60    fused order ['d1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd5', 'd4']  top score 0.0323
k=1000  fused order ['d1', 'd2', 'd3', 'd5', 'd4']  top score 0.0020

Read it line by line:

  • With k=0, a first place is worth 1, a second place 1/2 and a fifth place 1/5. First places dominate: d2 and d3, each first once, take the top two spots, and d1 drops to third.
  • With k=60 you get the fused order from above, with d1 on top.
  • With k=1000 the order is the same as with 60, but every score is tiny and nearly equal. Rank barely matters any more, so the fusion is close to counting how often a document appears and adding up its positions.

The conventional 60 sits where agreement wins but a strong first place still counts. It is a reasonable default, not a law. Like every other knob in this section, measure before you tune it.

Hybrid is the default worth starting from, and not an optimisation to add later. It is a handful of lines on top of two retrievers you were going to build anyway, and it removes the single biggest failure mode of pure vector search, which is that exact identifiers become unfindable. It also protects you from the keyword side's blind spots: had the opening search for refund been hybrid, the vector half would not have cared about refund versus refunds, so d1 could still reach the top without a stemmer.

10.6 Reranking

Hybrid search gives you a good list of candidates. The next question is whether the best ones are at the top.

Retrieval optimises for recall, meaning it tries to get the right chunk into the top fifty. Ranking the top fifty well is a different problem, and a reranker is much better at it. A reranker is a model that scores query and document pairs directly and does not compare pre-computed vectors. In the archive picture, retrieval is the clerk who pulls fifty plausible papers off the shelves, and the reranker is the careful reader who sits down and reads each of the fifty against the question.

The reason it is better is structural. An embedding is computed without knowing the query, so it has to be a general-purpose summary of the chunk. It was made months ago, before anyone asked anything. A reranker sees the query and the document together and can judge this document against this question. That costs a model call per candidate, which is why it runs over fifty candidates and not over the whole corpus.

To measure what a reranker changes, you need one more term. Precision@k is the share of the top k results that are actually relevant: if three of the top five are relevant, precision@5 is 60%. The block below takes ten retrieved chunks, c1 to c10. Each has two scores: the retrieval score that put it in the list, and the score a reranker gave it. Three chunks are truly relevant. The block compares the two orders, then compares sending five chunks in retrieval order with sending three after reranking:

# Scores a reranker returned for one query over ten retrieved candidates,
# alongside the retrieval order that produced them.
RETRIEVED = [
    ("c1", 0.81, 0.12), ("c2", 0.79, 0.94), ("c3", 0.78, 0.31),
    ("c4", 0.77, 0.88), ("c5", 0.76, 0.09), ("c6", 0.75, 0.71),
    ("c7", 0.74, 0.05), ("c8", 0.73, 0.97), ("c9", 0.72, 0.22),
    ("c10", 0.71, 0.14),
]
RELEVANT = {"c2", "c4", "c8"}


def precision_at_k(order, k):
    return sum(c in RELEVANT for c in order[:k]) / k


by_retrieval = [c for c, _, _ in RETRIEVED]
by_rerank = [c for c, _, _ in sorted(RETRIEVED, key=lambda r: -r[2])]

print("retrieval order:", by_retrieval)
print("reranked order :", by_rerank)
print()
for k in (1, 3, 5):
    print(f"precision@{k}  retrieval {precision_at_k(by_retrieval, k):>5.0%}"
          f"   reranked {precision_at_k(by_rerank, k):>5.0%}")

print()
sent_without = 5
sent_with = 3
CHUNK_TOKENS = 240
print(f"send top {sent_without} unreranked: {sent_without * CHUNK_TOKENS:>5,} tokens, "
      f"{sum(c in RELEVANT for c in by_retrieval[:sent_without])} of 3 relevant")
print(f"send top {sent_with} reranked   : {sent_with * CHUNK_TOKENS:>5,} tokens, "
      f"{sum(c in RELEVANT for c in by_rerank[:sent_with])} of 3 relevant")

retrieval order: ['c1', 'c2', 'c3', 'c4', 'c5', 'c6', 'c7', 'c8', 'c9', 'c10']
reranked order : ['c8', 'c2', 'c4', 'c6', 'c3', 'c9', 'c10', 'c1', 'c5', 'c7']

precision@1  retrieval    0%   reranked  100%
precision@3  retrieval   33%   reranked  100%
precision@5  retrieval   40%   reranked   60%

send top 5 unreranked: 1,200 tokens, 2 of 3 relevant
send top 3 reranked   :   720 tokens, 3 of 3 relevant

Read it line by line:

  • The retrieval order is simply c1 to c10, because the retrieval scores fall steadily from 0.81 to 0.71.
  • The reranked order starts with c8, c2 and c4, the three relevant chunks. In retrieval order they were eighth, second and fourth.
  • Precision@1 goes from 0% to 100%. Retrieval's first choice, c1, is irrelevant; the reranker's first choice is relevant.
  • Precision@3 goes from 33% to 100%, and precision@5 from 40% to 60%. At 5 the reranked list can only reach 60%, because only three chunks are relevant at all.
  • The last two lines are the practical result. Sending the top 5 in retrieval order costs 1,200 tokens and carries 2 of the 3 relevant chunks. Sending the top 3 after reranking costs 720 tokens and carries all 3.

The figure lines up the two orders side by side, with the relevant chunks marked.

Reranking lets you send fewer chunks and get better ones. That is the whole value proposition, and it compounds. Fewer chunks means fewer tokens, lower latency and, per §9, a context in which the relevant passage is easier for the model to use.

Notice that the retrieval scores in that data are all between 0.71 and 0.81. Vector similarity is poor at fine-grained ordering, because those scores are nearly indistinguishable and the differences are noise. Retrieval is a coarse filter that is very good at its job, and treating its ordering as a ranking is asking it for something it does not provide. The shelving clerk is good at bringing back the right armful of papers. Asking which paper in the armful is best is a job for the reader.

The practical shape is to retrieve 50 with hybrid search, rerank to 5, and send those. Treat both numbers as starting points and measure them. Anthropic's 2024 contextual retrieval tests tried sending 5, 10 and 20 chunks, and 20 performed best for their data, so the right number to send depends on your corpus and your chunk size. §10.8 shows how to measure it.

For the reranker itself, the documentation points at Voyage again. Its current rerankers are rerank-3, for the highest accuracy, and rerank-3-lite, for lower latency and cost. Each takes up to 32,000 tokens of query and documents. rerank-2.5 and rerank-2.5-lite are the previous generation, and you will still see them in older examples.

10.7 Grounding the Answer

Retrieval puts passages in the window. Nothing so far makes the model use them, or makes its use checkable. Grounding means tying each claim in the answer to a passage it came from. Two features do this, and they are the difference between a RAG system you can audit and one you have to trust:

  • search result blocks, a content block type that carries a passage together with where it came from;
  • citations, which the model attaches to the parts of its answer that draw on those passages.

In the archive picture, every clipping now has a source tag stapled to it, and the writer must footnote each claim with the tag of the clipping it came from.

Search result blocks carry a source and a title alongside the text, and Claude cites them automatically. Each one has three required fields and one setting:

  • source: where the passage came from, a URL or your own identifier;
  • title: a human-readable name for it;
  • content: a list of text blocks holding the passage itself;
  • citations: set {"enabled": True} to have the model cite it.

The block below sends two search results, one about the refund policy and one about processing times, followed by a question. Then it prints each text block of the answer, with any citations under it:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

RESULTS = [
    {"type": "search_result",
     "source": "kb://refund-policy",
     "title": "Refund Policy",
     "content": [{"type": "text",
                  "text": "Customers may request a refund within 30 days of "
                          "delivery. Perishable goods are not refundable."}],
     "citations": {"enabled": True}},
    {"type": "search_result",
     "source": "kb://processing-times",
     "title": "Processing Times",
     "content": [{"type": "text",
                  "text": "Refunds are processed within 5 business days of "
                          "approval."}],
     "citations": {"enabled": True}},
]

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": [*RESULTS,
                           {"type": "text",
                            "text": "How long does a refund take?"}]}],
)

for block in response.content:
    if block.type != "text":
        continue
    print("text:", block.text)
    for citation in (block.citations or []):
        print(f"  cited: {citation.source} — {citation.cited_text!r}")

text: Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.
  cited: kb://processing-times — 'Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.'

Read it line by line. The answer is one sentence, and under it is one citation. The citation names kb://processing-times, the source you supplied, and quotes the passage the sentence came from. The refund policy result was not cited, because the answer did not use it. You did not prompt for any of this; no instruction in the request says "cite your sources". Enabling citations on the search results was enough.

Each citation is a small object. Its type is search_result_location, and it carries the source and title you supplied, the cited_text, a search_result_index that counts every search result in the request from 0, and block indices saying which of the result's content blocks it covers. A few rules decide how you build the blocks.

source can be any stable string. It can be a URL or an internal identifier like kb://article-1234. It does not have to resolve to anything, because it is the handle your application uses to link back. Keep it permanent: a source that changes when you re-index breaks every link you already showed a user.

Citations are off by default and must be enabled per result, and all search results in one request must agree. Mixing enabled and disabled is rejected. One more case forces the choice: if the web search tool (§7) is enabled in the same request, citations must be enabled on all search result blocks.

Search results hold text only. No images inside the content array.

There is one more rule, and it decides how you should shape the content list. The model cites whole content blocks, never part of one. cited_text is the full text of the blocks a citation covers. So if a search result holds two facts in one text block, a citation of either fact quotes both. The block below is a toy of that documented rule, with no API call. It shows the same passage as one block and as two, and the slice that a citation of the perishable goods rule would carry in each case:

# A toy of the documented rule: a citation names a slice of a search
# result's content blocks, and cited_text is the text of that slice.
# Claude cites whole blocks, never part of one.
ONE_BLOCK = ["Customers may request a refund within 30 days of delivery. "
             "Perishable goods are not refundable."]
TWO_BLOCKS = ["Customers may request a refund within 30 days of delivery.",
              "Perishable goods are not refundable."]


def cited_text(content, start_block_index, end_block_index):
    return "".join(content[start_block_index:end_block_index])


# The claim being supported: "Perishable goods are not refundable."
print("one block :", repr(cited_text(ONE_BLOCK, 0, 1)))
print("two blocks:", repr(cited_text(TWO_BLOCKS, 1, 2)))

one block : 'Customers may request a refund within 30 days of delivery. Perishable goods are not refundable.'
two blocks: 'Perishable goods are not refundable.'

With one block, the citation for "Perishable goods are not refundable" also quotes the 30-day rule, which is not what the claim rests on. With two blocks, it quotes exactly the sentence it needs. So break long passages into several smaller text blocks, one idea each, and your citations become precise.

The rest of the rules are about where search results can go:

  • Two places to put them. You can send them directly in a user message, as above, for results you fetched before calling the model. Or your own search tool can return them inside a tool_result (§6), which lets the model search as it works.
  • Only in user turns. That includes tool results. An assistant message containing search results is rejected.
  • A tool result is all or nothing. If any block in a tool_result's content is a search result, every block in it must be one. To add a note alongside them, put it inside one of the results as another text block, where it also becomes citable.
  • An empty search is not an error. When your search finds nothing, return a plain text block such as "No results found." The model then tells the user, and the conversation carries on.
  • They can be cached. A cache_control setting goes on the search result block, next to citations, exactly as in §9.4.

What this buys you is mechanical. Every text block carries the passages it drew on, so a claim with no citation is detectable by code. That is §13's faithfulness check without needing a judge, and it is the strongest anti-hallucination measure available in a RAG system. Faithfulness means the answer says only what its sources say; a hallucination is a claim the model made up. A judge is a second model asked to grade the first one's answer, which §13 builds. Here you do not need one, because the check is a simple question that code can answer: does this sentence have a citation?

The block below runs that check over three claims from an imagined answer. Two carry a source; one carries none:

# The check that becomes possible once every claim carries its source.
BLOCKS = [
    ("Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.",
     ["kb://processing-times"]),
    ("Your bank may take a further week to post the credit.", []),
    ("Perishable goods are not refundable.", ["kb://refund-policy"]),
]

uncited = [text for text, cites in BLOCKS if not cites]
print(f"{'cited?':<8}{'claim'}")
for text, cites in BLOCKS:
    print(f"{('yes' if cites else 'NO'):<8}{text}")
print(f"\n{len(uncited)} of {len(BLOCKS)} claims rest on nothing in the sources:")
for text in uncited:
    print(f"  {text}")
print("\nthat is a code-based grader, not a judge (13.4)")

cited?  claim
yes     Refunds are processed within 5 business days of approval.
NO      Your bank may take a further week to post the credit.
yes     Perishable goods are not refundable.

1 of 3 claims rest on nothing in the sources:
  Your bank may take a further week to post the credit.

that is a code-based grader, not a judge (13.4)

Read it line by line. Two claims are marked yes and one NO. The uncited one, "Your bank may take a further week to post the credit", sounds reasonable and is not in either source. The refund policy in §10.2 says 3 to 5 days, and that sentence was not among the passages the model was sent. That is exactly the kind of plausible, specific, unsupported claim that ships to users unnoticed. Code found it in one line, with no model call. What you do next is a product decision: drop the sentence, flag it to the user, or send the answer back for another try.

10.8 Evaluating a Retrieval Pipeline

A RAG system can fail in two different places. In the archive picture: either the right clipping never made it into the envelope, or it did and the writer misread it. A RAG system has two failure modes, and they need separate measurement because the fixes are unrelated:

  • Retrieval failure: the answer was not in the retrieved chunks. The fix is in chunking or search.
  • Generation failure: it was, and the model did not use it or used it wrongly. The fix is in the prompt or the model.

Conflating them is how teams spend a month tuning a prompt to fix a chunker.

To tell them apart you need a gold set: test questions where you know which chunk holds the answer (the gold chunk). Then two numbers fall out. Recall@k is the share of questions where the gold chunk appears in the top k retrieved. End-to-end accuracy is the share where the final answer was correct. The block below has six test cases. Each records the gold chunk, the three chunks retrieved, and whether the answer was right. It computes both numbers and sorts every failure into one kind or the other:

CASES = [
    # (id, gold chunk, retrieved chunks, answer was correct)
    ("q1", "c2", ["c2", "c7", "c9"], True),
    ("q2", "c4", ["c1", "c3", "c8"], False),
    ("q3", "c5", ["c5", "c2", "c1"], False),
    ("q4", "c1", ["c1", "c4", "c6"], True),
    ("q5", "c9", ["c3", "c7", "c2"], False),
    ("q6", "c3", ["c3", "c9", "c5"], True),
]

retrieved_ok = [c for c in CASES if c[1] in c[2]]
answered_ok = [c for c in CASES if c[3]]
retrieval_failures = [c[0] for c in CASES if c[1] not in c[2]]
generation_failures = [c[0] for c in CASES if c[1] in c[2] and not c[3]]

print(f"recall@3 (gold chunk retrieved) : "
      f"{len(retrieved_ok)}/{len(CASES)} = {len(retrieved_ok) / len(CASES):.0%}")
print(f"end-to-end answer accuracy      : "
      f"{len(answered_ok)}/{len(CASES)} = {len(answered_ok) / len(CASES):.0%}")
print()
print(f"retrieval failures  {retrieval_failures}  -> fix chunking or search")
print(f"generation failures {generation_failures}  -> fix the prompt or the model")
print()
ceiling = len(retrieved_ok) / len(CASES)
print(f"answer accuracy can never exceed recall: ceiling is {ceiling:.0%}")
print("no prompt change moves a case whose answer was never in the window")

recall@3 (gold chunk retrieved) : 4/6 = 67%
end-to-end answer accuracy      : 3/6 = 50%

retrieval failures  ['q2', 'q5']  -> fix chunking or search
generation failures ['q3']  -> fix the prompt or the model

answer accuracy can never exceed recall: ceiling is 67%
no prompt change moves a case whose answer was never in the window

Read it line by line:

  • Recall@3 is 4 out of 6, 67%. In four cases the gold chunk was among the three retrieved.
  • Answer accuracy is 3 out of 6, 50%.
  • q2 and q5 are retrieval failures. Their gold chunks, c4 and c9, were never retrieved, so no model could have answered them from the window.
  • q3 is a generation failure. Its gold chunk c5 was retrieved, first even, and the answer was still wrong.
  • The last two lines are the important ones. Accuracy can never be higher than recall. Recall is 67%, so even a perfect model would top out at 67% on this set.

The figure draws the same six cases as bars: everything, then what was retrieved, then what was answered correctly.

Recall is a ceiling on end-to-end accuracy, and that single fact tells you where to work. (Recall@k is the share of questions where the right chunk appears in the top k results.) If recall@k is 67% and accuracy is 50%, the largest available gain is in retrieval, because no amount of prompt engineering reaches a passage that was never retrieved. The gap between the two numbers, 17 points here, is all the prompt work can ever recover.

Measure recall@k, not precision, at the retrieval stage. Getting the gold chunk (the correct answer's source) into the candidate set is the job, and ordering it is the reranker's (§10.6). A retriever tuned for precision@3 will discard candidates a reranker would have promoted. So the stages split the metrics between them:

  • measure the retriever by recall@50, or whatever number you hand to the reranker;
  • measure the reranker by precision at the number you send, for example precision@5;
  • measure the whole system by end-to-end accuracy.

This is also how you settle the open numbers from earlier in the section: chunk size, overlap, dimensions, quantization, k, and how many chunks to send. Change one, re-run the same gold set, and compare.

Building the gold set is the expensive part, and there is a shortcut. For each chunk, have a model generate a question that chunk answers, and the chunk is then the gold label for that question. It produces a large synthetic set for the cost of one pass over the corpus.

It is biased, though. The questions are phrased like the chunk, using the chunk's own words, so it flatters semantic search and understates the paraphrase gap. Real users say "can I return a cake", not "are perishable goods refundable". So pair it with a smaller hand-written set drawn from real user queries. §13.3's rule about edge cases coming from people who saw the system fail applies exactly here.

Back to the opening puzzle one last time. A search for refund gave the document that begins "Refunds are issued…" a score of exactly zero. You can now name every step. BM25 matches exact strings (§10.3). The tokeniser kept refunds and refund as different words, because there was no stemmer, so the document never matched. A stemmer fixes the keyword side, and hybrid search (§10.5) covers it from the semantic side, where refund and refunds sit almost on top of each other. In this section's evaluation terms, it was a retrieval failure: a recall@k check with that document as the gold chunk would have flagged it, and no prompt change could have fixed it.

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Diagnose four failures. A RAG assistant over an engineering handbook produces these. For each, say which stage is at fault and what you would change.

(a) Asked "what is our on-call escalation path?", it answers about incident severity levels — a real section, wrong one. (b) Asked "what does ERR_4471 mean?", it says the handbook does not cover it. It does. (c) Asked "can contractors approve deploys?", it retrieves the right section and answers "yes", where the section says contractors may approve deploys to staging. (d) Asked about a policy changed last week, it gives the old answer.

Solution 
DIAGNOSES = [
    ("a  wrong-but-related section", "retrieval: ranking",
     "The right chunk was probably retrieved and ranked below a plausible "
     "neighbour. Add a reranker (10.6) before touching anything else."),
    ("b  exact identifier not found", "retrieval: no keyword search",
     "ERR_4471 is a rare token. Pure vector search cannot find it. Add BM25 "
     "and fuse (10.3, 10.5) — this is the single most common RAG defect."),
    ("c  right chunk, wrong answer", "generation, or chunking",
     "The qualifier was either split off by the chunker or present and "
     "ignored. Look at the retrieved chunk first: it decides which."),
    ("d  stale answer", "indexing, not retrieval at all",
     "The pipeline is working perfectly on an index that is out of date. "
     "Nothing in the retrieval stack can fix it."),
]

for case, stage, action in DIAGNOSES:
    print(f"{case:<32} {stage}")
    print(f"{'':32} {action}")

a  wrong-but-related section     retrieval: ranking
                                 The right chunk was probably retrieved and ranked below a plausible neighbour. Add a reranker (10.6) before touching anything else.
b  exact identifier not found    retrieval: no keyword search
                                 ERR_4471 is a rare token. Pure vector search cannot find it. Add BM25 and fuse (10.3, 10.5) — this is the single most common RAG defect.
c  right chunk, wrong answer     generation, or chunking
                                 The qualifier was either split off by the chunker or present and ignored. Look at the retrieved chunk first: it decides which.
d  stale answer                  indexing, not retrieval at all
                                 The pipeline is working perfectly on an index that is out of date. Nothing in the retrieval stack can fix it.

(a) is a ranking failure, and the tell is that the retrieved section is related. Incident severity and on-call escalation sit near each other in embedding space, and cosine similarity is poor at fine-grained ordering (§10.6), so the scores for the two are probably within a few hundredths. A reranker sees the query and the candidate together and separates them easily. Before that, confirm the right chunk was in the candidate set at all. If recall@50 already contains it, this is a reranking job. If not, it is a chunking or search job, and reranking will not help.

(b) is the textbook argument for hybrid search. ERR_4471 is one rare token whose embedding carries almost no usable meaning, while its BM25 IDF is as high as it gets. A pure vector pipeline finds it by accident or not at all. Add keyword search and fuse with RRF (reciprocal rank fusion). This failure is common enough that "our RAG cannot find error codes" is close to a diagnosis on its own.

(c) needs the retrieved chunk before you can diagnose it, and that is the point of the exercise. Two very different bugs look identical from outside. If the chunk contains "contractors may approve deploys to staging", the model dropped a qualifier, and the fix is on the generation side: a prompt that requires quoting the passage (§14.5), or a judge in the eval that checks qualifiers survive. If the chunk contains only "contractors may approve deploys" with the qualifier in an adjacent chunk, the chunker split a sentence from its condition, and the fix is structural chunking (§10.2). Always look at the retrieved text before theorising about the model.

(d) is not a retrieval problem at all, and it is the one most likely to waste a week. Every stage did its job, and the index is stale. The fixes are operational: re-index on write and not on a schedule, or record an updated_at per chunk and surface it so the model can say how current its source is. It is worth adding a case like this to the eval set precisely because it is invisible to every retrieval metric. Recall@k is 100% against an index that is a week out of date.

Exercise 10.2 — Size a pipeline. 200,000 documents averaging 1,800 tokens. Chunk at 300 tokens with 15% overlap. Compute the chunk count, storage at 1024 dimensions, and decide whether to embed the whole corpus. Then compute what a hybrid + rerank query costs against a pure vector one.

Solution 
DOCS, DOC_TOKENS = 200_000, 1_800
CHUNK, OVERLAP_PCT, DIMS, BYTES = 300, 15, 1024, 4

step = CHUNK * (1 - OVERLAP_PCT / 100)
chunks_per_doc = max(1, round(DOC_TOKENS / step))
chunks = DOCS * chunks_per_doc
stored_tokens = chunks * CHUNK
raw_tokens = DOCS * DOC_TOKENS

print(f"chunks per document : {chunks_per_doc:>12,}")
print(f"total chunks        : {chunks:>12,}")
print(f"tokens embedded     : {stored_tokens:>12,}  "
      f"({stored_tokens / raw_tokens:.2f}x the corpus, from overlap)")
print(f"vector storage      : {chunks * DIMS * BYTES / 1e9:>12.2f} GB")
print(f"  at 256 dimensions : {chunks * 256 * BYTES / 1e9:>12.2f} GB")
print()

# Per query, in model calls and added latency.
CANDIDATES, FINAL = 50, 5
RERANK_MS, SEARCH_MS = 180, 40
CHUNK_TOKENS_SENT = {"vector only": 10 * CHUNK, "hybrid + rerank": FINAL * CHUNK}
INPUT_PER_MTOK = 5.00

print(f"{'pipeline':<20}{'chunks sent':>13}{'tokens':>9}"
      f"{'added latency':>15}{'cost/query':>12}")
for name, tokens in CHUNK_TOKENS_SENT.items():
    latency = SEARCH_MS if name == "vector only" else SEARCH_MS * 2 + RERANK_MS
    print(f"{name:<20}{tokens // CHUNK:>13}{tokens:>9,}{str(latency) + ' ms':>15}"
          f"{'$%.5f' % (tokens / 1e6 * INPUT_PER_MTOK):>12}")

print()
print(f"reranking costs ~{RERANK_MS + SEARCH_MS} ms and saves "
      f"{(10 - FINAL) * CHUNK:,} tokens per query")

chunks per document :            7
total chunks        :    1,400,000
tokens embedded     :  420,000,000  (1.17x the corpus, from overlap)
vector storage      :         5.73 GB
  at 256 dimensions :         1.43 GB

pipeline              chunks sent   tokens  added latency  cost/query
vector only                    10    3,000          40 ms    $0.01500
hybrid + rerank                 5    1,500         260 ms    $0.00750

reranking costs ~220 ms and saves 1,500 tokens per query

Yes, embed it. The corpus is far past the point where retrieval is optional. 360 million tokens does not fit in any context window, so §10.1's question answers itself. The storage is unremarkable by database standards, and the 256-dimension row is worth noting: if quality holds, it is a four-fold saving in storage and a proportional speed-up in search. Measure it with §10.8's recall@k and do not assume.

The overlap costs 17% more embedding and storage than the raw corpus, and that is the honest price of not cutting sentences at boundaries. It is usually worth paying. If it were not, the alternative is structural chunking, which needs no overlap because it splits where a human would.

Reranking looks expensive per query and is not. It adds roughly 220 ms and one model call, and it halves the tokens sent to the main model. The token saving alone roughly pays for it, and the accuracy gain (§10.6) is the actual reason to do it. Against a 1,400 ms model turn, 220 ms is a fraction of the total the user perceives.

What the arithmetic leaves out, and it is the expensive part. Embedding 360 million tokens once is a batch job with a real invoice, and, more importantly, the corpus changes. The recurring cost is re-embedding what changed, and the recurring engineering cost is keeping the index in step with the source of truth. Exercise 10.1(d) is what happens when that slips. Budget for the pipeline, and not just for the query.

One decision I would revisit. 300-token chunks with 15% overlap is a reasonable default for prose and a poor one for a corpus with structure. Before accepting it, check whether these documents have headings or sections. If they do, structural chunking (§10.2) will beat this on both recall and cost, because it needs no overlap at all.

SECTION 11

Building Agents

Start with a puzzle. You give a program that runs a model in a loop a strict budget: at most $1.00, and at most 200,000 tokens. Before every turn, the program checks the budget. The run lasts seven turns and ends with the words "finished normally". Its final bill is $1.343, and it used 250,530 tokens. Nothing crashed, no check was skipped, and no line of code has a bug in the usual sense. So how did it spend a third more than its limit? Guess before you read on. §11.3 runs that exact loop and answers it, and the answer changes where you put every limit in this section.

To see why this matters, recall where §6 and §9 left off:

  • Section 6 built a loop that lets the model call tools again and again. It pointed out that the loop has no stop condition.
  • Section 9 explained why the conversation inside that loop keeps growing, and what to do about it.

This section turns that loop into something you would let near production, meaning near real customers, real money and real data. To get there, the loop needs four properties:

  • bounded: it stops, always, and you know in advance the most it can spend;
  • observable: you can see afterwards what it did, and why;
  • recoverable: when it goes wrong, the damage can be caught and undone;
  • scoped: it is aimed at a job it can actually do.

The first three are code, and most of this section writes that code. The fourth takes judgement, not code, and it comes first.

Here is the picture for the whole section. Since §1 the model has been a ghostwriter you can only reach by telegram. In §6 the writer learned to hand request slips out of the window, and you decided whether a clerk ran each errand. Until now you read every slip yourself. In this section you stop doing that. You let the writer decide which errands to send, one after another, while you are away. That only works if you first build the office around the writer: the rulebook, the locks, the ledger and the logbook. Every part of this section has a place in that picture:

In the telegram office In this section Section
A list of errands you wrote down in advance a chain or a workflow §11.1
Letting the writer choose the next errand, with nobody reading the slips an agent §11.1
The office around the writer: rules, locks, ledger, logbook the harness §11.2
A spending limit, a shift length and a cap on the number of errands the loop's bounds §11.3
A note on the desk: "you have this many words for the whole job" a task budget §11.3
Which errands the clerks will run at all the tool surface §11.4
Everything those errands together could break the blast radius §11.4
A clerk who checks each slip against the rulebook first the gate §11.5
A bank that refuses any cheque over the limit, whoever signed it a check inside the tool's own code §11.5
A manager who must countersign some slips human in the loop §11.6
A logbook of every slip, every report and every signature the trace §11.7
Junior readers who read the files and send back one-page notes sub-agents §11.8
A clerk who notices the same slip coming back for the third time stall detection §11.9

It starts with the question most projects skip.

11.1 Should This Be an Agent?

Start with what the word means. An agent is a loop in which the model decides what happens next. In ordinary code, you decide the order of the steps: first this, then that. In an agent, the model reads what has happened so far and picks the next step itself.

Here is that difference in a few lines. The pick_next_step function stands in for the model. It is plain code, so the output is the same on every run, but it plays the model's role: it looks at what has happened and chooses. Two orders go through two designs:

ORDERS = {"ord_1": "delivered", "ord_2": "lost in transit"}


def chain(order_id):
    # You wrote the steps down. The same three run for every order.
    return ["get_order", "check_refund_policy", "write_reply"]


def pick_next_step(order_id, done):
    # Stands in for the model: it looks at what has happened so far and chooses.
    if not done:
        return "get_order"
    if done[-1] == "get_order" and ORDERS[order_id] == "lost in transit":
        return "open_courier_claim"
    if "check_refund_policy" not in done:
        return "check_refund_policy"
    if "write_reply" not in done:
        return "write_reply"
    return None


def agent(order_id, max_steps=10):
    done = []
    while len(done) < max_steps and (step := pick_next_step(order_id, done)):
        done.append(step)
    return done


for order_id, status in ORDERS.items():
    print(f"{order_id} ({status})")
    print("  chain:", " -> ".join(chain(order_id)))
    print("  agent:", " -> ".join(agent(order_id)))

ord_1 (delivered)
  chain: get_order -> check_refund_policy -> write_reply
  agent: get_order -> check_refund_policy -> write_reply
ord_2 (lost in transit)
  chain: get_order -> check_refund_policy -> write_reply
  agent: get_order -> open_courier_claim -> check_refund_policy -> write_reply

Read the output line by line:

  • For ord_1, the order that arrived, both designs run the same three steps.
  • For ord_2, the parcel lost in transit, the chain still runs its three steps. It cannot do anything else, because you wrote the list.
  • The agent, for the same order, adds open_courier_claim. That step is in no list. It was chosen at run time, after the agent saw the order's status.

That one extra step is the whole story of agents, in both directions. The agent handled a case you did not plan for, which is the attraction. It also ran a step nobody wrote down, which is the risk. If open_courier_claim had been create_refund, the agent would have moved money on its own judgement.

That freedom has a name: autonomy. It is the definition of an agent, and it is also the entire cost. You have given up control of the control flow, which means the decision of which step runs next. Every later design decision in this section is about bounding what that autonomy can reach. Everything that makes agents attractive, and everything that makes them expensive, comes from that one trade.

Most tasks do not need it. Think of a ladder with four rungs. Each rung up gives the model more control and costs you more predictability. The right answer is usually the lowest rung that works:

One call
Classification, extraction, summarisation, a question with an answer. One request, one response, predictable cost, testable with §13's machinery. Most production LLM traffic is this and should be.
A chain
Several calls in an order you decide. Extract, then validate, then draft. The control flow is yours; the model fills in steps. Debuggable, cheap, and covers far more than people expect.
A workflow with tools
A loop you drive, over a small fixed tool set, with a shape you know. "Look up the order, then answer." The model chooses arguments, not the plan.
An agent
The model chooses the plan. Open-ended, variable cost, variable latency, and only testable through §13.10's trajectory evaluation. Correct when the task genuinely cannot be specified in advance.

Before you leave the third rung for the fourth, ask four questions. A "no" to any one of them means stop.

Complexity. Is the task genuinely hard to specify in advance? To specify a task is to write down its steps. "Turn this design document into a pull request" is hard to specify, because nobody can list the steps before reading the document. "Extract the title from this PDF" is easy. If you can write the steps down, write them down. A chain of three calls beats an agent that rediscovers your process on every run.

Value. Does the outcome justify a bill and a wait that change from run to run? Picture an agent that takes 40 seconds and $0.30 to do something a single call does in 2 seconds for $0.004. It has to be much better to be worth it.

Viability. Is the model actually good at this task? An agent amplifies what the model can do. It does not create new ability. If a single call cannot do a step, a loop that calls it eleven times will not either. It will just be wrong at greater length.

Cost of error. Can mistakes be caught and undone? This is the question people weigh last, and it should be weighed first. Compare two agents:

  • An agent that writes code you review is safe, because the review is a gate: nothing happens until a person says yes.
  • An agent that issues refunds is safe only if you built the gate. §11.6 builds it.

The block below runs the four questions over five candidate tasks. Each task is a row of answers: can the steps be specified, how valuable is it, can the model do it, and can mistakes be undone. The if chain applies the questions in order and stops at the first one that fails:

CANDIDATES = [
    # (task, specifiable, value, viable, recoverable)
    ("extract invoice totals from PDFs",      True,  "high",   True,  True),
    ("negotiate with a supplier by email",    False, "high",   False, False),
    ("reconcile unmatched payments",          False, "high",   True,  False),
    ("tidy variable names across the repo",   False, "low",    True,  True),
    ("investigate a failing test and fix it", False, "high",   True,  True),
]

print(f"{'task':<40}{'verdict'}")
for task, specifiable, value, viable, recoverable in CANDIDATES:
    if not viable:
        verdict = "no — the model cannot do the underlying job"
    elif specifiable:
        verdict = "no — write the steps down; use a chain or a workflow"
    elif not recoverable:
        verdict = "only with a human gate on every irreversible step"
    elif value == "low":
        verdict = "no — the value does not justify the variance"
    else:
        verdict = "YES — this is what agents are for"
    print(f"{task:<40}{verdict}")

task                                    verdict
extract invoice totals from PDFs        no — write the steps down; use a chain or a workflow
negotiate with a supplier by email      no — the model cannot do the underlying job
reconcile unmatched payments            only with a human gate on every irreversible step
tidy variable names across the repo     no — the value does not justify the variance
investigate a failing test and fix it   YES — this is what agents are for

Each row fails on a different question, and that is the useful part. Read it top to bottom:

  • invoice totals fail on complexity: the steps can be written down, so a chain does it.
  • supplier negotiation fails on viability: the model cannot do the underlying job well enough.
  • payment reconciliation passes, but only with a person approving every step that cannot be undone.
  • renaming variables fails on value: it is not worth a variable bill.
  • fixing a failing test survives all four.

So a "no" arrives for four distinct reasons, and only the last row survives every question. That ratio is roughly right in practice too.

11.2 The Harness

Now suppose the answer was yes. What do you actually build?

Think back to the office. The writer is talented, but the writer is one part of the office. The locks on the doors, the spending limits, the countersigning rules and the logbook are what make it safe to leave the writer alone overnight. None of those live in the writer's head. They live in the building.

An agent is the same. It is a loop plus the scaffolding that makes the loop safe. That scaffolding has a name, the agent harness, and it is the part you actually write. The model is a component, and the agent harness is the system. Everything that makes an agent trustworthy lives in the harness and not in the model.

The harness has five parts. Each row names one, says what it holds, and points to where this course builds it:

Budget
Turns, tokens, wall-clock, money. Every one of them bounded, and every bound producing a defined outcome rather than an exception. §11.3.
Execution
Dispatch, authorisation, error shaping. The only place with the session, the permissions and the real world. §6.5 and §6.10 built most of this.
Context policy
What is cached, cleared, compacted, remembered. §9, applied rather than discussed.
Gates
What requires a human. Not a nice-to-have on anything irreversible. §11.6.
Observability
A record of every turn, every call, every argument. Without it, an agent that misbehaves once is not debuggable at all. §11.7.

The mistake worth naming early is treating the system prompt as the harness. The system prompt (§2.4) is the instruction text you send with every request. Suppose it says "never refund more than €100 without approval". That sentence is guidance to a component that produces text. It is not a control. In office terms, it is a sign on the writer's wall. A persuasive letter can talk the writer past a sign.

The €100 check belongs in create_refund, the function that actually moves the money. There it is code. Code runs the same way every time, and no amount of clever input can talk it out of firing.

11.3 Bounding the Loop

A bound is a limit with an action attached: when you reach this, stop. Here is §6.4's loop with the missing half added. It has four bounds: turns, tokens, seconds and money.

To keep the run repeatable, the model is replaced by a fixed list, TURN_COST. Each entry is what one turn would really use: input tokens read and output tokens written. The cost uses Opus 5's prices from §2, $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output. One more design choice matters later: the clock is a parameter, now, so the example can use a fake clock that moves exactly 9.5 seconds per turn:

import time


class Budget:
    """Turns, tokens, seconds and money, each with a defined outcome when hit."""

    def __init__(self, max_turns, max_tokens, max_seconds, max_cost,
                 now=lambda: 0.0):
        self.max_turns, self.max_tokens = max_turns, max_tokens
        self.max_seconds, self.max_cost = max_seconds, max_cost
        self.turns = self.tokens = 0
        self.cost = 0.0
        self._now = now
        self.started = now()

    def spend(self, input_tokens, output_tokens):
        self.turns += 1
        self.tokens += input_tokens + output_tokens
        self.cost += input_tokens / 1e6 * 5.0 + output_tokens / 1e6 * 25.0

    def exhausted(self):
        if self.turns >= self.max_turns:
            return "turn_limit"
        if self.tokens >= self.max_tokens:
            return "token_limit"
        if self._now() - self.started >= self.max_seconds:
            return "time_limit"
        if self.cost >= self.max_cost:
            return "cost_limit"
        return None


clock = {"t": 0.0}
budget = Budget(max_turns=20, max_tokens=200_000, max_seconds=120, max_cost=1.00,
                now=lambda: clock["t"])

TURN_COST = [(4_000, 300), (9_000, 450), (16_000, 380), (30_000, 900),
             (52_000, 700), (61_000, 1_200), (74_000, 600)]

for input_tokens, output_tokens in TURN_COST:
    stop = budget.exhausted()
    if stop:
        print(f"stopped after {budget.turns} turns: {stop}")
        break
    budget.spend(input_tokens, output_tokens)
    clock["t"] += 9.5
    print(f"turn {budget.turns:>2}  tokens {budget.tokens:>7,}  "
          f"cost ${budget.cost:>5.3f}  elapsed {clock['t']:>5.1f}s")
else:
    print(f"finished normally after {budget.turns} turns "
          f"(${budget.cost:.3f}, {budget.tokens:,} tokens)")

turn  1  tokens   4,300  cost $0.028  elapsed   9.5s
turn  2  tokens  13,750  cost $0.084  elapsed  19.0s
turn  3  tokens  30,130  cost $0.173  elapsed  28.5s
turn  4  tokens  61,030  cost $0.346  elapsed  38.0s
turn  5  tokens 113,730  cost $0.623  elapsed  47.5s
turn  6  tokens 175,930  cost $0.958  elapsed  57.0s
turn  7  tokens 250,530  cost $1.343  elapsed  66.5s
finished normally after 7 turns ($1.343, 250,530 tokens)

This is the puzzle from the start of the section. Look at the last two lines. The budget allowed $1.00 and 200,000 tokens, and the run ended at $1.343 and 250,530 tokens, with the words "finished normally". How?

Follow the numbers turn by turn:

  1. Before turn 7, exhausted() runs. The totals so far are 175,930 tokens and $0.958. Both are under the limits, so the check passes, correctly.
  2. Turn 7 runs. On its own it reads 74,000 tokens and writes 600, which costs about $0.385. A turn cannot be stopped halfway. Once the request is sent, it is spent.
  3. The list of turns ends, so the loop's else branch prints "finished normally". Nothing checks the budget again.

So nothing was broken. The check only looks backwards. It can judge the turns already paid for, and it knows nothing about the turn it is about to allow. Think of a shop assistant who checks your card balance after each purchase. Every check is honest, and the last purchase can still take you over.

The fix is to look forwards. Before you send a turn, work out the worst it could cost. Half of that is known exactly: the input is the conversation you are about to send, and §9.2 showed how to count its tokens before sending. The other half has a ceiling: the reply can be no longer than the max_tokens you put in the request (§2.1). Add both to what you have already spent, and refuse the turn if the total would cross a limit:

TURN_COST = [(4_000, 300), (9_000, 450), (16_000, 380), (30_000, 900),
             (52_000, 700), (61_000, 1_200), (74_000, 600)]
MAX_TOKENS, MAX_COST = 200_000, 1.00
MAX_OUTPUT = 1_500          # the max_tokens you send: no reply can be longer


def price(input_tokens, output_tokens):
    return input_tokens / 1e6 * 5.0 + output_tokens / 1e6 * 25.0


tokens, cost = 0, 0.0
for turn, (input_tokens, output_tokens) in enumerate(TURN_COST, 1):
    # Before sending: the input is known (§9.2 counts it), the output is not,
    # so assume the worst reply the request allows.
    worst_tokens = tokens + input_tokens + MAX_OUTPUT
    worst_cost = cost + price(input_tokens, MAX_OUTPUT)
    if worst_tokens > MAX_TOKENS or worst_cost > MAX_COST:
        print(f"refused turn {turn}: it could reach {worst_tokens:,} tokens "
              f"and ${worst_cost:.3f}")
        break
    tokens += input_tokens + output_tokens
    cost += price(input_tokens, output_tokens)
    print(f"turn {turn}  tokens {tokens:>7,}  cost ${cost:.3f}")

print(f"final: {tokens:,} tokens, ${cost:.3f}, both under the limits")

turn 1  tokens   4,300  cost $0.028
turn 2  tokens  13,750  cost $0.084
turn 3  tokens  30,130  cost $0.173
turn 4  tokens  61,030  cost $0.346
turn 5  tokens 113,730  cost $0.623
turn 6  tokens 175,930  cost $0.958
refused turn 7: it could reach 251,430 tokens and $1.366
final: 175,930 tokens, $0.958, both under the limits

This time the run stops before turn 7, because that turn could have reached 251,430 tokens and $1.366. The final totals stay under both limits. That is what a bound should mean: the limit is never crossed, not merely noticed afterwards.

With that in place, here are the three rules the Budget class encodes.

Four bounds, not one, because they fail in different ways:

  • A turn cap does not stop one turn that reads a 400,000-token file.
  • A token cap does not stop an agent waiting on a slow tool.
  • A time cap does not stop something cheap and fast that loops forever within budget.
  • Money is the one your finance team cares about, and the one nobody adds until an incident.

A bound must produce an outcome, not an exception. An exception is Python's way of stopping with an error, such as RuntimeError. Compare two endings:

  • stopped: turn_limit is a state your caller can handle. It can show partial results, escalate to a human, or resume with a raised budget.
  • A raised RuntimeError in the middle of a loop that has already issued a refund is not a state. It is a mess: the money has moved, and the code that knew why has crashed.

Inject the clock. To inject something is to pass it in as a parameter, and not let the code reach for it itself. The now parameter is what makes this testable, and it is what makes the output above identical on every run. A real clock would make the time limit depend on how busy the machine was. §13 cannot evaluate an agent like that.

There is a related feature worth knowing about, and it solves a different problem: task budgets. Back in the office, every bound above is a rule the office enforces: the ledger stops paying, the door locks at six. The writer does not see them coming. A task budget is a note on the writer's desk instead: "you have this many words for the whole job". The writer can see it, and plan around it.

A task budget differs from every bound above in exactly that respect, and it changes how it behaves. A task_budget inside output_config tells the model how many tokens it has for the whole job. So the model paces itself and finishes gracefully, and is not cut off mid-thought. It is advisory: the model aims for it, and nothing enforces it. It complements the hard bounds above and does not replace them.

A few facts from the documentation, before the example:

  • It is a beta feature, switched on with the task-budgets-2026-03-13 beta flag. A beta feature is released for use but still allowed to change, as §7.7 explained.
  • It takes three fields: type, always "tokens"; total, which must be at least 20,000; and an optional remaining, which you leave out in a normal loop because the server keeps the countdown itself.
  • It counts what the model writes and the tool results it reads. It does not count the history you resend on every turn.
  • It works on Opus 5 and several other current models, but not on Sonnet 5.

Here it is on a request with one tool:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with client.beta.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=64000,
    betas=["task-budgets-2026-03-13"],
    output_config={"effort": "high",
                   "task_budget": {"type": "tokens", "total": 40000}},
    tools=[{"name": "read_file",
            "description": "Read a file from the repository.",
            "input_schema": {"type": "object",
                             "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
                             "required": ["path"]}}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Audit the auth module for bugs."}],
) as stream:
    response = stream.get_final_message()

print("stop_reason:", response.stop_reason)
print("output tokens:", response.usage.output_tokens)

stop_reason: end_turn
output tokens: 11840

Read the output first. The response ended with end_turn, the model's own choice to stop, and it wrote 11,840 tokens against a budget of 40,000. That is a single-response run; in a loop you would add up output_tokens across turns to watch the budget being used.

Note the streaming. Streaming means receiving the response piece by piece as it is written (§2.7). A max_tokens that large on a non-streaming request risks an HTTP timeout: the connection gives up before the long reply is finished. That is why the budget example uses .stream() and get_final_message(), and not create().

max_tokens and task_budget are not the same thing, and the difference matters.

  • max_tokens is a hard ceiling on one response, and the model does not know about it. Hitting it gives you a sentence cut in half.
  • task_budget is a figure the model can see and pace against across the whole loop.

Use both. The task budget is there so the model lands the plane. The ceiling is there so it cannot run away.

11.4 Designing the Tool Surface for an Agent

A tool surface is the full set of tools an agent can call. §6.10 covered tool design in general. Agents add one question that single-call systems never face: how much of the world should this loop be able to touch?

The instinct is to give the agent everything it might need. The better instinct is the opposite. In the office, you would not hand a new clerk every key in the building on day one. You would hand over the keys for the rooms the job needs.

There is a concrete rule that captures this. An agent's blast radius is everything all its tools together can do. Blast radius is a term borrowed from explosives: how far the damage spreads if something goes wrong. Two words in that rule matter:

  • together: the tools combine. Each tool may look harmless alone.
  • can: the rule is about what is possible, not what is intended.

So size the blast radius to the worst plausible sequence of calls, not the intended one. A tool set of read_file, write_file and run_shell is, whatever the system prompt says, an agent that can do anything to that machine.

The block below makes the rule mechanical. TOOLSETS lists three agents and their tools. CAPABILITY labels every tool with two things: its kind (does it read, write, or execute?) and its reach (what does it touch?). The loop then lists, for each agent, every tool that reaches money, sends something out, or runs commands on the host machine, because those are the calls that cannot be taken back:

TOOLSETS = {
    "reader": ["search_docs", "read_file"],
    "support": ["get_order", "check_refund_policy", "create_refund",
                "send_email"],
    "dev": ["read_file", "write_file", "run_tests", "run_shell"],
}

CAPABILITY = {
    "search_docs": ("read", "public"), "read_file": ("read", "repo"),
    "get_order": ("read", "customer"), "check_refund_policy": ("read", "public"),
    "create_refund": ("write", "money"), "send_email": ("write", "outbound"),
    "write_file": ("write", "repo"), "run_tests": ("execute", "sandbox"),
    "run_shell": ("execute", "host"),
}

for name, tools in TOOLSETS.items():
    kinds = {CAPABILITY[t][0] for t in tools}
    reach = sorted({CAPABILITY[t][1] for t in tools})
    irreversible = [t for t in tools
                    if CAPABILITY[t] in (("write", "money"), ("write", "outbound"),
                                         ("execute", "host"))]
    print(f"{name:<9} kinds={','.join(sorted(kinds)):<20} reach={','.join(reach)}")
    print(f"{'':9} needs a gate: {irreversible or 'nothing — safe to run unattended'}")

reader    kinds=read                 reach=public,repo
          needs a gate: nothing — safe to run unattended
support   kinds=read,write           reach=customer,money,outbound,public
          needs a gate: ['create_refund', 'send_email']
dev       kinds=execute,read,write   reach=host,repo,sandbox
          needs a gate: ['run_shell']

Read it one agent at a time:

  • reader only reads, and only public documents and the repository. Nothing on its list needs a gate.
  • support can move money and send email. Two tools need a gate.
  • dev can run shell commands on the host. One tool needs a gate, and it is the one that makes the other three irrelevant.

The reader agent can be run unattended on a schedule, and nobody needs to think about it again. The other two cannot. The reason is visible in one line of output, not buried in a system prompt.

Two agent-specific tool design rules follow.

Split read from write, and make the write tools narrow. Compare one wide tool with two narrow ones:

  • update_order(fields) accepts arbitrary fields. It can change the price, the status, the customer, anything.
  • cancel_order(id) and change_address(id, address) can each do one thing.

The single wide tool has a much larger blast radius. Narrow tools are also easier for the model to call correctly, so this is not purely a safety trade.

Give the agent a way to finish. An explicit done(summary) tool is often better than relying on the model to simply stop calling tools. It makes completion an observable event: something you can log, gate and evaluate. Without it, "the agent finished" and "the agent gave up" look identical from outside.

11.5 A Complete Harness

Here is the whole thing, assembled. It is longer than the loop in §6.4 by roughly the amount of scaffolding a production system needs, and that is the point.

One note before the code. The SDK's tool runner, from §6.4, can drive this loop for you, and its per-turn hooks are a place to put a gate or a log line. Whoever drives the loop, the pieces below are still yours to write. Here they are written out by hand, so you can see each one.

The block is long, so read it in four parts:

  1. Halt is a custom exception. A tool raises it to say "this call must not go ahead".
  2. Agent._execute runs one tool call, checking in this order: does the tool exist, does the gate allow it, does the tool itself refuse with Halt, does anything else go wrong. Every failure becomes a sentence and an error flag, never a crash.
  3. Agent.run is the loop. To keep the run repeatable, it takes a scripted list of what the model asks for on each turn. Replacing that list with real API calls changes nothing else. Every step is reported through on_event, which here appends to a list.
  4. The setup at the bottom gives the agent two tools and a gate, then plays out six turns: one lookup, three refunds of different sizes, one tool that does not exist, and "done".

The two refund rules are in different places on purpose. The gate asks for approval for refunds above 5,000 cents (€50) and up to 10,000 (€100). The hard ceiling of €100 lives inside create_refund:

class Halt(Exception):
    """Raised by the executor when a call must not proceed. Never reaches the model."""


class Agent:
    def __init__(self, tools, implementations, *, max_turns=12,
                 gate=None, on_event=None):
        self.tools = tools
        self.implementations = implementations
        self.max_turns = max_turns
        self.gate = gate or (lambda name, args: True)
        self.on_event = on_event or (lambda *a: None)
